paragraphs.text: "Hurry up, Tyler! My mom's waiting in the car." Matt Whitman gathered up his backpack and sleeping bag. It was Saturday morning, and the two boys had just spent the night at their friend Brian's house.
"Great sleepover, Brian," Matt said. "That movie was the scariest one yet!"
"It was pretty good," Brian said. "Even I was frightened!"
Tyler was still fumbling with his sleeping bag. "Well, I wasn't scared at all."
Brian grinned at Tyler. "No, you just happened to go into the kitchen for more popcorn at the exact moment when those kids were walking into that haunted house."
"Okay, maybe I was a little scared," Tyler admitted. "But you should have seen your face when that zombie jumped out of the bushes."
They all laughed. Brian's phone buzzed. He frowned as he quickly read the text message. Then he put the phone back in his pocket.
"Who was that?" Tyler asked.
"Just Becky breaking up with me."
"Didn't you two already break up twice this week?" Matt said.
"Yeah, but we got back together."
"Apparently you forgot to tell her," Matt said.
Brian scowled at the joke, but Tyler laughed. Outside, Matt's mother honked the car horn.
"See you later, Brian." Matt opened the front door. Tyler followed Matt as he ran down the walk and jumped into the back seat of the car.
"Hi, guys," Mrs. Whitman said. "Did you get any sleep last night?"
"Of course not, Mom. No one sleeps at a sleepover."
"Especially when we're watching really scary movies," Tyler said.

"Now you admit they were really scary," Matt teased his friend as they drove away. "I thought you were just a little scared. Oh, wait a minute. Weren't you the one hiding your face in your pillow when the monster grabbed those kids? I thought you—"
"My pillow! I forgot my pillow!" Tyler cried. "I couldn't find my backpack this morning, so I took off the pillowcase to use as a sack. We have to go back."
Mrs. Whitman turned the car around and drove to Brian's house. Tyler ran in and soon returned with his pillow and backpack.
"Brian's mom found my backpack underneath a chair," he explained happily as he buckled his seatbelt.
"Are we all set now?" Mrs. Whitman turned on the car radio. "Matt, it's almost time for your favorite program. They're doing Don Carlo today."
Matt's eyes widened in horror. He couldn't believe his mother had just said that in front of Tyler.
"What's wrong with you?" Tyler pointed at Matt. "You look like you just saw a ghost."
"Nothing." Matt concentrated on staring out the window. "Did you ever notice how many silver cars there are?" he said quickly. "That's probably the most popular color, don't you think?"
But Tyler wasn't about to be distracted, especially after Matt had just been teasing him for being afraid. "What's your favorite show? Who's Don Carlo, and what are they doing to him?"
"Don Carlo is the main character in an opera," Mrs. Whitman explained. "It takes place in the 1500s, during the Spanish Inquisition, but it's really a tragic love story."
Matt stayed silent. It was bad enough that his mother had jumped into the conversation, but did she have to embarrass him too?
"You like opera?" Now it was Tyler's turn to widen his eyes in horror.
"Matt loves opera." Mrs. Whitman corrected him. "We always listen to the opera program when we're driving around, doing errands on Saturdays. Right, Matt?"

Matt just grunted. His mom was making things worse. They needed to get onto another topic immediately. His mind whirred with possibilities, but he quickly settled on the local baseball team, the Philadelphia Phillies. "Did you see that outfielder—"

"You do mean opera as in . . ." Tyler cleared his throat, clasped his hands together, and made a serious face. "Mi-mi-mi-mi-mi," he sang, imitating an opera star warming up. "Something like that?" He looked at Matt with a huge grin on his face.
"Not exactly." Matt could tell that Tyler was enjoying this way too much.
"Or is it more like this? La-la-la-la-la-la-la-la." Tyler used as deep a voice as possible to sing down the scale.
"No. Not at all."
"You should try listening to an opera, Tyler," Mrs. Whitman said as they arrived in front of Tyler's house. "You might actually enjoy it."

"No, thanks, but thanks for the ride," Tyler said. He pulled his backpack and the pillow and his sleeping bag and the bulging pillowcase from the car. He struggled up the driveway, but Matt didn't offer to help.
Instead Matt got out of the car and switched to the front seat. "How could you do that to me, Mom?" he said in a loud, angry voice. "Now everybody knows I like opera!"
"Not everybody, just Tyler," Mrs. Whitman said as she drove away from the curb.
"Believe me, it'll be everybody soon enough. I'm sure Tyler can't wait to tell people."
"I'm sorry I embarrassed you, but liking opera is nothing to be ashamed of. Plenty of people enjoy opera."

"Adults like opera," Matt corrected her. "Kids think it's weird. Weren't you listening to Tyler? Everyone will be making fun of me as soon as he starts spreading the news. I don't want to go to school on Monday."

"Oh, Matt, that's two days away. I'm sure Tyler will have forgotten all about it by then." Mrs. Whitman looked over at Matt. "What's that old expression? 'He'd forget his head if it wasn't attached.' That's Tyler. Now let's enjoy the opera."
The orchestra was playing the overture, which ended in an ominous thunder of drums.
"I can already tell from the music that this is going to be a dark opera." Mrs. Whitman smiled at Matt. "You know you'll like this once it gets started."
"I don't even know who's singing today," Matt grumbled. "And thanks to you and Tyler, I missed the synopsis of act 1, so I'll have no idea what's going on until they give the synopsis of act 2."
"Well, Don Carlo is the son of the king of Spain, and his father—"
"Never mind," snapped Matt. "I'll figure it out as we go along."
"But it's in Italian!"
Matt rolled his eyes. "I don't have to understand the words to enjoy the music!" He reached over and turned up the volume on the radio.
As soon as Tyler and Brian walked into music class on Monday, they ambushed Matt.
"So, I hear you're a real opera fan." Brian grinned. "Did your car windows shatter while you were listening on Saturday?"
"Ah-ah-ah-ah-ah-ah-ah-ACK!" Tyler sang, sliding up the scale until he ended in a high-pitched squeak. "I'm glad I left the car before the shrieking—I mean singing —started."
Matt put his books under his chair and sat down. "Nobody broke any glass, you guys. That only happens in cartoons."
"Well, how long did that opera last anyway?" Brian said. "They usually go on for hours and hours, right?"
"Days and nights!" Tyler chimed in.
"It didn't last that long." Matt tried to peer around them to see what the teacher, Mrs. Menendez, had written on the board.
"How can you even understand what's happening when it's all in a foreign language?" Tyler said.
Matt sighed heavily. "You two are awfully curious about opera for people who can't stand it."
"Oh, we're just trying to keep up with your latest activity," Brian said in a mockingly cheerful voice. "We want—"
"Time for class!" Mrs. Menendez clapped her hands.
Brian took his seat next to Matt while Tyler sat behind them.
"Before we return to our discussion of Baroque music, I'd like to make a plea for your help," Mrs. Menendez said. "I desperately need more people to join the school chorus, especially boys."
"No way," Tyler muttered.
Mrs. Menendez went on. "I don't know what any of you sound like because we don't sing in this class. But I'm sure there's some real talent lurking out there, just waiting to be discovered."
Brian elbowed Matt. "Sounds like something you should try, Opera Fan."
"No way! I'm not doing that !" Matt said.
Tyler and Brian snickered loudly, and the teacher looked in their direction. "Is there a problem, boys?"
"No, Mrs. Menendez," Matt said.
"We thought Matt was volunteering for chorus," Brian said as Matt glared at him.
"Well, you should all consider trying out." Mrs. Menendez smiled hopefully at the boys.

Matt ducked his head and stared at his hands. He liked to sing, but he wasn't going to give his friends any more ammunition in their war on opera. He also liked Mrs. Menendez's class. He especially enjoyed it when she played recordings to illustrate her points about composers. Today she was talking about Handel.
"You might know him from Messiah , his famous choral piece that's often performed at Christmas," Mrs. Menendez said. "But Handel composed other kinds of music, too, including many operas."
At the word "operas," Tyler leaned forward and tapped Matt on the head with his pencil.
"Ow!" Matt rubbed his head. This was going to be a long class.
When music finally ended, Matt braced himself for another round of teasing from his friends.
But Tyler was too busy searching through his books and notebooks to say anything. "I know it's here somewhere," he mumbled as he opened his social studies book and shook it.
"What did you lose?" Matt asked.
"My social studies homework. It's not here, so I must have left it at home."
"Well, you're in trouble now," Brian said. "You know homework counts as part of our grade."
"Yeah, thanks, I'm aware of that."
"Maybe you could call home and have someone send it by drone," Matt said as they left the music room. "It'll take us a few minutes to walk to class."
"Great idea!" Brian laughed, but Tyler was not amused.
"Hey, look!" Matt grabbed Brian's arm. "Isn't that Becky walking with Jameson? She keeps looking over here like she wants to make sure you see she has a new boyfriend."
Brian pretended to be very interested in getting a drink from the water fountain. "What's she doing now?" he whispered.
"Whoa! She's kissing him right here in the hall!" Matt exclaimed.
"What?" Brian stood up so quickly that he lost his grip on his books. They tumbled to the floor.
This time it was Tyler's turn to laugh.
"Gotcha!" Matt said as Brian frantically scanned the crowded hallway for his Becky. "You deserved that for volunteering me for chorus."

Matt was glad to be the one doing the teasing instead of getting grief from his friends. For the rest of the day he laughed every time Tyler made kissing noises at Brian, or Brian waved his hand like a drone circling for a landing.

After school Matt had to see his science teacher to make up a test. When he finished, he still had fifteen minutes before the late bus arrived to take him home. It was raining pretty hard, so he decided to wait inside the school. He was feeling happy because the science test had been easy. So, as he waited, he hummed a song to himself. Actually it was more than just a song. It was "Nessun Dorma," an aria from Turandot , a famous opera. Matt had listened to it so many times that he knew most of the words, even though they were in Italian.

He started out humming softly, but gradually he sang louder and louder as he realized the empty corridor had great acoustics. Just as he reached the highest note, the door to the teachers' lounge flew open and Mrs. Menendez rushed out.
"Was that you singing, Matt?"
"Uh . . . well . . . um." Matt didn't know what to say, but then he remembered what his mother always said: you can never go wrong with an apology. "I'm so sorry. I didn't mean to disturb anyone."
"You weren't disturbing me at all. I had to come out and see who was singing. You have a fabulous soprano voice! You absolutely have to join chorus!"
Matt was flattered, but there was no way he was doing anything musical after the way his friends had reacted today. "Oh, no, I couldn't possibly do that because I have—"
He stopped while he tried to think up an excuse.
Mrs. Menendez jumped right in. "Whatever you're doing, cancel it! Chorus is the activity for you!"

Matt wished she would go back into the teachers' room, but she kept talking to him and piling on the compliments. "That's amazing that you can sing 'Nessun Dorma'! Most kids have never heard of it. And your voice—so beautiful! You have a wonderful gift that you should share with everyone before your voice changes."
"I think my bus is coming!" Matt finally said in desperation. Then he ran outside into the pouring rain.

Matt spent the rest of the week trying to avoid Mrs. Menendez. Normally he looked forward to music class, but now he was glad he only had it once a week. He didn't want his friends to hear her praising his voice and pressuring him to join chorus. She really was his favorite teacher, and he hated saying no to her, and he did like to sing, but . . . He liked to sing by himself, not with a group of kids, and certainly not where Tyler and Brian could hear him.
All of a sudden, Mrs. Menendez seemed to be everywhere Matt was: in the school library, the cafeteria, and especially the hallways.

But somehow Matt managed to stay out of her way—even when he panicked on Wednesday and came within an inch of walking into the girls' bathroom by mistake. By the time Friday came, he was exhausted from dodging her.
So he was happy when his mother announced at breakfast on Saturday that she had a nice surprise for him. "Instead of listening to an opera on the radio today, how would you like to actually see one?"

"Great!" Matt said. "Do you mean the opera in Philadelphia? Or—" He paused because the other possibility was so exciting, he could barely say the words. "Or are we going to the Metropolitan Opera in New York City?"
"No, we're not going to the Met." Mrs. Whitman laughed. "That's way too expensive, and besides we couldn't get there in time. We're going to see an opera at a movie theater."
"Oh." Matt made a face as he scooped up another spoonful of cereal.

"Now don't be disappointed." Matt's mom explained that the movie theater was showing a series of operas broadcast live from famous opera houses. "Today's opera is The Barber of Seville , and it'll be just like seeing the live production. You might even like it more because you'll have a better view of the stage."
"Oh! That would be great!" Matt said enthusiastically. "Which movie theater are we going to?"
"The one near the mall."
"Oh, no! We definitely can't go there. What if we run into someone I know?"

"How is that a problem?" Mrs. Whitman looked puzzled. "If we see friends of yours, that just means they like opera too. In fact, would you like to invite Tyler to come along? He seemed curious about Don Carlo last week. I could try to get another ticket online."
"No! No! No! That wouldn't be good at all."
Mrs. Whitman crossed her arms and gave an annoyed sigh. "I thought you'd like to do this, but if you don't want to go—"
"You don't understand, Mom. Zombie Invasion 4 is opening this weekend, and everyone will be going to see it."
"Do you really think your friends would go without you? You won't run into them."

Matt had to admit it was highly unlikely that Brian and Tyler would see the movie without him, but that still didn't solve his problem. "That movie theater has a dozen screens! The odds we'll run into somebody I know in the lobby or parking lot are huge!"
"And if we do—"
"You just don't get it!" Matt slammed his spoon so hard, milk splashed out of his bowl. He stormed out of the kitchen.

Up in his room, he turned on his computer. He'd seen clips of operas online before, but he'd never watched an entire production. The trouble was that he did want to see this opera; he just didn't want to see it at that theater. Maybe it was playing somewhere else. He went online and quickly found The Barber of Seville and where it was showing. Now all he had to do was persuade his mother to go to one of those other theaters.

He came back downstairs, where she had just finished breakfast. "I know you don't like driving on highways, and there's no other way to get to that theater," he began. "But what if we went to the movies in Doylestown? You always say you like the drive up there."
"That's almost an hour away!" Mrs. Whitman said. "Besides, I already bought tickets to this theater."

Matt and his mom stood in the kitchen, staring at each other. He didn't know what else to say, but she did. "Be ready to go at 11 o'clock or I'm leaving without you. I've heard these shows are crowded, so we need to get there early to find good seats."
Matt went back to his room. There had to be some way that he could go to the opera without anyone seeing him. But he had no idea how to do that.
With a sigh, he went back online and browsed his favorite websites. He was looking at some photos from famous operas when he had an idea.

"I'll go in disguise!" he thought. "People do that all the time in operas." He remembered how a character in The Magic Flute , a beautiful young girl, disguised herself as an old woman. Suddenly he realized how easy it would be to disguise himself as an old man.

Matt's grandfather had lived with them until he died. "I think we still have some of his old clothes in the spare bedroom," Matt thought. He went off to explore the bureau and closet. He was so busy digging around that he almost didn't hear his mother.
"Matt!" she called from downstairs. "It's after 11 o'clock! Are you coming or not?"
"Coming!" he shouted.

A few minutes later, he ran downstairs wearing his grandfather's hat with a scarf wrapped around the lower part of his face. He was also wearing his own sunglasses and carrying his grandfather's cane.
"A disguise?" Matt's mom just shook her head. "I guess you were serious about not wanting anyone to see you at the opera."
At the theater Mrs. Whitman stopped to buy some snacks at the counter in the lobby. Matt looked around nervously. "Do you have to do that?" he asked.
"You'll want something to eat later on," she said. "This opera lasts two and a half hours, and that doesn't include intermission."

By the time they walked into the theater where the opera was showing, it was full. The only seats left were in the front row, but Matt didn't mind one bit! As the overture started, he removed his sunglasses and settled back in his seat, ready to enjoy the show.

Although Matt was in a movie theater, he felt as if he were watching The Barber of Seville at an opera house. On the screen the curtains opened to reveal an elaborate set—a two-story house on a plaza.
"Whoa! That looks so real! Where is that?" he whispered to his mother.
"Seville, a city in Spain."

It took Matt a few minutes to get used to watching the action and reading the English subtitles at the same time. But he soon caught on to the story, even though the performers were singing in Italian. The wealthy Count Almaviva had fallen in love with Rosina, the daughter of Dr. Bartolo. The count followed Rosina home and stood under her window, serenading her.
"He's a good singer!" Matt whispered. His mom nodded.

Along came Figaro, the barber of Seville, a clever fellow who seemed to know all the local gossip. Figaro told the count that Dr. Bartolo was not Rosina's father, but was instead her guardian, who intended to marry her. Meanwhile Rosina looked out her window and fell instantly in love with the count.
"Opera characters are always falling in love at first sight." Mrs. Whitman shook her head. "I'm not sure that's a good thing."

Matt knew they shouldn't be talking, but he was having fun and so far, no one seemed to mind. The rich count was now telling Rosina that he was a poor music student. He wanted to be sure that she loved him and not his money.

"I'm not the only one in disguise today," Matt thought. He felt hot in the crowded theater, so he looked around to make sure there was no one he knew. Then he took off his grandfather's hat and scarf.

On-screen the two men plotted how the count could get into Rosina's house to meet her. Figaro suggested the count disguise himself as a soldier who needed a place to stay; the law required citizens to host soldiers.
"Wait!" Matt said loudly. "Now the count is pretending to be a soldier? This guy has two disguises, and we're only at the beginning of this thing!"
"Shh!" a woman behind him said.
"Yes," his mom whispered, putting her finger to her lips.

Matt watched the rest of the first act in silence. He liked the colorful costumes and the gigantic set, and he recognized some of the music from TV ads. He especially liked when a donkey danced across the stage. Rosina and the count's romance grew more complicated as the doctor became suspicious of them. The count abandoned his military disguise. Matt laughed at the twists and turns of the plot.

At intermission Mrs. Whitman got up to stretch her legs, but Matt remained in his seat, sipping soda and munching popcorn. The theater lights stayed low because there was still action on-screen. Cameras backstage at the opera house showed breathless singers hurrying offstage. Stagehands in black shirts and pants moved the next set into place. After a few more minutes, singers began to step into position for Act Two.
Matt was so fascinated by what was happening behind the scenes that he almost didn't recognize the woman who walked in front of him.
"Mrs. Menendez?" he thought as the woman dropped into a seat. He wanted to turn to look at her, but he was afraid she'd notice him. As Act Two began, he slipped on his grandfather's hat and scarf.

This time the count was disguised as a new music teacher who came to Rosina's house. The count told Rosina's father that the regular teacher was too sick to give her a lesson. The young couple sang a duet.
"Oh, that was lovely!" Matt's mom whispered after they had finished.

Matt liked the music, but he also liked that the piano moved around the stage. He could see there was someone underneath it, but that only made it funnier. The real music teacher soon showed up, and the count and Figaro had to persuade him to pretend he was deathly ill. Matt laughed as characters dressed as gravediggers chased the music teacher around the stage. He was so involved in the story and the music that he forgot all about Mrs. Menendez until the count and Rosina were happily married. But then he suddenly remembered.
"Come on! Let's get out of here," he said to his mother as the singers took their curtain call.
"Just a minute. Don't forget Grandpa's cane, and make sure you pick up your cup and—"
"Matt? Mrs. Whitman?"
Matt groaned as Mrs. Menendez bustled over to greet them.

"At first I didn't recognize you under that hat," she said to Matt. "I like your scarf. You look like an opera star! Did you know that one of the greatest tenors of all time—Luciano Pavarotti—always wore a scarf?"
"Yeah, I know who he was." Matt looked longingly toward the exit.
"I love his recording of 'Nessun Dorma.' Nobody can sing that aria like Pavarotti." Mrs. Menendez sighed.
"It's the best version I've ever heard!" Matt said before he could stop himself.
"Well, it sounds like you're a guy who really loves opera!"
Matt's mom gave him an encouraging look. There was nothing embarrassing about admitting he liked opera to an adult, but he still swallowed hard before he replied.
"I do. We listen to the opera on the radio every Saturday."
"I thought Matt would have fun actually seeing an opera," Mrs. Whitman said.
"What did you think?" Mrs. Menendez asked Matt.
"It's so much better than just listening to the opera. The sets and the costumes and the acting . . . Everything was amazing!"

"And you can see how much effort singing takes at that level," Mrs. Menendez said. She went on about the opera, and Matt was actually enjoying himself. He was just about to ask a question when the conversation suddenly turned dangerous.
"You know, Mrs. Whitman, Matt has such a wonderful voice. I've been trying to get him to join chorus."
"Really?" Matt's mom stared at him in surprise. "You never told me that, Matt."
He felt like he was in a horror movie, watching himself get eaten up by a monster.
"I overheard him singing 'Nessun Dorma,' and I couldn't believe his voice. You're his mother. Perhaps you can persuade him to sing with us."
"Don't worry, Mrs. Menendez. He'll be at chorus from now on. Right, Matt?"
Matt stayed silent. "Ugh," he thought with dread. "Wait till Tyler and Brian hear about this. They're going to give me such a hard time."

Twice a week Matt and his friends spent the last period of the day goofing around in study hall while pretending to do homework. But now Matt had chorus—a change he dreaded mentioning to Brian and Tyler.
On Matt's first day of rehearsal, the three boys were walking toward study hall as usual, when Matt stopped outside Mrs. Menendez's room.
"I'm in chorus now, so I can't go to study hall anymore." He quickly pivoted toward the door. "Bye."
"Wait! What do you mean you're in chorus now?" Brian asked.
"Are you saying that for real?" Tyler asked.
Matt nodded. "When my mom found out that Mrs. Menendez was looking for guys to join chorus, she made me sign up."

Okay, that wasn't exactly the whole truth. But there was no way he was confessing that he'd run into Mrs. Menendez while watching an opera with his mother. Or that Mrs. Menendez had caught him belting out an aria. Or that ever since The Barber of Seville , he'd been thinking he might like to try chorus after all.

"I mean if it was just my mom, I could probably talk her out of it. Or if it was just Mrs. Menendez, but both of them together . . ." Matt nervously shifted his books to his left arm. "I didn't stand a chance."

"Sounds like that time my dad and the band teacher made me take trombone lessons in fourth grade," said Brian. "I couldn't argue my way out of that for anything. What you have to do in this situation is fail, and then they'll let you quit."
Tyler agreed. "Start forgetting to bring your music all the time, and you'll be back hanging around with us in no time."
"Thanks, guys." Matt felt relieved. He had no intention of failing at chorus, but now he could enjoy singing without worrying about his friends making fun of him.

The bell rang for the start of class, and Matt ducked inside Mrs. Menendez's room. There was only one empty chair near the back, so Matt took that seat. The girl to his left immediately started talking to him.
"Hi! You must be new! I'm Dede! I mean, my real name's Elizabeth, but everybody calls me Dede. I'm not sure why—because it's not the usual nickname for Elizabeth—but everybody does."
Dede paused to take a breath, and Matt stared at the girl in the Phillies T-shirt who'd just given him such an enthusiastic welcome.
"Dede." He repeated slowly. "Oh, like Mimi!"
Dede looked confused.
"You have an unexpected nickname like Mimi in the opera La Bohème . Her real name is Lucia." Matt instantly regretted that he'd mentioned an opera. Now Dede probably thought he was showing off.

But Dede's face lit up with recognition. "Oh, Mimi in the opera! Now I get it. I thought you were talking about somebody named Mimi here at school, and I couldn't think who that would be. I love that opera, don't you? My dad says there's going to be a production of La Bohème in Philadelphia, and I'm hoping we can go. It's so sad when Mimi dies at the end, don't you think? And what's your name?"
Matt grinned and told her his name. He wanted to ask if she had a favorite Phillies player, but Mrs. Menendez was starting to lead the chorus in warm-up exercises.

The weeks passed. Matt began to look forward to rehearsals with Dede, who always had lots to say about the Phillies and their most recent game. The other kids in chorus were nice too, and some of the guys even wore hats. Most teachers made kids leave their hats in their lockers, but Mrs. Menendez liked to encourage her students' individuality. Matt took to smuggling his grandfather's hat into class, careful that Brian and Tyler never saw it.
In fact, it had been a long time since either friend had mentioned chorus. So Matt was caught off guard one day at lunch.
"Haven't you failed chorus yet? How can you stand those chorus kids?" Brian asked.
"They're the worst." Matt blurted out, hoping that would end the conversation.
"What do you mean?"

"Oh, you know . . ." Matt was trying to be vague because he had no idea what he meant. He liked chorus because he liked singing, and he liked Dede and the other kids. But he could never tell Brian and Tyler that. He was still trying to think of what to say when Brian suddenly leaped up and ran across the cafeteria.
"What's with him?" Matt asked.
Tyler turned around to look at Brian, who was now talking to Becky. "Jameson broke up with Becky, so Brian's trying to win her back."
Matt shook his head. "It's like . . ." He started to say something but stopped.
"Like what?"
It was like the on-again, off-again romance of some of the characters in La Bohème ! Matt was thinking. But Matt knew better than to say that to Tyler.
"Nothing," Matt said quickly. "Did you watch the Phillies game last night?"
That afternoon Mrs. Menendez had an exciting announcement at rehearsal. An opera company in Philadelphia needed sopranos to play street urchins in La Bohème .
"I encourage you all to try out—boys as well as girls—and I'll be happy to help you with audition music."
Some kids announced they didn't like opera, and some said they couldn't attend all the rehearsals in Philadelphia. But Matt and Dede high-fived and said together, "We're doing this!"

For two weeks Mrs. Menendez worked with them every day after school. As they learned the music, she helped them improve their pronunciation of the Italian lyrics. On the afternoon of the audition, she even drove them to Philadelphia. Matt and Dede were both nervous, but their teacher reassured them that they were prepared—and they were. After the audition she took them to a café near the theater.

"We'll go here every day after rehearsals," said Dede, dipping a French fry in ketchup. "Oh! We have to plan how we'll get to rehearsals because we'll have to leave school early. My dad can drive us sometimes, but can your mom take us some days? This is going to be so much fun!"
"Assuming we get parts," Matt said cautiously.
"We'll get parts." Dede smiled and popped another French fry into her mouth.
A few days later, Matt received an email from the opera company. He immediately texted Dede. "I got a part! Did you?"
"NO!" She texted back, sending a sad face too.
"What?" Matt stared at his phone in disappointment. This wasn't in their plans at all.

"Who am I supposed to hang out with?" Matt grumbled. It was the first day of rehearsals for La Bohème , and Matt wasn't happy. Without Dede as a fellow street urchin, he had to go to Philadelphia all by himself. Inside the theater he walked through a maze of corridors.
He came to a dead end near the costume shop. "Where is this rehearsal room anyway?"

If Dede were there, they'd be laughing about getting lost, but now Matt felt anxious. He retraced his steps and finally found the right door. Matt took a deep breath to calm himself and walked into a room filled with kids, all talking at once.
Mr. Lorenzo, the chorus master, gave a shrill whistle. "Okay, people, let's get started! Settle down and introduce yourselves."
One by one, the kids stood up and said their own names as well as the names of any operas they'd appeared in. One girl had been in six operas! Matt sighed loudly, and the boy next to him leaned over.
"Not everyone has that much experience," he reassured Matt. "If you're here, you're a good singer. I'm Tim, by the way."
"Thanks, Tim," Matt said.

Following the introductions, Mr. Lorenzo welcomed the new singers. "You'll be working with some of the best professionals in the business, and they don't have time for any nonsense. While we'll have fun, I expect you to take your roles seriously. Now I assume you know the story of La Bohème , but for those who don't . . ."

Mr. Lorenzo said that act 1 takes place on Christmas Eve in 1830. Four poor artists live in a garret in Paris. Because it's a holiday, they decide to eat at a café. Rodolfo stays behind for a few minutes to finish his writing and soon hears a knock at the door. It's Mimi, a young woman who lives in the same building; her candle has blown out and she needs a flame to relight it.
"As soon as Rodolfo and Mimi meet, they instantly fall in love," Mr. Lorenzo said.
"Love at first sight!" Matt and Tim exclaimed together, and they burst out laughing.
"Exactly!" Mr. Lorenzo said. "Do you think this romance will end happily?"
"Nooo!" the kids roared.
"She dies!" someone called from the back of the room.

"That's right, but not yet," Mr. Lorenzo said. "First we have to get through act 2, and that's where you come in. The street urchins join the crowd outside the café, where the artists are dining. We also meet Musetta, who loves Marcello, one of Rodolfo's roommates. They're always breaking up and getting back together again."
"Brian and Becky!" Matt thought.
Mr. Lorenzo explained that in act 3, Marcello and Rodolfo are having trouble with their girlfriends, and by the start of act 4, both couples have broken up.
"Musetta brings Mimi to the artists' garret because she's very sick and wants to be with Rodolfo. Mimi and Rodolfo remember the night they fell in love, and then she dies."
"Ohh," everyone said at once.
"All right, people, enough about the plot. Let's get to the music."
Mr. Lorenzo sat at the piano and played scales, followed by some warm-up exercises that Matt recognized from chorus.
"Maybe this will be fun, after all," he thought.

By the next rehearsal, Matt felt at home. Most of the opera kids seemed nice, and Brian and Tyler believed his excuse for leaving school early for rehearsals. He simply said he had to go to physical therapy because he'd hurt his left elbow throwing curve balls.
For the first few weeks, the urchins concentrated on learning their music. But this was an opera, not a concert, so they also had to learn what to do onstage.
"From now on, you need to pay attention to Mr. Berman. He's the director." Mr. Lorenzo led the urchins onstage for their first rehearsal with the entire cast and orchestra.

The urchins sat in a circle while Mr. Berman talked. "Once you've run onstage, you can pretty much do as you like. Keep moving and fit into the spirit of the scene. But whatever you do, don't draw attention to yourself!"
Matt had no idea what to do or where to go.
Tim slapped him on the back. "Don't look so worried. It always takes a while to figure out where everyone belongs. Just keep singing!"
"Okay!" Matt tried to sound confident, but he really wished Dede were there.
They did one run-through of the scene. The kids were supposed to scatter among the crowd strolling the street and the vendors selling fruit, candy, and toys.
"This is hard!" Matt said breathlessly to Tim as they waited backstage to rehearse the scene again. "So many people are singing, it's impossible to hear our part."
"I know. Just follow me."
But an assistant director came backstage and took Tim and a few more kids to the other side of the stage.
When the scene started again, Matt decided to go in a different direction. He was so busy running, singing, and looking for Tim that he didn't see one of the stars of the opera!
"Oof!" Rodolfo cried as Matt hit him in the stomach.
"Oh!" Mimi said as she stumbled.
"Ow!" Matt said as he fell to the stage, hitting his right elbow.
The orchestra stopped playing and Mr. Berman started yelling.
"You! Street urchin!" the director bellowed at Matt. "What did I say about not drawing attention to yourself?"
"I'm sorry," Matt said weakly as everyone looked at him. He turned red with embarrassment.
"Don't apologize! Just do it right! As for the rest of you, was anyone paying any attention to the beat?"

Matt felt frozen in place. A vendor stretched out a hand and helped him to his feet. As the director continued yelling at the cast, Matt slipped to the back of the crowd. He moved offstage and ran to collect his things in the chorus room.
"I hate this opera!" he muttered. "Why did I think I could be a singer? I don't know what I'm doing, and the director obviously hates me!"

Even leaving school early wasn't fun anymore. He'd missed so much math that he was way behind everyone else. Not to mention he was tired of lying to Tyler and Brian. As for Dede, well, she'd barely spoken to him since he'd joined the opera company.
Matt pulled his phone out of his backpack and rubbed his elbow. He'd call his mother to come get him, and then he'd be done with this stupid opera forever.
The next day Matt needed to talk to Dede as soon as possible. He found her at her locker before homeroom started.
"I'm quitting La Bohème !" he announced dramatically.
"Why would you do that? Are you sick or something?" Dede blinked, as if she couldn't believe what she was hearing.
"No, I'm fine. I just don't want to do it anymore. It's too hard."
"You get to sing with a major opera company, and you want to quit just because it's hard?" Dede shook her head. "Of course it's hard. It's opera!"
It was Matt's turn to be surprised. "You've hardly said a word to me since I got the part. I thought you'd be happy I'm quitting."
"Happy? I'm horrified!"
"Fine. I don't care what you think anyway," Matt said angrily, and he started to walk away. He'd expected Dede to be more sympathetic.
"Wait! Let me explain."

Matt turned around and leaned on the locker next to Dede's. "Look, I admit I was jealous when you got the part. I thought either we'd both get into the chorus, or we'd both be rejected. I was really down on myself for failing. But then Mrs. Menendez explained that they'd had a lot of girls try out, and they needed more guys, so . . ."
"So you're saying I only got a part because I'm a guy?"
"No! You're an awesome singer! I'm saying that knowing they needed boys helped me to get over my rejection. Besides, I've got some other stuff going on right now. I don't have time to do everything."
"Oh." Matt stared at his shoes. For the past few weeks, he'd been so busy thinking about himself that he hadn't stopped to consider how Dede might be feeling.
"I know it must be hard sometimes, but you can't throw away an amazing opportunity. Now tell me why you want to quit the opera."
"Yes, do tell us!" some familiar voices said from behind Matt. He turned around to find Tyler and Brian grinning at him.
"Mi-mi-mi-mi-mi. I'm a famous opera star," Tyler sang.
"But I don't want to be a star!" Brian sang.
"Oh, this is tragic!" Tyler sang, touching the back of his hand to his forehead.
"Tragic," Brian echoed. "What will I do?"
"Stop it right now!" Dede was furious. "You guys don't realize how good Matt is, how much talent he has. I don't know why he's friends with people who don't appreciate him!"
The bell rang for the start of homeroom, and Dede stormed off.
"Whoa!" Tyler said. "She must really like you, Matt. Who was that?"
"A friend. A real friend." Matt reached into his backpack and tossed a book at Tyler. "Here, you left this at my house." Then he ran after Dede.

"You really don't know who she is, do you?" Brian said to Tyler. "She's that pitcher I was telling you about. My sister's on the high school softball team, and that girl Dede is so good that she practices with them sometimes."
"You're talking about the player with the killer fastball, right?"

"Yeah, that's the one, and now she's defending Matt. Did you also notice that he threw that book with his left arm? The one with the bad elbow? Dude, I think our man has been doing opera for a long time."
"Whoa!" Tyler said again as he watched Matt catch up with Dede.

Matt was not looking forward to his next rehearsal. Ever since the last one, he'd been arguing with his mother about quitting. She finally agreed that he could, but only if he told the director in person. As Matt walked into the theater, he practiced his speech under his breath. He'd get this over quickly and then he'd text his mom at the café where she was waiting.
"Hey, urchin!" a soft voice called as Matt walked down the aisle.

He turned around and was startled to see the singer who played Mimi. His words came tumbling out. "Oh! Were you talking to me? I'm so sorry I bumped into you last rehearsal. I didn't mean to. I was only trying—"
Mimi laughed. "I'm fine. I just wanted to check how you're doing. Don't let Bob get to you."
Matt looked confused. "Bob?"
"Mr. Berman. He yells at everybody. He's a director, and that's what directors do. If you're going to be an opera singer, you have to get used to directors yelling. Now tell me you're okay."
Mimi smiled kindly at Matt, and he smiled back. "I'm okay."
As the opera star walked away, Tim came up to Matt.
"She spoke to you!" Tim said in amazement. "She has an unbelievable voice, and she's so pretty, and . . ." His voice trailed off as he watched Mimi talking to the director.
"And you have a crush on her!"
Tim laughed and gave Matt a little punch on the arm. "So why'd you run off the other day?"
"I didn't run off. I—"

But before Matt could explain, Mr. Berman was calling them all to gather round. "We have a special guest performer today!" he announced with a flourish. "Nigel the horse will be pulling Musetta's carriage. Now let's try to get through the entire act with no stopping. Is everybody ready?"
"A real horse?" Matt raised his eyebrows at Tim. "When I saw The Barber of Seville , two guys in a costume played the dancing donkey."
"Let's hope this horse doesn't have to dance."

Matt took his place offstage. As the orchestra played the opening notes, he realized that he liked this strange world that combined singing and drama and even an occasional live animal. He couldn't wait to try on his costume later that day.

When he heard his cue, Matt ran onstage without bumping into anyone. He sang every note perfectly. The act was going so well, he couldn't understand why the director was suddenly shouting for them all to stop. Then people started laughing, and Matt realized the horse had pooped right in the middle of the stage.
"Stagehands!" the director yelled.
Mimi winked at Matt. "I guess you're not the worst performer today."

Matt laughed. As the stagehands cleaned up the mess, he realized something else. He liked singing and he was good at it. He'd made some new friends here, and he didn't care what his friends at school thought. He wasn't going to give up opera.
"I'll show them," he thought. Then he realized that he really could show them. "I'll give them tickets!"
"Everyone, gather round!" Mr. Berman called out to the cast and crew.

It was a couple of weeks later, and Matt was standing backstage, feeling sad and nervous. Sad, because the last performance of La Bohème had just ended. He was going to miss his new friends, kids who loved opera as much as he did. Nervous, because he knew Brian and Tyler had been in the audience, and he was anxious to hear what they'd say about the opera. He tried to tell himself that their opinions didn't matter, but he really hoped they'd enjoyed it.

Mr. Berman looked happy. "I have some exciting news! Mimi and La Bohème live on for another night! As you may know, the city of Philadelphia is hosting an outdoor arts festival this weekend. One of the acts has canceled, and we've been invited to perform a scene tomorrow night."
The cast cheered while members of the crew groaned.
"Does that mean we have to move everything outside?" one of the stagehands asked.
"Just the set for the beginning of act 2. I think that one will look best on TV."
"That's our scene!" Matt whispered to Tim.
"TV?" a few singers echoed.
"Oh, didn't I mention TV?" the director said. "You're going to be on live TV."
"We're going to be on TV!" Tim shouted. "Come on!" He grabbed Matt and another urchin. Together they led a chain of kids dancing and laughing their way through the backstage crowd.
Matt was still feeling pumped up as he ran to find his friends and family in the lobby.
"I'm so proud of you," his mom said, giving him a hug.
"You were great!" Dede said with a big smile.
"It's not over yet. We're going to be on live TV tomorrow night!" Matt handed his mom a paper with all the details.
He craned his neck, looking around the lobby. "Have you seen Brian and Tyler?"
Dede's face fell. "Uh . . . I don't know how to say this . . . Tyler had the tickets, but he forgot to bring them. He and Brian got all the way here, and had to go home because they couldn't get in."

"Are you serious?" Matt couldn't believe what he was hearing. "This was important to me! I had four free tickets, and I gave two of them to Tyler and Brian. If I'd known they weren't coming, I'd have given them to someone who actually likes opera!"
When he checked his phone on the way home, he saw numerous texts from Brian and Tyler. But he was too angry to read them, never mind reply.
The next day was a busy one. Even though the opera wouldn't air until that night, Matt had to be in Philadelphia that afternoon.
"Wow! And I thought our theater was amazing!" Tim said as they walked onto the stage that had been built in front of the art museum. "This is—"
"Outstanding!" Matt completed his sentence. Standing onstage, they had a spectacular view down a grand boulevard toward Philadelphia's city hall.

The cast did a run-through for the sound technicians. Sound traveled differently outside, so it took a bit of adjusting to hear the orchestra. Afterward Matt remained at the side of the stage, gazing at the incredible scene before him. The road was closed to traffic. In a few hours there would be a crowd as far as he could see.
"Imagine being an opera star and singing to a crowd like that!" Matt said to himself.
He began to hum "Nessun Dorma," and then the urge to sing became overpowering. Matt closed his eyes and imagined he was standing in front of a huge crowd that had come to see him perform.
When he finished singing the aria, he heard someone applauding. Matt's eyes flew open.
"Bravo!" Mr. Berman said. "You have a fine voice."
"Oh!" Matt was startled. "Thanks!"
A few hours later Matt was hanging around backstage with the rest of the urchins. They were all in their costumes, ready for the performance, which would begin in half an hour.
Suddenly a stage manager came running. "Matt, come with me! Mr. Berman wants to see you right away!"
"Uh-oh," Tim said. "You're in trouble."
"But I haven't done anything wrong!"
Matt followed the stage manager to the spot where the director was consulting a woman holding a clipboard.

"Ah, Matt," the director said. "I'm wondering if you could do me a favor. Ms. Chang here from the TV station says we'll have a few minutes of empty airtime while our set is moved into place. Do you think you could sing 'Nessun Dorma' to entertain the crowd? You'd have to do it a cappella because the orchestra doesn't have the music."
Matt gulped. His stomach did a flip-flop. Then he remembered what Dede had said when he wanted to quit, something about not throwing away "an amazing opportunity."
He took a deep breath. "Sure. I'm used to singing it by myself anyway."
And that's how Matt found himself at center stage, gazing out over an enormous crowd.

" Nessun dorma !" he sang in Italian. The words mean "No one will sleep." His voice sailed out into the darkness while the audience below sat transfixed. Matt tried not to think about how many people were watching him.
As he finished the aria, there was silence. Then people jumped to their feet and applauded. He left the stage, but the audience called him back again and again.
"Whoa!" Tim said. "We don't need to do our scene. They just want to listen to you!"
The rest of the evening was a blur for Matt. When he got home, he found Dede, Brian, and Tyler waiting for him.
"Dede made us watch you on TV! You were amazing!" Tyler squeaked. "How did you remember all those words in Italian? I have to admit that opera stuff is sort of cool!"
"Oh, I don't know," Brian said. "I thought it was pretty weird."
"Well, I can't believe you sang a solo in front of all those people," Dede said. "I couldn't do that."
She gave Matt a quick hug that knocked off his hat. Matt smiled.
"I did like that guy with the deep voice," Brian admitted "Maybe you'll sound like him after your voice changes."
"You mean the bass? Nah, I'd rather be a tenor." Matt grinned. "They always get the girl!"
For almost an hour, Amy Kim had been sitting in the audience at the middle school talent show, waiting for her turn to perform. She'd been watching the show. But mostly she'd been feeling nervous.

Holding a deck of cards in her right hand, she practiced cutting the deck with one hand. Then she shifted the deck to her left hand and practiced that way. When that didn't calm her down, she shuffled the cards again and again.
"Stop that!" her best friend, Megan Sanchez, hissed. "You're even making me nervous, and I don't get nervous before a show!"

"Sorry!" Amy put the cards in her duffel bag and tried to concentrate on the talent show. But so many of the acts seemed the same. Except for one boy who played the clarinet, all the guys were in rock bands. The girls were either singing or dancing. Megan was scheduled to sing and dance later on, so she was wearing a long coat to conceal her costume. Amy had a top hat and wand in her bag.
Megan glanced at the program and then nudged Amy. "Come on! It's time for us to get ready."
"I can't believe I let you talk me into this," Amy said as they made their way backstage.

Amy liked to do magic tricks, especially card tricks, and she sometimes performed for her family. But she'd been reluctant to perform in front of the whole school—until Megan persuaded her that it would be fun.

"Remember what I told you. Don't think about the audience." Megan removed her coat to reveal a red leotard covered in sequins. "Think about the party afterward. So many of the boys in the show are coming!"
"I'm glad I didn't eat any dinner because my stomach is churning. All I can hear is my heart pounding. Can you even hear me talking?"
"You'll be fine once you get onstage." Megan gave Amy a quick hug before plopping down on the floor.
"I sure hope so." Amy pulled her props from her duffel bag as she numbly watched Megan slipping into tap shoes.

Amy had been practicing her act for days. She was planning to do three card tricks followed by two coin tricks. If the audience demanded an encore, she was sort of ready to pull some colored scarves from a paper cone.
"I hope they don't want an encore,"Amy said to Megan. "I'm not too confident about that scarf trick."
But Megan wasn't listening. Or rather, she wasn't paying attention to Amy anymore because she was listening to someone on her phone. Megan giggled.

The plan was for Megan to act as Amy's assistant for the first card trick. Megan had suggested it. She said this would give Amy a chance to warm up and feel comfortable onstage. Then Amy would repeat the trick with a member of the audience. This would show that Megan hadn't helped her in any way.

Amy watched from the wings as yet another group of guitar-playing boys worked their way through a popular song. The crowd was going wild. Amy glanced over at Megan, who was still on the phone. They were up next!
"Megan!" Amy called. But her friend had a finger in one ear so she could hear better on the phone.

The music stopped and the boys came offstage. Mr. Carlson, who was announcing the show and was also Amy's math teacher, started to introduce her act to the audience. Amy looked over at Megan, who was too busy laughing into the phone to notice her.
"And now Amy Kim and her world of magic!" Mr. Carlson announced for the second time.

Amy had no choice but to step onstage. The bright lights blinded her. "Uh," she said into the microphone. Then she glanced into the wings, hoping Megan would appear. "Uh," she said again. "This is an ordinary deck of cards. Nothing unusual about it at all. I'm now going to—"
Megan suddenly rushed onstage, and someone whistled at her costume. "I'm here! Did I miss anything?"
The audience laughed, but Amy flashed an annoyed look at her friend. But she tried to carry on as if nothing was wrong. "I'm now going to ask my assistant to pick a card, any card."
Megan dutifully picked a card, just as they'd practiced so many times in Amy's bedroom.
"Please look at it and show the audience," Amy said.
Megan did as she was told, and Amy began to relax ever so slightly.
"Now cut the cards as many times as you want, and I'll find your card."
This was where things went suddenly, terribly wrong. As Megan cut the cards, she lost her grip on the deck. The cards scattered, with some even flying off the stage and into the audience.

Amy's eyes widened in horror. There were some card tricks where the assistant is supposed to drop the cards into a pile instead of cutting the deck. But this wasn't one of them. Meanwhile the crowd was laughing wildly and getting louder by the minute.
"Um, okay . . ." Amy stepped away from the microphone to pick up the cards.
"We can't hear you!" someone in the audience shouted.
Megan turned her back to the audience. "Just smile and keep going like nothing's wrong," she said to Amy. "They'll never know the difference."
"Yes, they will!"Amy said in a surprisingly loud voice. "I can't believe you dropped the cards! All you had to do was cut them!"
The kids in the front rows laughed.
"What did you say?" someone called from the back of the auditorium. "We can't hear you!"
"Louder!" someone else shouted.
"Let's start again," Megan suggested.
"No. Leave. I'll handle this myself," Amy said, though she had no idea how she was going to do that.
Megan gave a big smile and waved to the crowd as she tap-danced offstage.
Amy decided to abandon her card tricks and move on to the coin tricks. She pulled four quarters from her pocket. "As you can see, I have four ordinary quarters . . ."
But she had forgotten to step back to the microphone, and no one could hear her.
"Louder! Louder! Louder!" the crowd chanted.
Amy looked out into the audience in terror. Then she turned and fled the stage.
Megan was waiting in the wings. "You're still going to the party, right?"

On Saturday afternoon Amy watched Megan as her friend stood in front of the mirror in Amy's bedroom. Megan tilted her head, studying the French braid she'd just made in her hair. Usually Amy would have been right next to her, using the mirror to practice her latest trick. But today Amy was lying on her bed, moaning whenever Megan mentioned the previous night's talent show.

"Really, Amy, it wasn't so bad." Megan pulled out the braid and started brushing her hair. "You want to talk talent show disasters? You should have seen Brett Greenberg. He had his gigantic dog, Rex, onstage. Rex was supposed to bark on command and balance a treat on his nose. But Rex ran to Brett's sister in the audience. And then—"
Amy groaned loudly. "You're comparing me to a dog, Megan. This is not consoling me!"
"That's not what I meant. I know I've already apologized, but I'm really, really sorry for messing up your trick. I shouldn't have been talking on the phone, and I didn't mean to drop the cards."
Amy nodded. "I know you didn't mean to do all that stuff, Megan, but I looked like an idiot onstage! I haven't even turned on my phone today. I'm too afraid to see what everyone's saying about me."

"Well, you don't have to worry about that. Everybody's still talking about Brett's dog. Brett tried to go after Rex, but the dog ran up to Mrs. Antonelli. He put his paws right on her shoulders and licked her face and her glasses!"
Amy couldn't help laughing. "Who's Mrs. Antonelli?"
"She's substituting for that seventh-grade math teacher who just had twins."
"Oh." Amy sat up. "Speaking of math—remember the reason you're here? It's for help with your math homework."
Megan sighed and pulled her hair into a ponytail. "I hate math—absolutely, completely hate it. How can you stand it?"

Amy smiled happily at the thought of math problems. Now that she was in eighth grade, math class focused on algebra. Amy loved working with graphs and equations. "It's like doing a puzzle," she said to Megan, "and the best thing is there's only one right answer. So when you get that, you're done. None of that endless revision stuff like in English class."
"Yeah, but I can never find that one right answer." Megan made a frowning face in the mirror. "Even with a calculator."

On Monday morning it didn't take long for Amy to realize that Megan had been right. No one was talking about her because they were too busy laughing about Brett's dog. A rumor was even circulating that Rex had jumped into Mrs. Antonelli's car and driven her home! But then Amy got to math class.
"Hey, magician!" Frank Martin called from across the room. "How's that ordinary deck of cards?"
Amy turned red.
"Pretend you didn't hear him," Megan said. She sat behind Amy.
But Frank wasn't through yet. "Nope, nothing unusual about that deck of cards— except it leaped right off the stage!"
He laughed and the boys sitting near him joined in.
Megan jumped up and charged over to Frank. "Listen to me, fathead. That wasn't her fault!"
"Whoa! What's going on here?" Mr. Carlson hurried into his classroom. "Everybody should be in their seats."
"He means you, lovely assistant," Frank said in a mocking voice.
Megan glared at him before stomping back to her seat.
"Thanks, Megan," Amy whispered.
"It was the least I could do."
Amy immediately caught on to the day's lesson, but Megan seemed hopelessly lost. When Mr. Carlson gave permission to start the homework in class, Megan asked Amy for help.
"You're so smart!" she said as Amy showed her how to solve the first problem. "Why don't you raise your hand whenever Mr. Carlson asks a question?"
Amy shrugged. "I don't like talking in class."
"But you could have a million extra-credit points for class participation!"
Amy shrugged again."I don't need any extra credit."
The bell rang to signal the end of class. As Amy passed Mr. Carlson's desk, he called her over.
"That was a tough crowd you had the other night. Even the famous magician Houdini couldn't have controlled that group."
Amy nodded. She didn't know what to say.
Mr. Carlson went on. "You may not know this, but I'm an amateur magician. You probably would have had better luck with a trick that people could actually see."
"They saw the cards fall!" Amy blurted out.
Mr. Carlson smiled. "They sure did, but that wasn't your fault. Look, I want you to be the first to know something—I'm starting a magic club at school."
"Thanks, Mr. Carlson, but I don't want to do magic anymore. I have to go now or I'll be late for my next class."
"Think about it!" Mr. Carlson called after Amy.

Amy did think about it. She thought about how she loved magic and she wanted to learn some new tricks. But then she thought about how she didn't want to perform for an audience—no matter how small—ever again. When she mentioned her dilemma to her parents, they said it was up to her to decide.
Amy tried to forget about the club, but she passed the sign-up sheet on Mr. Carlson's bulletin board every day. After a week she stood there staring at it.
"Maybe I should just try it," she thought. But as she started to write her name, she noticed something: everyone on the sheet was a boy.
"You didn't sign up because it's all boys?" Megan squeaked at her later, when Amy sat down in math class. "That sounds like the perfect club to me!"
Amy shook her head, remembering Frank and the other boys laughing at her.
"Look, I'm trying out for the school musical, and once rehearsals start I won't have much time to hang out with you. Unless, of course, you do the musical too."
"No, no!" Amy shook her head vigorously. "Not a good idea."

"Amy, why are you shaking your head?" Mr. Carlson walked over and put his hand near her ear. "Oh, here's the problem!" He held out a quarter. "You had some money in your ear." He closed his hand around the coin. When he opened his fingers again, he was holding five nickels.
Amy laughed and Megan clapped her hands.
"So, Amy, how about joining magic club?" Mr. Carlson asked as he made all the coins disappear.
Amy put her name on the list.
On the first day of magic club, Amy peeked in the door of Mr. Carlson's room. "Ugh," she thought. "Ten boys and no girls."
Several boys were yelling and chasing one another around the room. A tall boy was tapping a short kid on the head with a magic wand. Amy didn't see Mr. Carlson anywhere.
"Okay, I can do this," Amy said to herself. "Remember what Megan said: this is a chance to do something I like and meet some new boys. Though I'm not sure I want to meet these boys."
Amy opened the door, and the room went quiet.
"Woo-hoo!" Frank grinned. "Now we have a woman to saw in half!"
For a moment Amy was too stunned to speak. But then she said, "Oh no, I'm not here to be somebody's assistant. I'm a magician. And, by the way, you'd actually need two women to perform that trick."
Frank laughed at her. "Right, we'd need a spare woman in case we couldn't put the original one back together again."
All the other boys were now laughing too. Except one.
"Frank obviously doesn't understand how that trick is done," Brett Greenberg said quietly to Amy.
"That's for sure," she agreed. At least she had one ally in the room.
"Sorry I'm late." Mr. Carlson came breezing in. "Emergency math department meeting. Okay, so let's lay down some club rules and talk about the kinds of magic we'll be learning."
"I saw the most amazing magic show this weekend!" Frank jumped in. "There were all these special effects. Explosions! Fireworks!"
"Rule number one," said Mr. Carlson, "no explosions and no fireworks."
"One of the magicians had to escape from a locked tank of water!"
"No dangerous escape acts," Mr. Carlson said.
"Then they did an incredible act with six live doves! I don't usually like animal acts, but—"
"We could use rabbits!"one boy shouted.
"Or snakes!" another suggested.
"No live animals!" Mr. Carlson said firmly. "Now someone, please tell me some basic kinds of magic acts."
The boys quieted down but most weren't looking at Mr. Carlson. Frank was staring at his phone, clearly bored now that he'd described the show he'd seen.
Amy put up her hand.
"You don't have to raise your hand during club meetings," Mr. Carlson said.

"Okay." Amy hesitated. The teacher's comment had thrown her off track. "Well, first there are illusions. Those are the big tricks you usually see onstage. Things like levitating a person or sawing a woman in half." She glared at Frank, but he was still looking at his phone. "You know, things with fireworks or explosives."
Frank was paying attention now.

"Right," said Mr. Carlson. "Illusions often use special equipment to achieve their effects. When the magician is onstage, he—and I use the word he because most magicians are men—doesn't really have to do much. He's more of a performer than someone who's mastered a set of skills. What else?"
"Escapes!" said Frank. "Tricks that make the audience worry the magician might die."
"Yeah!" a couple boys said.
"Escape tricks don't have to be dangerous," said Mr. Carlson. "Some of the most interesting and intricate escapes involve ropes and knots. Keep going."
"Does mind reading count?" Brett asked.
"It sure does," Mr. Carlson said. "Sometimes the magician is blindfolded or turns his back to the audience. Then he has to guess what kind of object an audience member is holding up."
Amy's hand shot up. "But there's no such thing as mind reading, right? I mean, nobody can really do that."
"You're correct." Mr. Carlson nodded at Amy. "Those tricks usually involve signals between the magician and his assistant. But we still haven't mentioned several kinds of magic."
"Making things appear and disappear!" Amy said.

"Right. They can be small things—like cards or coins—that you hold in your hand. Or big things like a person. One magician even made the Statue of Liberty disappear on TV! All right, who can define sleight of hand for me?"
Amy raised her hand again. Frank sighed. "You don't have to raise your hand, Ms. Encyclopedia of Magic. And you don't have to answer every question."

Amy could feel her anger rising, but then she remembered Megan's advice to ignore him. " Sleight of hand can actually be two different things," she said calmly. "Some people use the phrase to refer to those small tricks you mentioned. The ones with coins or cards or anything you can hide in your hand. But other people use it to describe any deceptive move a magician makes with her hands. The magician does that to misdirect the audience's attention."
Mr. Carlson smiled at Amy. "Excellent! Okay, everyone, let's see what you can do."
The teacher laid an assortment of props—cards, rings, scarves, and coins—on a table. "Who wants to go first?"

Frank strode confidently to the table and picked up the rings. He did a fast-paced routine, linking and unlinking them in the blink of an eye. When he finished, Amy joined in the applause. Frank was a pain, but she had to admit he was a good magician.
Next Brett picked up the cards and pulled out three. He held them out toward Amy. "Pick a card."
She picked the one on the left.
"No, not that one!"
She picked the one on the right.
He groaned "Not that one either!"
"Okay, time for our first lesson." Mr. Carlson grinned. "I assume you wanted her to pick the one in the middle?"
Brett nodded.

"So you have to do what magicians call the force . When she picks the first card, you say, 'Great! You've eliminated one.' Then when she picks the second card, you throw that one down, and say, 'Smart choice.' And then you use the third card to do your trick. Now, does anyone know why it's called the force ?"
Amy knew. "Because you're forcing the person to choose the card you need for your trick."
"And what was that trick anyway?" Frank rolled his eyes.
"Uh . . ." Brett stepped away from the table. "You know, I don't really remember how that one goes."

Amy felt bad for Brett. She also felt more and more nervous the closer it came to her turn. To calm herself, she picked up a card and practiced concealing it in her palm. By now seven kids had performed and only four were left.
Mr. Carlson glanced at the clock. "I'm afraid our time is up. The rest of you can show us your tricks next week."
"Whew!" Amy let out a loud sigh of relief.
As Amy was leaving the first meeting of the magic club, Mr. Carlson stopped her.

"I noticed that you seemed nervous about performing," the teacher said kindly. "You know, some people are really good at mastering the mechanics of a trick, while others are better at performing. It's the rare kid who's a skilled magician and a spellbinding performer."

Amy nervously shifted her backpack from one shoulder to the other. "Ugh," she thought. "Here comes another lecture on being more outgoing." Everyone—from her parents to her teachers to Megan—was always telling her that she needed to be bolder and speak up more.
"I watched how you were palming that card," Mr. Carlson said. "That takes a lot of skill. How did you learn to do that?"
Amy was puzzled by such an obvious question. "Practice, of course."

"That's exactly how you learn to be a better performer," Mr. Carlson went on. "I also saw that some of the boys weren't exactly welcoming you. What if you could use your fear of performing to your advantage? I think you could impress the boys at the same time. Are you familiar with the trick where you pass a coin through a table?"
"Oh, yeah!" Amy's eyes lit up with excitement. "I did that at a restaurant once to keep my little cousin amused while we were waiting for dinner."
"If you can do that trick well, the boys might start giving you more respect. It's often done at a dining table. But you could use my desk."
Amy looked at the jumble of papers, books, and office supplies covering her teacher's desk. She laughed. "I guess you'll have to clean it off first!"

The idea behind the coin trick was simple, but it required split-second timing. At the restaurant a saltshaker had played a key role; for school Amy decided to substitute Mr. Carlson's coffee cup. Over the next week, she practiced every spare moment. Mr. Carlson helped her to develop some patter. That was the magicians' word for the story that accompanies a trick.
At the next magic club meeting, Amy was nervous about the idea of outwitting the boys. But she also felt excited. If the trick went well, it would be fun to see their faces.
She sat behind Mr. Carlson's desk, which he had cleaned off. On the surface she placed a nickel and his coffee cup.

First, she rapped on his desk to show that it was solid. "Every day Mr. Carlson sits at this desk, correcting math homework. Little does he realize that it's more than a desk. It's actually a portal, a gateway that objects can pass through."
Amy looked at the boys, who were now staring at the gray metal desk. "All he needs is this magic poncho!" With a flourish, she laid a paper napkin on the desk.
Everyone laughed, but this time the boys weren't laughing at her. They were laughing at the "magic poncho" prop.
"I will now use this cup and this magic poncho to make this coin pass through the desk."

Amy covered the coin with the cup and then placed the napkin over the cup. She closed her eyes, waved her hands in circles, and tapped the cup. Her eyes flew open. She took a breath and reached for the cup.
The nickel was still there.
"I knew she couldn't do it." Frank smirked and looked at the other boys.

"Oh no! That didn't work!" Amy appeared flustered. But as she glanced at Mr. Carlson, he winked at her. They both knew this was part of the act. "Oh, please, Mr. Carlson. Let me try that again. I know I can do it right."
"Well, I don't know . . ." Mr. Carlson hesitated. The boys looked back and forth between the teacher and Amy, who seemed on the verge of tears. "All right. One more time, but that's it."

Amy placed the coin under the cup and the cup under the napkin. She closed her eyes, waved her hands in circles, and tapped the cup. As her eyes popped open, she slammed her hand on the napkin-covered cup. She lifted the napkin. The coin was still there, but the cup was gone.
"Ahh!" the boys gasped.
"Sorry, Mr. Carlson." Amy pulled his coffee cup from under the desk. "I guess that portal only works for cups!"
The boys broke into applause. Even Frank admitted it was a pretty good trick. "Do it again," he demanded.
"Oh, no," Mr. Carlson said. "Never repeat a trick. Surprise is one of the elements that make a trick work. If you repeat it, people will be watching to see how it's done."
"Besides"—Amy grinned—"a magician never reveals her secrets."

Every week Mr. Carlson taught the kids a new trick and had them perform the previous week's trick. Frank usually performed best when they first learned a trick. But Amy was the one who always mastered the trick. That was because, unlike Frank, she went home and practiced until she could do the trick effortlessly. Meanwhile poor Brett struggled, and Amy tried to help him.

As the weeks passed, Amy began to look forward to magic club. She got better at making up patter for the tricks. But she still wasn't comfortable talking to any of the boys except Brett. Until someone arrived unexpectedly one afternoon.

The club was in the middle of a meeting when Megan burst through the door. "I just quit the musical!" she announced breathlessly. "Ms. Patel—she's the director—didn't think I was serious enough! Can you believe that? She said I was always talking. And she was mad that I missed two rehearsals in a row!"
All the boys were staring wide-eyed at Megan. Mr. Carlson started to speak. "Well—"

"Ms. Patel gave my part to somebody else and put me in the chorus. It's so unfair! I've had more years of voice and dance lessons than everybody else combined! So I quit. And now I can join magic club!" Megan flopped into a seat.
"Well, the more the merrier," Mr. Carlson said. "Welcome!"
Frank rolled his eyes and muttered, "Another girl magician."
Amy broke into a grin. Now there was another girl in the club, and she wasn't just any girl. She was Amy's best friend.
At first Amy thought it would be fun to have Megan in magic club, but she quickly began to change her mind.

As soon as Megan showed up, she was a distraction. Mr. Carlson had been in the middle of demonstrating a rope trick, but he had to stop to introduce Megan. Then Megan couldn't just sit quietly; she had to say something special to each boy.
"As I was saying . . ." Mr. Carlson picked up the rope again. "This is a classic example of something appearing other than it is. This looks like a rope with a knot in it, but—"
"Brett keeps glancing over here," Megan whispered to Amy.
"Uh-huh." Amy was trying to pay attention to the teacher.
Megan nudged Amy in the side. "I think he's looking at you ! Maybe he likes—"
"Please be quiet, Megan! I can't concentrate on this trick!" Amy burst out.
Suddenly everyone—not just Brett—was looking at the two girls.
"Um . . ." Amy felt her face growing hot with embarrassment.
"Girls!" Frank grinned and pretended to scold them. "Some of us are actually trying to learn something here."
Megan frowned at Frank. "Mr. Carlson, when do we learn how to make people disappear?"
"That's an advanced lesson, and you have to learn how to make them reappear."
"Maybe not," Megan said in a low voice that the teacher couldn't hear.
But everyone around her heard, and all the boys laughed. Frank just glared at her.

As the weeks passed, Amy continued to have mixed feelings about Megan's joining the club. On the one hand, it was nice to have another girl around. But it was clear to Amy that Megan was only there to meet boys. She had no real interest in magic.
"Do we have to go to magic club this afternoon?" Megan asked Amy as they opened their lockers at the end of school one day.
"Of course!" Amy was looking forward to going.

Megan threw her books in her locker and took out her coat. "That stuff Mr. Carlson shows us is too difficult. He says you always have to be two steps ahead of the audience, but I feel like I'm two steps behind. I don't want to learn those tricks. I just want to be onstage."
Amy felt annoyed. "Look, Megan, you don't have to come if you don't want to. But I don't want to miss this meeting. Mr. Carlson said we're having a special guest."
"It's probably a rabbit." Megan closed her locker and followed Amy, who was already walking down the hall.
Amy turned around. "No, it won't be a rabbit. Mr. Carlson banned live animals from our acts on the first day."
When they arrived at magic club, an older woman was talking to the teacher. She had short gray hair and a big smile. Once everyone arrived, Mr. Carlson introduced his guest.

"Kids, I'd like you to welcome Olga Lapinski, assistant to the late, great Marvin Marvelo, who traveled the world, astounding people with his feats of magic. Besides being Marvin's wife and assistant, she helped to develop some of his most famous tricks. Since his tragic death, Olga is the only one who knows the secrets of his tricks."
Olga smiled. "Thank you for inviting me to your meeting."
All the kids applauded except for Frank. He shook his head and muttered, "She's just an assistant. What a waste of time!"
But Megan tapped Amy's arm excitedly. "An assistant! That's what I should do. I'd be a great assistant!"

Olga began speaking. "An assistant is an important part of any magic act. He or she helps with the trick directly, or helps by distracting the audience. You should always treat your assistants nicely and pay them well. It's the right thing to do—and you want to be sure they never betray you!"
"Betray you?" said Brett. "What are you talking about?"

"Well, magicians are just like anybody else. Whenever they see a new act, the first thing they ask is: How did the magician do that? Magicians are always trying to learn the secrets behind others' tricks, especially the big illusions. One way to do that is to bribe an assistant to reveal the information."
"That's pretty sneaky," Brett said.
"Can you tell us more about what assistants do?" Amy asked.
"They get sawed in half." Frank was now tapping away on his phone.

"That's true and sometimes they vanish. When the assistant walks in front of the magician, she may be acting as a screen between him and the audience. Or she may be passing him something he needs. Or," Olga said with a wink, "that may be what the magician wants you to think. Whenever assistants are onstage, they're there for a reason."
"Did you have a favorite costume?" Megan asked.
"Well, I always loved sequin-covered leotards," Olga said. "But—"
"Me too!" Megan interrupted.
"But my favorite costumes were the ones that were part of the act. I loved it when I dressed like Marvin. It seemed to the audience that he was one place onstage when he was really somewhere else."

"Now I have another surprise for you," Mr. Carlson said. "The school is having a carnival in a few weeks to raise funds for after-school activities. All the teams and clubs will get a portion of the money. With the help of Olga, I've come up with a grand illusion that we can perform in the auditorium."
"What is it?" a few kids yelled at once.

"In a minute. It will take everyone's help to build the illusion and to work behind the scenes on carnival night. But we need only one magician and one assistant onstage." Mr. Carlson paused. "After careful consideration, I've selected Amy as the magician."
"Go, Amy!" Megan cried.
Frank crossed his arms and scowled. "That's ridiculous! I'm the best magician in the room."
"Please stand up, Amy," Mr. Carlson said. "I chose you because I know you'll put in the practice time and your patter has really come a long way."
"Thanks," Amy mumbled. She looked down, struggling to decide if this was a good thing. Then Mr. Carlson made another announcement. "And now Amy will choose her assistant."
Megan popped up and stood next to Amy. She flashed her brightest smile.
"Uh . . . uh . . . actually . . ." Amy hesitated. Then she said in a strong voice, "I pick Brett."
Olga clapped her hands with delight. "A female magician with a male assistant—I love it!"
But not everyone was so happy.
Megan sank back into her seat with a shocked look on her face. Meanwhile Brett came forward and stood next to Amy.
"This is a joke, right?" Megan said. "You meant to choose me as your assistant."

"Sorry, Megan, but I need someone I can rely on, and you can be, well, kind of undependable sometimes." Amy felt awful. She knew the words were true, but she didn't want to hurt her friend's feelings.
"Well, then, I'm through with this stupid club!" Megan started to storm out of the room. When she reached the door, she turned back to Amy. "You wouldn't even be in magic club if it weren't for me!"
"I'm done too." Frank gathered up his backpack. "I don't have time for this bunch of losers. Hey, Megan, wait up!"
"Oh my!" Olga lifted her eyebrows. "I've seen temperamental behavior like that in the world of professional magic. But I thought kids would be more easygoing."
Brett let out his breath. "Megan and Frank—now, there's a pair who deserve each other."
Amy shook her head sadly. At that moment she had to agree.

"All right," Mr. Carlson said. "Before I describe the illusion for the carnival, does anyone else want to abandon us?" No one made a move to leave. "Good. Now here's what's going to happen. Amy, assisted by Brett, will make six people disappear."
"Wow!" everyone said at once.
"Obviously you kids can't be the people," Olga added, "because everyone would be suspicious of that."
"I'm leaning toward choosing players on the boys' and girls' soccer teams," Mr. Carlson said. "They're popular kids. Wouldn't a lot of people show up to see them disappear?"
"Yes," Amy said. "But we can't trust other kids to keep the secret behind the trick. They're not magicians like we are."
A few boys nodded.
"What about six teachers?" Brett said. "There are lots of them I'd like to see disappear!"
All the kids laughed and even Mr. Carlson did too.
"That's a great idea," Amy said, and everyone else agreed.
"Well, that's settled," Mr. Carlson said. "Now all you have to do, Amy, is find us some teachers who have the time to participate and can keep a secret."
