"Oh." Amy felt her heart sinking. She dreaded talking to teachers, never mind asking them for a favor.
"Don't worry!" Brett said cheerfully. "I'll help you."

With Brett at her side, Amy visited all the teachers she knew. Many of them were too busy to attend rehearsals for the magic trick. But slowly over the next couple weeks, Amy and Brett found six willing teachers. They got them to sign the secrecy agreement that Mr. Carlson had drafted.

Meanwhile, under the supervision of Olga Lapinski and Mr. Carlson, the other magicians built the frame for a large box. Instead of solid sides, it had four black curtains, which matched the curtain hanging across the back of the stage.
"How will the teachers escape?" Amy asked.
Olga whispered her response, and then said aloud, "That's why you need the teachers to rehearse, along with friends behind the big black curtain to assist them."
When everyone arrived in the auditorium for the first rehearsal, the box was standing on a low platform.
"Are you ready, Amy?" Mr. Carlson asked. "You're the magician, so you're in charge."
Amy nodded. "Okay, all kids should be offstage. Those of you who'll be wandering the carnival dressed as magicians can sit in the audience. The rest of you should be backstage."
The kids scrambled into position. Mr. Carlson opened the red curtain at the front of the stage.
"Teachers should be seated separately around the auditorium," Amy called out. But the teachers were too busy talking to pay attention to her.
"Mr. Carlson, they're not listening to me."
"You're the magician," he repeated.
"Attention, teachers!" Amy said in her loudest voice, but they kept on talking.
"Here, let me help." Brett stuck two fingers in his mouth and let out an ear-piercing whistle. The auditorium went silent, and Amy grinned at Brett.
She repeated her instructions to the teachers, who slowly took their seats. "And they complain when we don't respond right away!" she said to Brett.
"You're doing great! Just show them who's boss."
"Okay, let's practice getting onstage and into the box," she said. "Everybody walk around to the back and step in."

"Wait a minute!" Mr. Harrington called out. He was Amy's social studies teacher. "Why can't we be onstage at the beginning? Wouldn't it be better if everyone could get a good look at us before we disappear? Maybe each of us could say something as we enter the box."
Amy sighed and looked at Brett. "You're the boss," he whispered.
"I want you in the audience, so it looks like I've picked random volunteers."
"But you haven't picked us at random," Mr. Harrington insisted.
"True, but that's what I want it to look like."

"Always be suspicious of the volunteers, my dear Mr. Harrington." Olga came out from the wings and pointed toward the box. "Won't you come this way?" She herded him and the rest of the teachers into the box.
"Okay, teachers, close the curtains," said Amy.
The curtains on the back and one side closed; the curtain rods on the front and the other side fell off, taking the curtains with them.
Amy sighed again and called out, "Magic crew! Curtain repair!"

That was pretty much how rehearsals went. The teachers showed up on time, but that was about all they did right. They talked among themselves and didn't listen to instructions. Mr. Harrington was full of ideas to improve the act, but none of his ideas were really useful. Amy finally thought of a special role he could play at the start of the act, and that seemed to satisfy his need to stand out.
Olga worked with Amy on her patter, reminding her to fill the auditorium with her voice and her presence. "You don't have to do much magic, but you do have to perform," Olga said.
Amy felt smaller and smaller as every day passed. She wished she had a best friend to talk to, but Megan had stopped speaking to her weeks ago.

After five rehearsals the only person performing well was Brett. He moved silently across the stage, escorting the teachers into the box. He whisked open the curtains when it was time to reveal that they had disappeared. He was perfect, which was a good thing because the carnival was the next night.

15.title: Now You See It, Now You Don't

paragraphs.text: On carnival night a steady line of people streamed into the school and bought tickets. By seven o'clock Amy and Brett were walking around the carnival, looking at what the other clubs and teams were presenting. The magic club's act wasn't scheduled until eight o'clock. Mr. Carlson figured a good crowd would have arrived by then.
Amy and Brett went outside, where the boys' soccer team was operating a dunk tank. Their coach was sitting on a small seat above a tank filled with water.
"That looks like fun," Brett said. "You want to try?"
"No, you go ahead." Amy was too nervous to do anything but watch.
Brett hurled a ball toward a round target on the tank. If he hit the target, the seat would flip down and dump the coach into the water. But Brett missed.
"It's probably a good thing I didn't dunk him. He's my gym teacher." Brett smiled at Amy, but she didn't respond. "Come on, lighten up! You're going to be great!"
Amy groaned. "I don't want to talk about it. Let's go inside."
But inside the school, posters for their magic act hung everywhere. Magic club members were walking around, dressed in capes and top hats, encouraging people to attend the show.
"I wonder if Frank and Megan will come," Brett said.
"I hope Megan comes." Amy scanned the hallway for her friend. "I can do without Frank."

Amy and Brett went into the gym, where the girls' basketball team was sponsoring a contest to see who could score the most baskets in one minute. While Brett lined up to take a turn, Amy sat glumly in the bleachers.
"Hey, Amy!"
Amy turned. "Megan!"
"I just wanted to wish you luck. I—"
"Oh, Megan, I've missed you!" Amy hugged her friend. "I'm so nervous! Please tell me you'll come to the show."
"Of course I'll come! Are you sure you want me there? I've been acting like such a jerk."
Amy patted the spot next to her. "Sit while I wait for Brett."
Megan sat down, and the two friends watched the action on the court. When it was Brett's turn to shoot, he searched the bleachers for Amy. He finally spotted her and gave her a thumbs-up.
"Well, that's interesting," Megan said. "I'm sure he likes you."
"I can't think about that now."
The two girls watched as Brett missed every basket.
"I want to sample some of the cooking club's food." Megan stood up as Brett came over. "But I'll be at your show."

Amy and Brett made their way to the auditorium, where they went backstage and checked that everything was ready. Amy put on her top hat and picked up her magic wand. At ten minutes before show time, she peeked into the audience.
"I see all the teachers except Mr. Harrington."
Brett sighed in exasperation. "I'll find him. And if I can't, we'll go on without him."
Five minutes later Brett returned. "He was in the teachers' lounge. By the way, I saw Frank lurking in the back of the auditorium. The place is packed!"
Amy nervously tapped her wand against her leg. "Great! More people to watch me fail."
"You want to go over your patter one more time?" Brett asked.
"No, that'll only make things worse."
Mr. Carlson came backstage. He checked in with the kids who were positioned behind the black curtain at the rear of the stage, and then he came over to Amy and Brett. "You two ready?"
Amy hid her shaking hands behind her back so he couldn't see them. "I guess so."
"She's ready, Mr. Carlson. She'll be great!" Brett said.
"Then it's showtime!"

Mr. Carlson stepped before the red stage curtain at the front of the stage. "Good evening! Tonight the magic club has a special treat for you. The Amazing Amy will make someone disappear right before your eyes! Or as we magicians say, 'Now you see it, now you don't.'"
As the crowd politely clapped, Amy and Brett stepped in front of the red curtain. The lights were bright, but Amy could see Megan smiling in the front row. She took a deep breath and began.
"A magician usually makes his lovely female assistant vanish. But as you can see, I don't have a female assistant." She held out her hand and Brett bowed.
"He's still lovely!" someone called out from the audience.
Mr. Carlson had told Amy to anticipate that response, so she was ready.
"He sure is!" she replied, and Brett took another bow.
"But I think it'd be more interesting to make a whole group of people disappear, don't you?"
"Yes!" the crowd roared.
The red curtain opened to reveal the box with its black curtains open.
"The only question is: Which group?"
"Cheerleaders!" someone called out.
"Baseball players!"
"Teachers!"
Amy smiled slowly as if that were the first time she'd considered this idea. "Ah, yes, teachers!" Amy turned to Brett. "Please find six brave volunteers."
Brett went into the audience and returned with the teachers. He escorted them to the box and helped them step inside.

"Wait! There are only five teachers!" Amy pretended to sigh with annoyance as she looked into the audience. "I need one more volunteer." She shielded her eyes from the light with her hand. "Aha! There's one!"
Mr. Harrington left his seat and hurried onstage. So far the act was going according to plan.
"If I disappear forever, my classes still have a test on Monday!" Mr. Harrington shouted.
Amy was annoyed by his ad-lib. "Should I make him disappear forever?" she asked the crowd.
"Yes!" they roared.
"You wouldn't do that to your favorite teacher," he said.
"Into the box!" Amy pointed her wand at Mr. Harrington, and the audience laughed at their banter.
"Teachers! Close the curtains!" Amy commanded.
Brett walked around the box to show that there was no way the teachers could secretly slip behind the stage curtains.

"Making people disappear is a time-honored tradition in the magic world," Amy said. "But where do they go when they vanish? Do they momentarily step into another dimension? Who knows? None of them ever recall where they've been." She waved her wand. "Abracadabra! Make these teachers disappear!"
She faced the audience as Brett dramatically pulled all the box's curtains open. "Ohh!" the audience cried.
Amy smiled and turned toward the box. The teachers had disappeared.
With the exception of Mr. Harrington. Amy looked at Brett in horror. That wasn't supposed to happen!
For a moment Amy stood frozen in the spotlight. Why hadn't Mr. Harrington disappeared? Her heart sank. What was she going to do now?
Finally she just shrugged. "Why is there always a teacher around when you don't want one?"
The audience burst into loud laughter, and Mr. Carlson returned to the stage. "Let's give a big hand for the Amazing Amy!" he said to the crowd. "Nice recovery," he said to her.
Brett reached up and helped Mr. Harrington down from the box. They joined Amy at the front of the stage, where the three of them bowed.
"It was so dark in there!" a flustered Mr. Harrington whispered to Amy. "I don't know what went wrong, but I didn't have time to escape."
"Don't worry about it. Just keep smiling."

Amy waved as they left the stage. But the audience was demanding a curtain call, so Amy, Brett, and Mr. Harrington held hands and came out for another bow. This time the five teachers who had disappeared ran into the auditorium from the main doors.
"Boo! The teachers are back!" someone yelled.
Amy grinned. "Yep. I didn't really make them disappear forever!"
The teachers joined her and the others onstage. Everyone in the audience leaped to their feet and began clapping wildly.
Brett squeezed Amy’s hand. "I told you that you’d be great!" She smiled and took another bow.

After the show Megan rushed to congratulate Amy outside the auditorium. "That was unbelievable! I saw the teachers go into the box, but I didn't see them get out. I'm thinking they must have exited from the back of the box, but how?"
Amy smiled mysteriously. "It was magic!"
"So you can't even tell your best friend?"
"Nope." Amy laughed.
"That was sensational!" a parent said as he passed by in the crowded hallway.
"Thanks!" Amy replied.
A little girl ran up to Amy with a scrap of paper and a pen. "Can I have your autograph? I want to be a girl magician too!"
Amy smiled and signed her name.

"Everybody is talking about you!" Megan held up her phone so Amy could see the screen. "You should ask Mr. Carlson if you can do another magic act for the whole school. That would make a great assembly!"

Amy shook her head. "I proved to everyone that I could pull off a big illusion and entertain an auditorium full of people. But I didn't really enjoy it. I don't like depending on an assistant or a group of volunteers. And I don't like waiting for somebody to build an illusion for me. I like—"
"Oh, I get it." Megan cut her off. "You want to be a star all by yourself."
"That's not it at all." Amy put down the duffel bag containing her hat and wand, and pulled out her phone. "Look at this."
Megan's eyes widened as she watched a kid doing an amazing series of card tricks. His hands were constantly in motion as he silently spun and flipped the cards, making them fly across the screen.
"How is that even possible?" Megan asked.
"I don't know, but that's what I want to find out. And that's something else I love about magic: Figuring out a trick is like doing a puzzle. It's the same thing I love about math."
"I'll never understand why you like math. But I can see the appeal of magic."

"Hey, you want to see some more magic? Next weekend Mr. Carlson has invited us all to participate in A Night of Magic at the park. He belongs to a magic club with Olga Lapinski. You remember her, the assistant?"
"Sure. I'll be there!" Megan nodded.

All week kids kept coming up to Amy at school and telling her how much they'd liked her performance at the carnival. Mr. Carlson mentioned A Night of Magic in his math classes, so by the time Friday came, he had a built-in audience for his show.

Wearing a dark suit, Mr. Carlson appeared in the park as Math Man the Magnificent. Amy planned to sit at a table and do card and coin tricks for a few people at a time. What she hadn't counted on was Megan's enthusiasm. Megan showed up with a bullhorn and acted as Amy's barker.
"Step right up! See the Amazing Amy! Straight from her sold-out performance at the middle school carnival!"

Amy enjoyed watching people's reactions as she made cards and coins disappear and reappear right before their eyes. She even performed the coin trick she'd done on Mr. Carlson's desk, this time using a saltshaker instead of a cup. Thanks to Megan, there was a line of people waiting to watch Amy all night. When the crowd finally thinned out, Amy looked up to see Brett coming toward her.
Megan giggled. "Here comes your boyfriend."
"We're just friends." Amy muttered. She ran her hand through her hair and then nervously shuffled the cards.
"Right. For somebody who's so smart, you can be totally clueless sometimes." Megan started to walk away.
"Wait, Meg—" Amy called out as her friend melted into the dark.
"Hey, Amy, how's it going?" Brett sat down at her table with his hand behind his back.
"Oh, okay, um …" She felt herself flush, suddenly feeling awkward around Brett.
"I want to show you a trick I've been practicing." Brett pulled a paper cone from behind his back. "There's nothing in the cone and nothing up my sleeve, of course."
Amy smiled. "Of course."
"Abracadabra!" Brett waved his hand over the cone and poured a handful of paper flowers onto the table. "For you!"
Amy laughed in delight. "That was awesome! You did the trick perfectly."
"Do you want to go to the movies sometime?" Brett blurted out.
Amy looked at him in surprise. "Sure. That would be nice."
"Great!" Brett stood up. "Okay then, see you at school on Monday."
Amy hummed happily to herself as she scooped up the paper flowers and put them in the duffel bag with her props. She was zipping up her bag when Megan returned.
"So, did I miss anything?" Megan was grinning.

"Actually, you did. Brett asked me to go to the movies. It was kind of out of the blue." Amy paused as she noticed a funny look on Megan's face. "Wait a minute. Did you have anything to do with that?"
"Maybe." Megan smiled mysteriously. "Or maybe it was magic!"
"Hey, Mr. D.!" Javier called out as he entered the school gym.

Most of the dance crew was already at hip-hop practice. Javier's best friend, Will, was plugging his phone into a speaker so they'd have some music. Marty was stretching to loosen up. Malcolm, the best dancer at Benjamin Franklin Middle School, was practicing a new move. And Mr. D'Alessandro, English teacher and the crew's adviser, was grading essays in the gym office.
Mr. D'Alessandro looked up and gave Javier a wave through the office window.
Javier dropped his backpack on the floor and walked over to Will. "Where's Ian?"
Will shrugged. "I texted him twice, but he didn't reply."
"So, are we waiting for him or what?" Javier asked as the other two boys joined them.
"I guess." Malcolm shrugged. "Let's battle while we wait."
"Great idea!" Marty said. He always followed Malcolm's lead—and not just when the crew was dancing.
Will groaned loudly. Javier knew it was because Malcom always won the battles.
"I challenge Javier," Malcolm said. "Will, have you downloaded that new song by Urban Independence? Play that, and I'll go first."
"Orders . . . always giving orders," Will muttered, searching for the music on his phone.
Javier smiled. "Chill out, Will. Maybe Malcom will show us a new move." Javier wasn't the best dancer, but he loved hip-hop and learning new moves.

Will rolled his eyes as Malcolm began to freestyle, making up a dance on the spot. Malcolm had all the moves, and he did everything with style. His fast-paced toprocking, a basic skill that hip-hop dancers performed upright, was perfect. Then he dropped to the floor for a flare.
"Whoa!" Javier said. "It's so hard to execute a flare. You need strong arms to do that!"
When Malcolm finished, it was Javier's turn. He moved crisply to the beat, but he simply couldn't compete with Malcolm's flashy moves.
Marty announced his vote for the winner of the battle. "Malcolm!"
Will let out a sigh. "Malcolm, as usual. I don't know why we even bother with battles."
"Because someday one of us will beat him!" Javier said. He was always the optimist.
"That'll never happen," Marty said.
"Never." Malcolm smiled. "Who's next?"
But before anyone could take up the challenge, Mr. D. emerged from the gym office. "How's it going, guys? Or should I say B-boys ? By the way, does anyone know the origins of that word?"
The B-boys shook their heads.

"Back in the 1970s, city kids started doing amazing dance moves during the instrumental parts—or breaks—of songs. That style became known as breakdancing, and the dancers were called B-boys." There was an awkward silence. "Well, have a good practice. I'm here if you need me." He turned and walked back into the office.
"And thus concludes today's educational moment," Malcolm joked under his breath. Marty laughed.
"Oh, Mr. D.'s not so bad," said Javier. "You know the rules. We need a teacher here for any after-school activity, and he's the only one who volunteered for dance crew."
"Whatever." Malcolm bent down to tie his shoe. "Who's ready to challenge me now?"
"Forget about the battle," Will said. "I don't think Ian will show up. Let's start practice. Everybody ready?" Without waiting for a reply, he cued up the music.
The boys took their places on the gym floor. As soon as they started dancing, things went wrong.
"Everybody stop!" Malcolm shouted.
"What's the matter?" Marty asked. "Are you okay?"
" I'm fine here in front. But without Ian, there are two of you behind me on one side and only one of you on my other side. We look stupid!"
Will stopped the music. "Maybe you shouldn't be out in front."
"Yeah! You could teach us that toprocking you were doing, and we could all do it together in a line," Javier suggested.

Malcolm looked at the three of them doubtfully for a second. Then he said, "Okay, watch me." He demonstrated the toprocking again. Will caught on right away, but Marty and Javier were still stumbling after several tries.
"Look, it's like this ," Malcolm said impatiently, starting all over again.

While Malcolm worked one-on-one with Marty, Javier pulled out his phone. After checking for texts, he looked at the website for Best American Talent . There was usually something interesting posted there—an interview with a performer, outtakes from last week's TV show. But this time Javier couldn't believe what he was seeing.
"Guess what! Best American Talent is coming to town, and they're holding open auditions! We have to try out!"
"Can anybody try out?" Will asked.
"Yes, that's what 'open auditions' means. All you have to do is show up."
Marty stopped dancing. "What's the grand prize?"
"One hundred thousand dollars! But even if we don't win, there's still a chance we could be on TV, once we make it out of the early rounds."
Malcolm snorted. "You losers won't win the grand prize. And forget about being on TV."
"We might not win," Javier said, "but I bet we could get on TV. You're really good, Malcolm, and so is Will, and if we practiced—"
"Look, I haven't said anything before," Malcolm interrupted. "But some of the guys from Octagonal have been trying to recruit me."
"Octagonal? Isn't that a high school crew?" Will asked.

"Yeah, but now that Best American Talent is holding auditions, I'll have a better shot at winning with them. In fact, they're practicing at the high school right now. I'll see you later." Malcolm grabbed his backpack and was gone before anyone could react.
"Well, that's the end of this crew." Will threw his hands up in disgust. "He was the best dancer we had."
But Javier saw the bright side. "Maybe it's not such a bad thing that he's leaving. Malcolm wasn't exactly a real team player, as they say in sports. We'll be fine, right, Marty?"
"Uh . . . uh . . ." Marty glanced at his phone. "Wow, it's late. I have to go."

"Okay, see you tomorrow," Javier said cheerfully. "Will, we might need some new music and choreography since there are only four of us. You got any ideas?" He started searching a playlist on his phone. "Something with a good beat."
"Did you notice that Marty didn't answer when you said we'd be fine?" Will asked.
Javier shrugged and started dancing across the gym. He was trying out some new steps and thinking hard about the audition.
"We'll be fine," he said again.

That night at home, Javier went back to the Best American Talent website. He wanted to learn more about the audition process. Stretched out on his bed, he watched a video called "All You Need to Know." It featured Alana Hendricks, one of the TV show's hosts.
"Contestants don't need to submit a video before the audition," Alana said. "The judges want to see your performance live."
"That's good. It gives us more time to practice," Javier said to himself. He opened a bag of pretzels and popped one into his mouth.

"As a contestant, you don't have to register in advance, but doing so will give you priority on audition day. So you'll only have to wait eight hours instead of twelve!" Alana said cheerfully. "And if you register in advance, the show will email daily tryout tips to you."

"Will won't like all that waiting. I'd better register our crew right now." Javier made note of the audition date before clicking on "Advance Registration." He was almost finished filling out the form when he spotted a notice: "At least one contact person must be 18 years of age or older. School groups must be registered by a teacher or coach."

"Ugh." Javier sighed. Everyone in his crew was 13. "I guess I can't finish this tonight. I'll have to get Mr. D. to help." He emailed Mr. D. the link to the Best American Talent site. He included the name of the crew and all the necessary details to fill out the registration form.

The next morning Javier checked his phone as soon as he woke up. He saw an email from Mr. D., saying that he'd already filled out the form. Javier couldn't wait to get to school and tell Will the good news.
"So, thanks to Mr. D., we're all signed up!" Javier said. Will was pulling books from his locker. "Now all we have to do is figure out some choreography that'll work for four people."
Will stood up and faced Javier. "And exactly who is going to do that? Have you ever noticed that Malcolm did most of our choreography?"
"Yes, and Malcolm also rejected any ideas that didn't showcase him. Now that he's gone, we can do whatever we want. You have to think positively here, Will. This is an opportunity."
"I don't know, Javier. What about—"
"Hey, guys!" Marty came running over. "Look, I hate to tell you this, but I'm quitting your hip-hop crew."
"What?" Will blinked in surprise.
"It's not our crew," Javier said. "It's yours too."

"Not anymore. You know how Malcolm was going to Octagonal's practice at the high school?" Marty spoke in a rush, as if he wanted to get this over with. "Well, it turns out a couple of guys had quit, so they asked him to join, and they still needed another guy, and he recommended me, so I went over to the high school after your practice and showed them what I could do." He paused for breath.
"But you can't quit!" Will protested. "That leaves us with only three dancers. Where's your loyalty?"
Before Marty could reply, the bell rang for homeroom. "See you around," he said over his shoulder as he hurried away.
Will slammed his locker shut. "So, Javier, exactly what kind of opportunity is this?"
"One that we can still do with three guys instead of five. You'll see. We'll be fine."
Will raised a skeptical eyebrow.
After school Javier met Will in the gym. Ian wasn't there yet, and neither was Mr. D. Unlike the day before, Will was not plugging his phone into a speaker.
"What's the point?" he muttered to Javier. "We're the only ones here."
"Where's Ian?" Javier dropped his things on the bleachers.
"Right here! Sorry I'm late!" Ian came running into the gym but didn't bother to remove his backpack or his jacket.
"Where were you yesterday?" Javier asked.
"My mom made me text her a photo of my latest math test. When she saw the big, red 46 percent on top, she made me come home right away. Then she took away my phone and said—"
"Did you hear that Malcolm and Marty quit?" Will interrupted him. "They've joined Octagonal!"

"Really? Wow!" Ian looked surprised. "Well, Malcolm is really good, but still . . . I'm surprised the high school guys would want them. Anyway . . ." He paused and took a deep breath. "This probably isn't the best time to tell you, but my mom is making me quit hip-hop."
"What?" Javier felt his jaw drop. "Why?"
"You can't do that to us!" Will said.
"My mom said I need to spend more time concentrating on my schoolwork. Listen, I have to go. She also said if I'm not home right after school, she'll take away my phone forever."
Will turned slowly to Javier. "So now what, Mr. Optimism? Looks like hip-hop crew is over."
"I don't know. I really don't know. Maybe we could—"

"Hello! I have some great news for you!" Mr. D. walked into the gym and motioned for them to follow him into the office. He dropped a pile of papers on the desk. "I'm sorry I'm late, but Ms. Cushman, the girls' basketball coach, stopped me. The team's new season starts soon. She was complaining about the low attendance at games—apparently very few people come to watch."
"Well, most games are right after school, and people do have other activities," Will said.
Javier heard the faint sound of a coach's whistle from another gym next door.
"It’s weird that not many people go to the games," Javier said. "Basketball can be really exciting to watch."

Mr. D. agreed. "That's exactly what I told her. I said she needs some sort of gimmick to draw a bigger crowd. Then I said I was sorry I couldn't help her right now, because I needed to be in the gym for you guys. And suddenly her eyes lit up. The next thing I knew, she was asking if you'd consider performing during halftime. I said sure! This will give you some great experience before the TV show audition." Mr. D. beamed at them, obviously pleased with himself. "I got you your first gig! What do you think of that, guys?"
Will groaned. "Well, it would be great if we still had a crew."
"What do you mean if you still had a crew?" Mr. D.'s smile faded.
"We had a small problem with guys dropping out," Javier said quickly. "But don't worry. Everything will be fine."

Javier was feeling a bit discouraged now that the dance crew was down to two guys. But he didn't want to admit that to Will or Mr. D. "Something good will happen," he thought as he arrived home from school. "Things always work out."
He checked his phone while he sat at the kitchen table, eating a snack of cold leftover chicken. There was an email from Best American Talent .
Today's Tryout Tip: Make your act original—no matter if you’re singing, dancing, drumming, or juggling things on fire! Don't copy what past winners have done. Be fresh and have fun!
"Right! Have fun!" Javier suddenly felt inspired to dance. "Maybe I can figure out those steps that Malcolm was trying to teach us yesterday."

Javier left his plate on the table and went upstairs, where he dropped his backpack in his room. Then he picked up his laptop and walked down the hall to his older sister Tessa's room. That was the only room in the house with a big mirror. He sat on Tessa's bed while he hunted online for toprocking videos. He was looking for moves similar to Malcolm's during the battle. After Javier watched a few videos, he put on his headphones and turned on some music. He was ready to dance!

Javier concentrated. He thought he was moving his arms the right way, but his feet kept getting tangled whenever he sped up. He could tell that his moves lacked the bounce of good toprocking. Javier sighed in frustration. Suddenly he heard laughter, and he caught Tessa's reflection in the mirror.
"What are you doing home?" He flushed with embarrassment and pulled off his headphones. "Shouldn't you be staying after school for some activity?"
"I should ask you the same questions," Tessa said. "Don't you have hip-hop practice today? And what are you doing in my room? Get your stuff off my bed right now!"
"Practice got canceled." Javier swept his computer off Tessa's bed and quickly smoothed the blanket where he'd been sitting. He needed to get out of there ASAP.
"What were you trying to do anyway? You looked like a chicken flapping its wings and scurrying around the barnyard."
"Oh, nothing."
"Tell me what you were doing, or I'll tell Mom you were in here."
Javier opened his computer and showed Tessa a video. "That. I was trying to do that, okay?"
Tessa studied the video for a few minutes and then stood in front of the mirror. "Oh, you mean something like this?" She flawlessly imitated the dancer on the first try.
"How did you do that?" Javier was stunned. He knew she'd had years of dance lessons, but he thought it was all ballet or tap.
"There are B-girls as well as B-boys, you know. I've done hip-hop before. Now do you want to learn how to do this or not? I'll break it down for you."
Slowly Javier learned each part of the step.
"Then you put it all together like this," Tessa said. "Come on, loosen up! Swing your hips a little more! Act like you know what you're doing! That's it! You've got it!"

Javier broke into a grin as he watched himself toprocking in the mirror. "Thanks, Tessa!" he said breathlessly. "This is the first good thing that's happened today. I mean, it would have been a good thing that Mr. D. got us a gig, performing at the girls' basketball games. But three guys quit, and we'd just signed up to audition for Best American Talent ! So we've only got two guys right now—Will and me—but everything will probably work out."

Tessa stared at him. "You're joking, right? Two guys don't make a hip-hop crew. You probably need at least four or five. I bet the show has regulations about the number of people for each kind of dance."
"It didn't say anything about that in the rules."
"Well, if you're serious about auditioning, you're going to have to do something besides think that everything will work out. You're going to have to take some action."
"It's so nice having an extra parent," Javier said in a sarcastic voice. But Tessa ignored him.

"Auditions are the fastest way to find the best dancers for your crew. Have you thought about the skills you're looking for? How will you score the dancers? Will you choose your crew after only one audition or will you have another round?"
"Uh . . . No . . . I hadn't thought about any of that."
"Well, you'd better think about it if you want to get on that TV show."
"At the beginning of the year, we just took whoever showed up for practice and wanted to dance. That worked out fine."
Tessa shook her head. "That'll never do now. You need to hold auditions. Let me show you how to make a score sheet. What qualities make the best hip-hop dancers?"
"Well, it's good if they can do some power moves like flares and headspins. But popping and locking and footwork are important too."
Tessa had grabbed his laptop and was typing notes. "From what I've seen, dancers need confidence and attitude. Yet they also need to be able to synchronize with the other dancers."
Javier named some more hip-hop moves. "And they need to do all this stuff to music!"
"Well, obviously," Tessa said.
Together the two of them came up with a list of eight traits that Javier should be looking for.
"So you rate each dancer on each of these skills, using a scale of one to five. Then total up the score, and you have a way to compare everyone who auditions."
Javier nodded.
"Just print this out, and you'll be all set," Tessa said. "By the way, how often do you guys practice?"
"Two days a week. But it's not like we compete against other schools or anything. We're just a bunch of guys who like to dance."

Tessa snorted. "You'll never get on Best American Talent until you start taking yourselves seriously. You need to practice four or five days a week. And you need to find a choreographer. It's way too much to do it all yourself. Now show me your pirouette."
"My what?"
"Your pirouette. No matter what kind of dance you're doing, it's good to know how to keep spinning without getting dizzy."
For the next ten minutes, Tessa made Javier spin and spin while she shouted instructions at him. Javier felt like his head was spinning—and not just from the pirouettes.

Javier and Will were in the gym, getting ready for their first audition day—the one at school. They knew what they were looking for in new dancers. They'd made copies of Tessa's score sheet, and they asked Mr. D. to help them evaluate dancers.
"Remember, you can't just choose your friends for dance crew," the teacher warned. He took a seat at the judging table.
"Okay, Mr. D.," Javier said cheerfully.
"I don't understand why he has to help us," Will complained as the boys walked toward the gym doors. "He doesn't know anything about hip-hop."
"That's true, but we have to be nice to him. We need him here—and at the Best American Talent audition."
"I know, but I still think . . ." Will opened a door and stopped. The hallway outside the gym was packed with guys. Some were dancing to music on their headphones; the rest were talking loudly.
"Whoa!" Javier shook his head in disbelief.
The two boys ran back to the judging table. "Mr. D., you should see all the guys out there!" Javier said. "Where did they come from?"
Mr. D. looked uncomfortable. "I might have mentioned Best American Talent to some of my classes."
"Mr. Deeeee!" Will groaned.
"Will, run into the office and make more copies of these." Mr. D. held out the score sheets. "Javier and I will get everybody organized."
By the time Will returned, all 32 guys had signed in and were ready to start the audition.
"There are too many dancers to evaluate at once," said Mr. D. "Break them into groups of eight, so we can get a good look at everybody."
"This will take forever!" Will moaned, but Javier was already dividing the crowd.
"Does everybody know how to kick step?" Javier asked the first group.
Most of the kids nodded, but a few shook their heads.
"All right, I'll show you. There are a couple of ways to do this—in place and traveling across the floor. Traveling is easier, so let's start with that."
Javier soon had everyone dancing across the gym floor. One tall kid kept bumping into the others.
"You in the middle." Mr. D. checked the names on his sheet. "Charlie, is it? Move to the end, so you don't bump into anyone."
Javier waited for Charlie to move. "Now let's try that faster this time with some upper body movements—like this—and some music."
Will started the music, and Javier demonstrated the step. "Come on, everybody!"
Charlie led the line of dancers across the gym, but he wasn't paying attention, and he crashed into the volleyball net. He fell to the floor with the netting draped around his shoulders.
"We should probably take that net down," said Mr. D. There was a break while two hip-hop hopefuls untangled Charlie. Then they helped Mr. D. put away the net.
"We're going to be here until midnight," Will said. "And I have no idea how to score these dancers. Charlie obviously scores low in the coordination category, but aside from that . . ."
"It's harder than I thought it would be, but we can do this," Javier said. "Why don't you take over demonstrating the steps? I'll help Mr. D. with the judging."

The afternoon wore on. One kid kept looking at his feet. Javier gave him a zero in the confidence and attitude category. Another dancer kept talking to his friend. Eventually the two of them stopped trying to keep up and sat on the bleachers. Javier rated them low on energy.
But then there were the kids who could really dance. One was amazing at freestyling and big moves like head spins and flares.
"He's even better than Malcolm!" Javier said excitedly.
When Will demonstrated some complicated choreography, one kid caught on right away. Another kid was really good at synchronizing his movements to the beat.
"I like him," said Mr. D., who'd been tapping his fingers to the music.
There were also kids who understood that they were all supposed to be moving as one unit. But by the end of the afternoon, there was still a big problem.
"We have some talented guys here." Will looked over the scores. "But nobody has all the skills we need."
"Maybe we should have another day of auditions?" Javier suggested. "We need the best guys to get on the show. What do you think, Mr. D.?"
"It's up to you two to decide."
Javier's phone buzzed. It was Today's Tryout Tip: A unifying look for your group makes a good impression on the judges.
Javier had no idea what their crew's look was, never mind if it was unified. But he was suddenly sure of one thing. "No more auditions. We need to decide today because we have a lot of work to do."
So Javier and Will chose three guys—Pablo, the freestyler with all the big moves; Christopher, whose footwork was amazing; and Harry, who paid close attention to the beat.
Tessa pounced on Javier as soon as he came upstairs. "How did it go? Did anybody show up to the audition?"
"Oh yeah, way too many guys."
Tessa followed him to his room. "Are you holding another audition?"

"No, it was pretty easy to find the best dancers." Javier tried to sound confident with Tessa. He didn't want to get into a discussion with her. Not now—when he was already overwhelmed by all this dance crew stuff. "Besides, we don't have time for more auditions," he added. " Best American Talent is coming to town in two months."
"That's no time at all!"
"We'll get lots of practice at basketball games."
Tessa looked skeptical. "When does basketball season start?"
"Two weeks."
"Two weeks?" Tessa squeaked. "Are you serious? Have you picked your music yet?"

"Well, sort of." Javier thought about the music they used to dance to—Malcolm's favorites. He hated Malcolm's taste in music. They should definitely throw everything out and start again, but that would require even more time.
"Do you know what you're going to wear?"
Javier wasn't sure. "Whatever we wear to school that day?"
"That's fine for the basketball games, but you'll need something special for the show. Masks are big in hip-hop right now."

"I'll keep that in mind." Javier shut the door and lay down on his bed. Music, clothes, choreography. There was too much to do. He'd never tell Tessa this, but he longed for the days when they were just a bunch of guys fooling around in the gym.
The next day at practice Javier didn't know where to start. Malcolm had always run the crew's practices.
"I guess we should talk about music first. We have to decide on that before we do any choreography, right?" Javier said as Will set up the speaker.
"Of course! And I've got some great suggestions." The enthusiasm on Will's face faded abruptly as he looked up. "Oh, no. What are they doing here?"
Javier turned to see Malcolm and Marty peering through the narrow windows on each side of the gym doors. "I'll go find out."
But by the time he reached the doors, the ex-members of the crew were gone. Javier spotted them at the end of the corridor, talking to Harry and Christopher.
"Time for practice!" Javier yelled to the new crew members.
"Your mother's calling. You'd better run," Malcolm said, which got a good laugh from Marty.
Harry and Christopher walked slowly down the corridor, as if to show Malcolm that they didn't need to hurry.
"What did Malcolm and Marty want?" Javier was worried that Malcolm was trying to lure away their new dancers.
"Not much." Christopher shrugged. "They were just trying to find out who joined the crew and what music we're using."
"It's none of their business!" Will snapped.
"We're experimenting with some new music right now," Javier said. "You ready, Will?"
Will tapped his phone, and the latest hit from his favorite group, Emerald Toast, filled the gym. All five guys started freestyling, each one making up his own dance.
"Turn off that music right this minute!" Mr. D. emerged from the gym office, his face red with anger. "You can't play that stuff at school! In fact, you shouldn't be listening to that at all."
Will quickly turned off the music. "What's wrong with it?"
"Have you actually listened to those lyrics? Do you hear what that guy is singing? You'll have to find something else to dance to around here."
"A lot of hip-hop music is like that," Christopher protested. "What are we supposed to use?"

"What about something by Happy Banter?" Mr. D. ran his hands through his hair. "Or something with no words? Just not that stuff you were playing. And don't pick something really popular. Give the judges a break. You don't want to be the fortieth crew dancing to Moldy Bread, or whatever that band's name is." He went back into the office, still shaking his head.
"Happy Banter? The boy band from the nineties?" Pablo said.
"Their lead singer must be as old as Mr. D.," Christopher said.
"Remember when he used to just sit in the office and not bother us?" Will said. "What are we going to do now, Javier?"
"I guess we'll have to find different music."
Harry, who hadn't said anything, nudged Javier and held out his phone.
"Hey, everybody, look at this!" Javier said. "It's that really cool hip-hop crew that won American Dance Off last year. And they're actually dancing to Happy Banter in this new video!"

As the guys gathered around, Javier noticed that all the dancers in the video were wearing masks. His crew could do that too. Javier felt a sudden wave of optimism. "Now we just need music," he told himself. "This is going to turn out fine!"

In the past Malcolm had simply chosen the music without any discussion among the crew. Now there were five strong opinions, and everyone's opinion counted. The crew finally picked an electronic piece without words and a Happy Banter song. Will edited the pieces together. The final cut was two minutes.

Javier started working out the choreography with some help from Tessa. Then the rest of the crew helped him iron it out. Over the next two weeks, the crew practiced almost every afternoon. They weren't perfect, but at least they had a new dance. And they even had a "unified look." They decided to wear jeans and plain black T-shirts along with gold masks that Christopher found online.
As the first girls' basketball game was about to start, Javier tried to pump up the crew. They were waiting with Mr. D. in the gym office. "Is everybody ready? We're going to kill this performance!"
"Yeah!" Christopher shouted.
"Shouldn't Pablo be here by now?" Will squinted at the wall clock.
"Don't worry. He'll be here." Javier handed out the masks. "Is the music ready?"
Will gave a quick nod, but he was clearly distracted. "I'm texting Pablo because he's never late. He's usually the first person at practice."
The game started with the Benjamin Franklin girls winning the ball. It was a close game, but the guys weren't paying attention to the score. They were just nervously waiting for halftime—and Pablo.

By now Will was pacing the office. "There are only three minutes left before we have to go out there, and Pablo's not answering his phone! What are we going to do, Mr. D.? Pablo's supposed to freestyle in the middle of the dance!"
"I'm sure you boys will think of something," Mr. D. said.
"Okay, don't panic," Javier said. "How about if we all take turns freestyling?"
"I don't know." Christopher hesitated. "I'm not the best freestyler . . ."
Harry stared out into the bleachers. He didn't have to say anything. It was clear he wasn't confident about his freestyling either.
"You'll both be fine," Javier said. "You only have to dance for a few seconds each. And if you run out of moves, well . . . Will can fill in. Right, Will?"
"I guess so. If I have to." Will didn't look happy.
The halftime buzzer sounded. As soon as the teams cleared the court, the crew's music started playing. The guys ran onto the floor and began to dance. The spectators cheered.
"Hey . . ." Javier thought. He suddenly realized that the right number of guys was dancing. But wait a minute . . . that freestyling guy wasn't Pablo.
Will danced over to Javier. "Who is that guy in the white T-shirt?"
"I have no idea, but he's not bad. He doesn't have any big moves, but his footwork is amazing!"
"His toprocking is better than yours!" Will said.
"Thanks!" Beneath his mask Javier made a face at his best friend. It was hard to watch the new "Pablo" and dance at the same time. But Javier tried.
At the end of the dance, the music stopped, and the guys pulled off their masks. Javier gasped. The mystery dancer was Mr. D.!
"Mr. D.! Mr. D.! Mr. D.!" the spectators chanted at the girls' basketball game. There weren't many people in the bleachers, but they were loud.
Mr. D. acknowledged his new fans with a wave while the hip-hop crew swarmed around him.
"Where did you learn to dance like that?" Javier still couldn't believe that their faculty adviser, who'd never shown much interest in dancing, had filled in for Pablo.
"Come on, guys, the second half of the game is about to start. Let's get off the court, and I'll explain."
Back in the gym office, the guys fired questions at the teacher.

"Whoa! One at a time!" Mr. D. held up his hands and laughed. "I believe the first question was about where I learned to dance. Well, I wasn't always an English teacher, you know. I was once a kid who—"
"No, that can't be true!" Will said in mock disbelief.
"And I used to do hip-hop."
"That's amazing," Christopher said.
Harry just nodded in agreement as Mr. D. continued talking about his longtime interest in hip-hop.
"But why didn't you tell us this before?" Javier asked.
"You guys needed to work things out on your own. But also, when I was 13, I wouldn't have wanted some teacher trying to be cool and telling me what to do."
"If Pablo doesn't come back, you'll have to join us," Javier joked.
"No, this was a onetime thing." Mr. D. handed his mask to Christopher.

At the next practice, Pablo showed up as usual. He'd missed the basketball game because his parents had grounded him that day. They'd also taken his phone, which explained why he couldn't answer Will's texts.

To Javier's surprise, Malcolm and Marty showed up for practice too. The two of them stayed outside the gym, though, peeking through the windows. Mr. D. finally covered the windows with brown paper, so they couldn't spy anymore.
"I don't know why they'd want to steal our choreography. We're nowhere near ready for Best American Talent ," Will complained. The boys were sitting on the floor, taking a break.
"Don't worry. We'll be fine for the audition." Javier took a long drink from his water bottle and wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. "We just need more practice."
"I'm not sure exactly what our problem is, but we've definitely got one," Christopher said.
Harry raised an eyebrow sharply.
Javier started to respond. "We'll be fine if we just—"
"No," Pablo interrupted firmly. "Will and Christopher are right. I have no idea what's wrong with our dance either. But we're not ready for that audition."

Javier suddenly realized that everybody was looking at him. "Why are you all staring at me? I was too busy dancing to even notice there was a problem. I don't know what to do . . ." He paused. "Unless . . . unless . . . what if we asked Mr. D. to help us?"
"Do you think he would?" Will mumbled.
"Go ask him, Javier! We'll wait here," Pablo said.
Javier rolled his eyes. "Why me? I just want to dance."
"Because you're good at talking to teachers," said Christopher.
Harry nudged Javier with his elbow.
"Okay, okay, I'm going!"
Ten minutes later Mr. D. was out on the gym floor, watching them dance. When they finished, he called them into a huddle.

"Well, I'm not sure where to begin . . ." Mr. D. ran his hands through his hair. "You've got some nice moves here, but you're not in sync. If everyone's moves are crisp and clean, the whole dance will look more harmonious. Turn on the music, Will." Mr. D. stepped away from the huddle and demonstrated a few steps. "Hit those beats precisely. Like this. All right, everybody, let's try that again."

Mr. D. made the crew run through the same moves again and again. By the end of the afternoon, they were tired of practicing. But Mr. D. was still full of energy. He seemed very enthusiastic about coaching!
Every afternoon, Mr. D. worked on a different aspect of their choreography. As it turned out, he knew a lot about hip-hop, and he had an eye for detail.
"Keep your spacing even!" he shouted at them one day.
"Don't you people ever count?" he roared in exasperation another day.

"We've created a monster," Will said to Javier at the end of that practice. It was right after Mr. D. had explained the importance of counting—with lots and lots of detail. "Mr. D. was right. No one wants a teacher telling them how to dance."
"Why did he say we should remember that we're dancing , not just doing tricks?" Pablo said. "He was picking on me for no good reason."
"Maybe we'd be better off without him," Christopher said. "What do you think?"
Nobody said anything for a moment.

"I think he's trying to show us that everything—down to the smallest gesture—has to be perfect." Javier looked directly at Pablo. "The big moves are really important. But so is everything else. And everybody on this crew has an important role to play."
Harry nodded quickly.
"We can take a vote, but I think we're getting better with Mr. D.," Javier said.
The guys decided to keep their coach.

As the weeks passed, the crew's dancing continued to improve under Mr. D.'s guidance. The crowd coming to the girls' basketball games kept growing, and it wasn't just because the team was winning. Word was getting around that the hip-hop crew was fun to watch. Everyone also knew that they were auditioning for Best American Talent .
On the day before the big audition, the crew practiced as usual. It was an extra-long practice, but Mr. D. wasn't finished yet.

"I've managed to find some video clips about what it's like when the show comes to town," said Mr. D. He'd hooked up a computer, so he could project the videos onto a screen in the gym. "You'll see interviews with performers and samples of the acts. There are even segments with the judges discussing the acts. You'll get a real sense of what the audition will be like tomorrow."
The five boys watched the videos in silence. At the end Mr. D. flipped on the lights. "So, what do you think? Are you ready for tomorrow?" He sounded excited.

Javier was almost always optimistic. But today no encouraging words came out of his mouth. He couldn't even speak. The rest of the crew sat there, looking just as stunned as he felt. They all knew it—tomorrow was going to be a disaster.
"What's wrong with you?" Tessa gave Javier a critical look as he slipped into the front seat of the car after practice.
"Nothing. Just drive me home." Javier was still thinking about the talent show videos. He didn't want to talk about how intimidating they were, but Tessa was persistent.

"Are you sure nothing's wrong?" Tessa drove away from the school. "You look like you've seen . . . oh, I don't know . . . a ghost or something. And you're really late tonight. I was getting tired of waiting for you. Did something bad happen at practice?"
Javier sighed. "The audition is tomorrow, and basically we're doomed," he blurted out. "Mr. D. freaked everybody out with some old videos of past auditions."
Tessa shot him a look. "What was he thinking? He waited until the day before the audition to show videos?"
"Yeah, we watched them right after our practice, which ran extra long."

Tessa shook her head in disbelief. "You should have been resting! You should have been breathing deeply and thinking calm, positive thoughts! Mr. D. should have been inspiring you, not scaring you! Do you want me to say something to him? I could email him tonight or . . ." She paused. "Or I could even come to your audition tomorrow!"

"No, no, that's okay! I'll take care of things." Javier was horrified at the idea of an angry Tessa trying to help. That wouldn't go well at all. He needed to think of something right now to keep her from interfering. "I'll text my crew and tell them to show up early tomorrow."
"For breathing and relaxation exercises." Tessa looked pleased with herself.
"Right!" Javier said as he texted his crew: ". . . show up early to warm up."

The next morning Javier arrived at school at seven. Nobody else was there, and it was cold waiting outside the locked building. He had a plan to motivate the crew, but he needed everyone to show up before Mr. D.
Will was the last to arrive. "Are we warming up outside?"

Javier shook his head. "I'm only jumping up and down because I'm cold." He took a deep breath. "Listen, the real reason I wanted everybody here early is because we need to talk. Mr. D. was trying to help us with those videos, but—"
"They made me want to quit!" Will said. "We can't compete with crews like that!"
Javier almost smiled—so far his plan was working perfectly. But he made himself nod gravely at Will. "Exactly. That's why we should quit."
"We can't quit!" Pablo said. "We've put in so much time and effort!"
"I've already told everyone that we're auditioning!" Christopher added.
Harry nodded vigorously.
"Hmm." Javier pretended to think. "Maybe we just need a new attitude. When we each started dancing, we were doing it for fun. We're still having fun, right?"
"Of course we're having fun," Pablo said. "We get to practice our favorite hip-hop moves every day."
"While hanging out with our friends," Will said.
"So let's just keep having fun," Javier said. "That was even a Tryout Tip from Best American Talent . And come on, guys, we're on our way to audition for a TV show! That has to be fun."
The guys high-fived just as Mr. D. pulled up in a van. "Talent show express to success!" he announced cheerfully. No one said anything about quitting as they piled in.
"Oof, I don't feel so good." Christopher sat down next to Javier. "My stomach—"
"Me too! It's probably just nerves." Javier was feeling super optimistic again. He'd even given himself a boost with his secret plan—that inspiring talk!
"Wow! There are tons of people here!" Pablo said as the crew entered the lobby of the convention center. "Look at those lines!"
"It's a good thing Javier registered your crew in advance," Mr. D. said.
Javier steered the crew to the advance check-in line. "This line is shorter, but not by much."
"What's that?" Will pointed to a grayish animal being led by twins.
"A big goat? A llama?" Javier shrugged. "I wonder what its talent is."
"We probably don't have to worry that it's on a hip-hop crew," Will said.

Javier laughed. It was fun to people-watch in this crowd. They saw a woman whose hair was as pink as her costume, and a man carrying a marionette that was bigger than he was. Everyone seemed to be covered in sequins and feathers.
"We're going to stand out by being boring," Will said.
"Uh-huh." Javier wasn't really listening. He was watching a member of the talent show staff walk around with a cameraperson.

She was interviewing contestants. Javier wished they could get on TV. But the woman was only talking to people with strange costumes or props. She talked for a long time to the twins with the grayish animal.
"Hey, what name did you use for our registration?" Will asked as the line inched forward.
"Benjamin Franklin Middle School Hip-Hop Crew," Javier said.
The other four boys groaned.
"Really? That was the best you could do?" Pablo said.
"How about B-Frank because we're the B-boys from Ben Franklin?" Harry blurted out.
"You talked!" Will said.
Harry turned bright red and looked at his shoes. "I had something important to say."
"Can I be frank with you?" Mr. D. joked. "I love that name! So many layers of meaning!"
"Sometimes it's almost too easy to tell he's an English teacher," Will whispered to Javier.
"It's the perfect name." Javier gave Harry a thumbs-up, and Harry grinned.
The guys were still talking and joking around when they finally reached the check-in table.

"You're assigned to Holding Room C." The woman behind the table handed an envelope to Javier. "Wait there until your audition number is called. And don't lose your wristbands. Those are for identification."
"Well, that line only took us an hour," Will said. "Let's go find our room."
Holding Room C was a lot bigger than Javier had imagined. Tables lined one wall. Above each table hung a mirror surrounded by lights.
"Makeup mirrors," Mr. D. said with a nod.
"Uh, we don't wear makeup," Javier said.
"Then we can just sit down," Mr. D. said.
The rest of the room was filled with chairs, and most of those chairs were filled with people. The room was hot and crowded.
"Oh, now I really don't feel good." Christopher had turned a strange pale color.
"You'll be fine as soon as you sit down," Javier said in an encouraging voice.
But it was too late. Before anyone could get out of the way, Christopher threw up.

"You can't go home now!" Javier pleaded with Christopher. They were in the restroom at the convention center. Christopher had run there after throwing up. "If you leave, and our crew moves on to the next round, you won't be allowed to participate. It's in the Best American Talent rules."
Christopher was too sick to care. "We aren't going to move on," he said weakly. "Did you see the other crews? The dancers all looked like high school kids. Everyone is older than we are."
Javier had to admit that B-Frank was probably the youngest hip-hop crew at the audition. Still, he tried not to feel discouraged, even though it was obvious that Christopher would soon be leaving.
After Christopher's father picked him up, Javier returned to Holding Room C.
"I can't believe our bad luck!" Will moaned.
"We're down to four dancers," Pablo said. "Now what?"
"It's a shame you wasted all that time for this," Mr. D. said.
But Javier was more determined than ever. "What if we did what we did before—have Mr. D. fill in?"
Will was doubtful. "Our audition choreography is much harder than what we did at that first basketball game."
Mr. D. shook his head. "I'm not sure I can do all the steps."
"Maybe you were right this morning—we should quit," Pablo said to Javier.
"No! I only said that to motivate everyone to keep going," Javier said firmly. "I didn't really believe it. Everybody sit down. We're not leaving!"

The guys sat in a circle on the floor. Meanwhile other contestants were going off to their auditions and then returning to the holding room. Some looked relieved; one or two came back in tears. Javier noticed that there were a lot of dancers among the acts: Irish dancers, tap dancers, flamenco dancers, ballroom dancers.
"Maybe the judges will be sick of dancers." Javier's voice was suddenly full of doubt. "They'll be bored by the time we compete."
"Even if we did use Mr. D., the judges would notice right away that he's old," Will said.
Harry elbowed Will and nodded in Mr. D.'s direction.
"I mean, older than we are," Will said.

"That's it!" Javier slapped Will on the back. "Instead of trying to make Mr. D. a perfect substitute for Christopher, we can take advantage of his age. We'd need to rework the sections of the dance that Mr. D. can't do. But we have plenty of time . . ." Javier gestured around the room. "Because we still have hours to wait."
All at once everybody started contributing ideas and trying out moves. At one point Will looked up and noticed that Octagonal was in the same room. Malcolm and Marty were watching them closely.
"Ignore those guys and concentrate!" Javier said. "We've got work to do."
At last it was time for B-Frank to go onstage. "You've got this!" said Mr. D. "I'll be out there with you in a minute."
"Actually, your entrance is at 38 seconds," Javier reminded him. "Don't be late!"

The dance began as it always had, with some big moves from Pablo. Then the other guys emerged from the shadows and started to dance. At exactly 38 seconds, Mr. D. walked onstage and pretended to watch. He tapped his foot in time to the music. Then he moved his upper body from side to side. When the guys spun around, so did he. Clearly, this was a man who was dying to dance.

Suddenly all four young guys raised their right arms and beckoned to Mr. D. to join them. With three quick steps, he was in the center of the line of b-boys, popping and locking. Javier noticed that the crew wasn't quite together. But it didn't matter because the crowd was going wild, cheering and clapping. And Javier was doing what he'd always done with hip-hop: he was having fun.
When the music came to an end, the crew froze in place. The audience stood and applauded.
Javier glanced at the judges, who wore large name tags with numbers.
"You were amazing!" Judge number one said.
"I love how your dance tells a story," Judge number two said. "The older gentleman used to be a dancer, and he longs to recapture his youth. Am I getting this right?"

"Sure." Javier laughed into the microphone. This was like English class when Mr. D. interpreted a poem in a way he'd never thought of. "Actually Mr. D., I mean Mr. D'Alessandro, only joined us because one of our dancers got sick this morning."

"He's only been part of your team since this morning?" Judge number three raised her eyebrows. "You aren't the best dancers we've seen today, but you certainly solved your problem in an original way."
Mr. D. leaned into the mic and pointed to Javier. "You have to credit this guy for that. He really kept this crew together."
"I think we know how this is going to end, panel, but are you ready to vote?" asked Judge number one.
The judges pressed their buzzers. B-Frank was moving on to the next round of auditions! They were being held next month in New York City!
"Alana, make sure you get these guys on camera!" Judge number one called to the show host who'd been interviewing contestants. "America will want to hear their story."
"We're going to be on TV! We're going to New York!" All the guys were jumping up and down—including Mr. D.
Later that afternoon, after they'd finished their interview, the crew went back to Holding Room C to pick up their things. Malcolm and Marty came over to offer some half-hearted congratulations.
"You guys were pretty good," Malcolm said.
"Yeah, pretty good," Marty echoed.

"But with the right coach, you could improve," Malcolm continued. "I've got some time on my hands since Octagonal didn't make the cut. I'm willing to quit that crew to coach yours. Marty can be your captain."
Javier shook his head. "Thanks, but no thanks. We've been through a lot together, so we're a really tight crew now. Besides, we already have Mr. D. as our coach."
"And Javier is our captain," Will said.
Javier looked at his friend in surprise. "What are you talking about?"
"Oh, didn't we tell you? We elected you captain while you were in the restroom cleaning up Christopher."
Javier grinned and held up a hand to share high fives with his crew. With a lot of hard work, everything had turned out fine in the end. Just as he'd always predicted.

Jackie tried not to worry as her black Labrador retriever, Poke, walked beside her into the show ring. The ring was a square grassy area surrounded by a low fence. Poke loved performing in dog shows, but he had a mischievous streak. And right now his eyes were sparkling with a familiar look. It said, "Watch this!"
"Stay," Jackie told Poke as they reached their spot in the ring.

Poke froze like a statue, but Jackie did not take her attention away from him. The seven other handlers entered the ring with their dogs. They lined up according to the size of their dogs, from biggest to smallest. A girl named Priscilla entered last with a small dog named Fluffy.
Jackie lightly touched Poke's chin. He lifted his head slightly, not moving the rest of his body. Only his eyes danced. Poke loved to show off as much as Jackie loved showing him.
"Please take your dogs around," the judge said.

"Go," Jackie said to Poke. The two of them led the way, trotting in a circle with the other dogs and handlers following. Spectators sat in folding chairs around the ring, including Jackie's friends and her grandmother. Grandma was the one who'd taught Jackie how to show dogs.
"You've got this!" Jackie's friend Hudson called.

Jackie kept her eyes on Poke. "I hope Hudson is right," she thought. All year she had watched her friends move up from the novice class for beginners to the open class for more experienced handlers. Jackie had felt left behind. But if she won this show, she could move up too!
Once the dogs were lined up again, the judge turned to Jackie. "Bring him up," she said.
"Please be good, Poke," Jackie muttered as Poke heeled at her side.
"Take him around the ring," the judge said.
"Go." Jackie broke into a run on the right side of the dog, holding the leash. Poke trotted slightly ahead of her around the ring. Jackie kept a steady pace to show off Poke's best gait.
"Up and back," the judge said.
Jackie and Poke trotted to the far side of the ring and back.
Next, Jackie stacked the dog. This meant putting Poke in the best standing position to show him off. She touched the dog's elbow so he'd move his front feet slightly forward, stretching out his body.

The judge walked around Poke, her expression serious. Jackie knew exactly what the judge was looking for. The American Kennel Club had a breed standard for every breed of dog. These standards defined the best traits of each breed. Poke was a champion—that meant he came close to what the AKC considered a perfect Labrador retriever.

At this show, however, Poke wasn't being judged. Jackie was. This show was for junior handlers, a competition for kids learning to show dogs. Junior handler shows judged the handler's knowledge of her breed and the rules and etiquette of the ring.
The judge knelt in front of Poke. She studied his broad head. She pulled back Poke's lips to look at his teeth.
The tip of Poke's tail quivered.
"Stand still," Jackie whispered.
Poke's tail stopped moving.
"Perfect," Jackie thought. She felt a thrill. Their turn was almost over, and she hadn't made a single mistake!
Then it happened. Jackie felt a slight movement on the leash . . . and Poke leaned forward and slathered the judge's face with his tongue!
"Oh no!" Jackie thought, but she stayed calm. She gave a gentle tug on the leash to bring Poke back into position. Poke obeyed, his mouth open in a big grin.
"He's certainly friendly." The judge wiped her face with a tissue.
Jackie nodded with a polite smile. She could feel that her own face was still beet red as she walked Poke toward the back of the line.
"Tough break," Priscilla whispered.
Jackie couldn't meet her eyes. She felt humiliated. The secret to handling a dog was staying in control so the dog would look its best. And she had just lost control of Poke.
Poke nudged her leg with his nose.
"You're not expecting a treat after that stunt, are you?" Jackie muttered.

Keeping a firm hold on Poke, Jackie watched as the rest of the handlers went before the judge. This was a novice class, so half the kids didn't know what they were doing. A boy with a basset hound did okay, but he handled the dog too roughly.

Jackie felt a trickle of hope. She needed a first-place finish today. But that depended on the other kids' performances. "We still have a chance, Poke," she muttered as Priscilla walked Fluffy to the judge.
Priscilla was good. Jackie didn't see her make any mistakes—but Jackie didn't know anything about showing smaller dogs.
The judge gave out the lower-place ribbons, and then walked toward Jackie and Priscilla, holding ribbons for first and second place. Jackie held her breath.

"Nice job," the judge said, handing Jackie second place. "Your dog displays just the right temperament for the breed. He's friendly and willing to please. But you have to make sure he doesn't get the last word. He took control for a moment there."
Jackie's heart plummeted, but she managed to hide her disappointment. "Thank you," she said, accepting the ribbon.
The judge handed Priscilla the rose ribbon for first place.
"Congratulations," Jackie said.
"Thanks!" Priscilla was beaming. "It's my second win!"
Jackie slowly walked Poke out of the ring.
"You'll make it next time," Grandma said, giving her a hug. Grandma rubbed Poke's head. "I think Poke pulled that stunt because he knew it was his last show."
"Last show?" Jackie felt the blood drain from her face. "What are you talking about, Grandma?"
"Most show dogs are younger than five," Grandma said. "Poke's older, so I'm going to retire him."
Tears filled Jackie's eyes as she hugged the big dog. She couldn't believe what she was hearing. "Why didn't you tell me, Grandma? I can't be in junior handlers without Poke!"
Grandma patted Jackie's shoulder. "I didn't want to make you nervous or upset before today's event. And a skilled handler can show more than one dog—and more than one breed. You'll be fine."

Jackie just shook her head. She knew what Grandma was saying was true. Plenty of kids changed dogs or worked with more than one. But Jackie had already been worried about advancing to open class. Now she was going to have to do it with a new dog!
"Hi, guys!" Jackie said, getting out of her dad's car a few days later.

Grandma had dozens of animals on her farm, and right now, most of her dogs wanted Jackie's attention. Poke reached the car first. Jackie scratched behind his ears. Next Esmerelda, a sleek Afghan hound, pushed forward for petting. Then Romper, a rat terrier, circled the car. The dogs wiggled and wagged, but none of them jumped on her. Grandma was strict about her dogs' behavior offstage as well as onstage. Jackie patted heads and stroked ears.
Her dad stood there, watching the scene with a grin. "Looks like you have a fan club, Jackie."
"Actually, I'm their fan," Jackie replied. "I love being around Grandma's dogs."
"Huh." Dad cocked his head, pretending to look surprised. "Is that so?" He gave her a quick kiss. "Have a good weekend, honey."
"You too. I'll see you on Sunday night."

Jackie's parents owned a busy Italian restaurant. They both worked long hours on weekends, so Jackie spent most weekends at the farm with her grandmother. The arrangement helped Grandma, and it gave Jackie a chance to be with the animals she loved.
Dad started the car, leaning out the window. "You sure you don't want to wash dishes at the restaurant this weekend?" He winked. "Your brother is helping out again. And we pay a fair wage."
Jackie laughed. "Thanks but I'd rather scoop poop. Especially since Grandma has a litter of adorable puppies right now!"

Jackie waved good-bye to her father, and then hurried toward the neat white house with red shutters. The rocking chairs on the wide front porch were empty. That meant Grandma was at the kennels, working with the dogs. As Jackie walked past the house, she breathed deeply, sniffing the fresh autumn air. The leaves of the giant oaks were turning red and gold. Soon the dogs would have their thick winter coats for her to brush.

Jackie headed toward the kennels with the pack trotting after her. A peacock screeched. Kitty Cat bounded up a tree and hissed at the dogs. The dogs dropped low to the ground, showing the old orange tabby that they were no threat at all.
Jackie stopped and looked up at the cat with a laugh. "There's no doubt who's boss around here!"
Poke bumped her leg, reminding her of where her attention should be. "I'll play with you later," she said. "I've got to see how much the pups have grown first."
The litter of five Labrador puppies was almost six weeks old. In just two more weeks, their new owners would pick them up.
As Jackie rounded the barn, she saw Grandma in the practice ring with one of the new pups. "Hi, Grandma!"
Grandma gave a quick wave in return. She was watching the puppy bounce around the ring.
"She's so cute!" Jackie whispered to Poke. "It's hard to remember when you were that little."
Poke entered the ring and gently nosed the puppy. The pup tumbled over and then scrambled to her feet, ready to attack Poke's ears.
Grandma laughed, picked up the puppy, and joined Jackie. "This little one has real potential," she said. "I had planned to sell all the puppies, but this one is hard for me to resist."
"I guess that means you're keeping her," Jackie said.
"Yep."
"Good," Jackie said. Grandma had a talent for choosing champion pups. Since Jackie wanted her own champion someday, she studied this pup more closely. "Can I hold her?"

"Sure." Grandma handed her the puppy. Jackie nuzzled her soft nose and then held the pup away from herself to get a better look. She had a hard time picturing an adult dog; all she could see was a pudgy snout, oversize feet, and a round belly.
"Her color is good," said Jackie. "Pure black. What else should I look at?"
"The shape of her head," suggested Grandma.
"Ears set back, good strong brow, brown eyes." Jackie recited the breed standards for Labradors.
"Exactly!" Grandma smiled. "So I think she's a keeper."
Jackie cuddled the puppy. "Let's call her Shadow."
"I like it," said Grandma. She turned to Poke. "What do you think of your daughter, Poke?"
"Whuff!" Poke replied.
Jackie's eyes glowed. "I can't wait to have another Labrador to train!"

Grandma paused. "We can get started with her soon," she said carefully. "But she won't be ready to show until next year. You need a dog right now if you want to compete in the junior handlers show next month."
"Right . . ." Jackie sighed and put the puppy back in the pen. "I want to move up to the open class."

"I've got several other dogs you can choose from for the next show," Grandma said. "One month should give you plenty of time to review the standards for a new breed. How about Esmerelda? She's been showing well—I think she may make champion next year."

Esmerelda was the three-year-old Afghan hound that had met Jackie at the car. She was a sweet dog and well trained, but Jackie wasn't crazy about the idea of showing a long-haired dog. She thought about Fluffy, the little dog that Priscilla showed. It probably took hours of washing, blow-drying, and brushing to get that dog ready to show. That didn't seem like much fun.
"Maybe," Jackie said as she considered her options. Besides Esmerelda, Grandma had the little rat terrier, Romper; two border collies; and a beagle.
Kitty Cat had climbed onto a beam above the puppies. Now she was looking at them and yawning as they yelped at her.
Jackie grinned. Kitty Cat wasn't impressed by dogs—or puppies.
"You should decide by the end of this weekend," Grandma said. "It's going to take a while to get used to working with a new dog."
"No problem. I'll think about it while I do chores." Today was bath day. Jackie called to Poke. "You can have the first bath today, buddy."
Poke grinned and wagged his thick tail. When Jackie opened the door to the bathhouse, Poke pushed ahead and jumped into the tub.
Jackie laughed. "You're eager today!"
"Whuff!"

Jackie turned on the spray nozzle and adjusted the temperature. But before she wet down the dog's thick black coat, she gave Poke a tight hug. "I'm going to miss showing you, Poke. You are absolutely the best dog ever."
Poke gave her a mournful look. Jackie knew exactly what he was saying: "I'll miss you too."

After lunch on Saturday, Jackie rolled her bike from Grandma's garage. She called Poke, and he ran alongside her as she biked to Hudson's house. Hudson's family lived less than a mile away in a log cabin tucked among some cedar trees. He'd asked Jackie to bring Poke over this afternoon. Poke was going to help with some dog training.

Jackie found her friend in the obstacle course behind the house. Hudson had built the course himself from old boards and other items he had found around the property. It was a crazy collection of bars, planks, tables, and tunnels. Hudson waved to Jackie and then turned back to his dog, Bart. He was running the beagle through the course.
"Sit," Jackie whispered to Poke, and together they watched the training session.

Hudson motioned at Bart to keep him moving through the course. When Bart tried to skip a tunnel, Hudson immediately stopped him. He showed the tunnel to the dog, and this time Bart followed the course properly.
"Good boy!" Hudson said as the dog leaped onto an end table and gobbled the treat Hudson held out.
"Yip! Yip!" Bart barked.
"Whuff." Poke looked at Jackie. She pulled a treat from her pocket. "Good boy. You sat quietly."
"Thanks for bringing Poke over," Hudson said. "Bart loves his buddy, Poke, but he needs to learn to ignore him when he is working."
"No problem," said Jackie. "It looks like you're doing a great job with Bart." She scratched the beagle's ears. "He seems really smart."
"He is. He still goes around some of the jumps," said Hudson, "but he's learning. He's just a little over a year old and already knows all the commands."

Hudson had shown his family's beagles in junior handlers events for years, but Bart was the first dog he had trained for agility competition. In agility, Hudson was going to compete against handlers of all ages. Jackie knew it would be challenging.
Hudson and Jackie let the two dogs play together for a few minutes. Bart ran circles around the bigger dog, bowing low and barking happily.
Hudson grinned. "They have different personalities, don't they?"

Jackie nodded. "I guess that's because Bart is younger than Poke. Plus, they were bred for different jobs. Labradors are supposed to retrieve ducks, and beagles are supposed to chase rabbits. Different jobs for different dogs."
The dogs stopped playing and lay there, panting. Then they took off together again.
"Speaking of different breeds," said Jackie, "I've got a little problem." She explained about Poke's retirement. "Grandma wants me to show Esmerelda, but I don't know . . ."
