Hudson raised his eyebrows. "All that blow-drying and brushing?"
Jackie laughed. "Exactly! I don't even like to comb my own hair!"
"Obviously," Hudson joked.

Jackie grinned. She was used to her friends teasing her about her messy hair. Then she elbowed Hudson in the side. "But seriously, I have a problem. The next junior handlers show is only a month away."

Jackie's throat tightened as she thought about her second-place ribbon from last week. Her friends had been kind and encouraging—after they had finished making jokes about Poke giving the judge a bath. But Jackie still felt like a failure. It was as if everybody could ride a real bike while she still had training wheels.
She swallowed hard. "I need a first-place win to make it to open class. But I don't have a dog."
Bart came running over, his body wiggling madly. Poke ambled behind the smaller dog and then plopped down beside Jackie.
"Didn't your grandma buy one of Bart's littermates?" Hudson asked.
"Yes. Grandma hasn't shown Howler yet, but she's been working with him a lot."
"Bart's doing his first junior handlers show next month. We'd both have beagles at the event. That would be fun."
Jackie stared at the little beagle chasing a leaf as it blew across the grass. "I don't know. I've never shown a small dog."
Hudson shrugged. "It's no big deal. You'll be competing in the novice class, so you won't compete against me. I compete in the open class."
Jackie raised her eyebrows. "Do you think I'm scared of competing against you?"
"Nope!" Hudson said quickly. "I didn't say that."
Jackie watched him out of the corner of her eye. He hadn't said it, but did he think it? After all, she was still stuck in novice class.
"I think it would be fun," Hudson repeated. "We could train the beagles together sometimes."
Jackie was still unsure. "I've always worked with Labradors. I'd be working with a totally different type of dog."
"You don't have a Labrador to show right now," Hudson said. "So you're definitely going to have to learn about a new breed. Why not beagles?"
Bart pounced on Poke's tail. The big dog lifted his head and then rolled over.
"The whole idea of junior handlers is to learn about showing dogs," Hudson went on. "You're not expected to be an expert. That's what novice class is for—being a beginner."
"But beagles—"
"Are fun," Hudson said firmly. "Plus, I'll help you. The secret to beagles is learning their personality."

"Hmm . . ." Jackie looked at her dog. "What do you think, Poke?" He rested his head on her leg. "I agree," she said with a laugh. "Nothing is better than a Labrador. I wish Shadow was older—she's one of Grandma's new Lab puppies."

"Well, keep thinking about beagles," Hudson said. He got up and took Bart back to the obstacle course. The little dog stood at the starting line, his gaze fixed on Hudson. He was obviously eager to please his master.
"I've got a whole month to practice," Jackie thought. "And I really want to enter the November show." Maybe Howler wasn't a bad choice.

Back at the obstacle course, Bart ran fast, panting all the way. At the end he stuck his nose in the air and howled. Hudson rubbed his head and gave him a treat. The little dog immediately bounded back to the starting line and looked at Hudson. He was ready to run the course again.
"Whoa," Jackie thought. "He's got so much energy!"
She sighed. Working with a beagle seemed very different from working with a Labrador retriever. If she did choose to work with Howler, Hudson had better keep his promise about helping her.
On Sunday, Grandma set two plates of eggs on the table as Jackie finished buttering toast. While they ate breakfast, Grandma went over the chores for the day.

"I'll wash down the kennels this afternoon," Jackie offered. She would rather be in the sunshine exercising dogs than hosing down the concrete floor in rubber boots. But she didn't want to stick Grandma with the worst job on the list.
Grandma nodded her appreciation. "Have you decided which dog to show next month?"
"Well . . ." Jackie put down her fork. "Hudson gave me an idea yesterday. Are you entering Howler in any shows?"
Grandma paused, her coffee cup cradled in her hands. "Howler's ready to go to a show. But I haven't signed him up for anything. Why are you asking?"
"Hudson thinks I should work with Howler. Hudson really likes beagles, and he's taking his beagle to the show. He's even been training him for agility."
Grandma set her cup down, looking interested. "Beagles aren't usually trained for agility." She smiled. "They get distracted when their noses override their brains."
"Bart is fantastic!" Jackie told Grandma about the beagle's practice the day before. "He's smart and he loves running the agility course."
"Howler's smart too, but he's a total beginner," Grandma said. "Are you sure you want to show him next month? Esmerelda is a pro. She practically shows herself."
Jackie nodded slowly. "I think I'd rather show a short-haired dog. There's less grooming involved."
Grandma smiled. "People often pick dogs that match their personality."
Jackie self-consciously pushed her hair from her face. She had remembered to brush it before breakfast—hadn't she?
"No matter which dog I choose," Jackie went on, "I'll have to learn about a new breed. Beagles and Afghan hounds are both very different from Labradors."
"Why don't you spend some time with Howler today and see how it goes," Grandma suggested. "You can decide after that."
"I'll unload your pickup truck first," Jackie said.

A short while later, Jackie slipped on a light jacket and went to the kennels. She unloaded the heavy dog food sacks from the truck, and then got the pooper-scooper and cleaned the yard. Back inside the kennels, she stopped at the new puppies' pen. They were snuggled in a ball against their mother.
"Aren't they cute, Poke?"
"Whoof!"
"I sure wish they were big enough to show."
Poke whined, ready to play.
"I don't have time to play yet," she said, stroking his head. "I need to see a dog about a show." She opened the gate. "Go out in the yard for a bit."
Poke looked confused as Jackie shut the gate behind her, but he ran off toward the house.

Jackie started letting dogs out into their exercise yards. They didn't have free run of the farm like Poke, but they all had lots of space to run. When Jackie got to Howler's kennel, he eagerly pawed the gate. He was a tricolor beagle, with a black, tan, and white coat and big dark eyes.
"Morning, Howler," Jackie said. "Want to hang out with me today?"
"Yip!" Howler darted from his kennel and took a lap around the large pen. Jackie gave him some time to run off energy and then called him back to her.
Howler immediately came to her side. He sat on command. Then he trotted at her side as she took a lap around the pen.
"Good job! I can tell Grandma's been working with you." Jackie gave the little beagle a treat.
"Yip!"
"Stay." Jackie turned her back to Howler and walked across the pen. When she turned to face him again, he was still sitting obediently in his place.
"Yes!" Jackie said. Howler quivered but didn't move. His eyes carefully watched her face.
"Come!"
Howler ran to her, stopping at her side. Jackie gave the dog a treat and then stroked his velvety ears. The beagle was sweet, and he seemed smart too.
Jackie's mind was made up. "We can do this! Howler, you and I are going to be a team!"
"Yip!"
While Howler munched on another treat, Jackie sent a text to Hudson.
"Decided to show Howler."
"Great! Beagles rock!"
"Need to study breed standard now."
Hudson sent her a huge thumbs-up emoji. Jackie sent back a face with sweat dripping down its cheeks. She hoped she wasn't making a big mistake!
Later, when Jackie left the kennels, she found Poke lying outside by the gate. His nose rested on his paws as he looked up at her. She had never seen such a sad look in his eyes.
"Ready for a walk?" she asked.
Poke bounced to his feet, wagging his tail.
Jackie laughed. "At least you don't hold a grudge."

Jackie jogged as Poke trotted beside her. They circled the yard and then headed down the path to the small pond at the back of Grandma's farm. Poke's ears pricked forward as he realized where they were going. The pond was one of his favorite places on the farm.

Jackie stopped to catch her breath. Poke stood waiting near the water. When she picked up a stick, his front feet pranced. No one had trained Poke to fetch—he was a retriever and did it as naturally as eating. Jackie flung the stick into the water, and the dog ran down the short dock and plunged in. He paddled out and returned, laying the stick at Jackie's feet.
Jackie threw the stick again and again, delighted by Poke's excitement. "We'll have more time for this now, buddy. We can play fetch instead of practicing for shows."
Jackie threw the stick a few more times, and then they left the pond. As they headed back to the kennels, Jackie looked at Poke. "You smell like fish, buddy! How about a bath?"
"Whoof!"
Poke closed his eyes as Jackie rinsed him off. From the wooden beams above, Kitty Cat watched them. She squatted on her haunches, looking ready to pounce right on top of the dog's broad black back.
"You do it, and you get the next bath," Jackie warned her with a grin.
Kitty Cat hissed and retreated.

Jackie finished drying Poke with a towel. "Now you have to find something to do," she said. "I need to use Grandma's computer to register Howler and myself for the show. Plus, I need to do some research on beagles."
"I'll let you run for a few minutes," Jackie said to Howler as he stared at her through the kennel gate. "But today is a work day, little buddy. No time for play."

It was the following Saturday. Jackie was glad to be back at the farm, but she was also worried. She'd gone to a football game last night instead of coming to the farm. It had been fun, but it had delayed the start of Howler's training.
Jackie opened the kennel door, and the little dog burst out. He moved at a quick trot, nose to the ground. Howler was a hound, and hounds depended on their noses for tracking.
The beagle twisted and turned as he ran, making it hard to judge his gait. She'd have to figure that out later.
While the beagle ran off some energy, Jackie went to visit the litter of puppies. Grandma had let Shadow out of the pen. The puppy was toddling after her.
"You're already training her!" Jackie said.
Grandma smiled. "She's learning to pay attention to the nice lady with the treats."
Shadow came to investigate Jackie. She gave the puppy a treat, laughing as Shadow snuffled along the ground for more. "Puppies are so cute!"
"You'll have lots of opportunity to play with this one later," Grandma said.
Jackie took the hint—she needed to focus on Howler today.

"Howler, come!" Jackie called. He came running, and she snapped on a leash. Then she ran a grooming glove over him, cleaning the dust from his black, tan, and white coat. She liked the way his tail had a white feathery banner at the tip like a tiny flag. Howler stood still for the grooming, but he definitely didn't like it as much as Poke did. His black nose quivered—he was eager to get moving again.

A few minutes later, Jackie took him into the training ring and lifted him onto a platform. Howler was a small beagle, so judges might choose to have him stacked on a table rather than on the ground. Jackie had to be ready for either possibility.
Howler made a circle on the table, sniffing for treats. Jackie caught sight of Grandma watching them from the entrance.
Jackie held a treat above Howler's nose. "Stay."
Howler froze, his nose pointed at the treat. Jackie ran her free hand over the dog's back and then up and down his legs. Howler obediently stayed still.
"Good boy." Jackie fed him the treat.
Howler surged forward, looking for another treat.
Jackie placed him back in the middle of the table. "Stay." He froze and she gave him the treat.

Jackie adjusted the dog's feet, remembering what she'd learned about the breed standard for beagles. Howler's legs were supposed to be straight, and his feet were supposed to point ahead. Putting one hand under the dog's chin and the other at the tip of his tail, Jackie looked toward Grandma. "What do you think?"
"Nice job." Grandma nodded. "You did a good job of keeping him focused."
Jackie beamed. Maybe working with a new dog was going to be easier than she had thought. "Showing him will be harder—there are other dogs and people around."
"True," Grandma said. "And Howler doesn't have the age or experience of Poke. You'll have to be patient with him. But you're off to a wonderful start."
Jackie glanced toward the gate as she patted Howler. Poke lay quietly watching her, his nose on his front paws.
"Should I check Howler's gait next?" Jackie asked Grandma. "I don't want to do too much on our first day. He'll get tired and frustrated."
"Go ahead and take him around a couple of times," Grandma said. "Then take a break."

Jackie led Howler to the side of the ring. With Poke, she knew just how fast to run to keep him at his best gait. She wasn't sure about her speed yet with Howler. This part of training Howler was probably going to take some time.

Holding the leash in her left hand, Jackie led Howler counterclockwise around the ring. It felt strange to walk with a smaller dog—Poke was taller than Howler. Jackie quickly increased her speed, and Howler moved into a trot. Then she saw Grandma watching them with a frown.
"Speed up a little," Grandma said.
Jackie sped up.
"Slow down," Grandma said. A minute later she walked into the ring. "He's pacing, not trotting."

Jackie groaned. The secret to properly gaiting a dog was making it trot—that meant it had to move its diagonal feet together, at the same time. When a dog was pacing, it was moving its feet on the same side together. Trotting made dogs move in a straight smooth line, which is what handlers wanted while showing their dogs.
"Let me try." Grandma took the leash and circled the ring. Howler trotted comfortably at her side.
"He looks good with you. Let me try again," Jackie said.
"Go!" Grandma commanded as Jackie took off, running around the ring. Jackie tried to keep her speed about the same as Grandma's had been. Then she looked down at Howler's legs.
The two legs on the dog's right side were moving forward together. "Ugh!" She groaned. "He's pacing again!"
Jackie halted. "What am I doing wrong?"
Grandma shook her head, a puzzled look on her face. "I'm not sure. Why don't you quit for now, and I'll think about it."

Jackie didn't like to quit training when things were going poorly. She knew it was better to end a session on a positive note. But she also knew that Grandma's suggestion was a good one. She didn't want to teach Howler bad habits. Plus, she could feel herself getting frustrated.
"We'll get it figured out," Grandma assured her.
Jackie praised Howler for the good work he had done and let him into the exercise yard. Howler took off like a kid let out of school early.
Jackie stared after him, trying to shake off her worry. They had worked well together on the stacking. Howler knew what to do and he did it—most of the time.
But gaiting was important during shows. Dogs looked stronger, and their backs were straighter when they were trotting, and it was the handler's job to ensure that the dog looked good.
"What if I can't get it right?" Jackie thought. "I'll be stuck in the novice class forever!"
The next day Jackie clipped on Howler's leash. "Grandma, I'm going to Hudson's house. He's going to help me with Howler's training."
"Good idea," Grandma said. "Hudson's one of the best young handlers I've seen."
Jackie nodded. "He is a good handler. And he knows beagles really well." After yesterday, she hoped she'd get good at handling beagles soon too.
As she approached Hudson's house, Jackie could see him at the obstacle course. Howler whined as they got closer, excited by another dog's scent.
"No," Jackie commanded. "Stand and wait."
Suddenly Bart's head popped from the end of a long tunnel. Howler immediately started barking.
Bart looked over, distracted by Howler's yipping.
"No," Jackie repeated. "Howler, stand and wait."
Hudson quickly got Bart's attention back, and they finished the course. Howler quivered with excitement as he watched the other dog race along, but he stayed at Jackie's side.
"Sorry for the interruption," Jackie said when Hudson brought Bart over. "But you did offer to help me with Howler!"
Hudson grinned. "Glad to help. Do you mind if Bart and I run through the course once more? Move Howler right next to the ring. It will be good practice for Bart. He has to learn to stay focused."

Jackie brought Howler to ringside as Hudson took Bart back to the starting line. Hudson made Bart sit and look at him as he talked. To Jackie, it seemed like a long discussion. She couldn't help giggling. Bart actually seemed to be following the conversation! "That's how you pay attention, Howler!" she said.
Finally Hudson and Bart were ready.

"Stand and wait," Jackie commanded. She wanted Howler to get used to standing near a show ring. Judges were always watching dogs and handlers, and a standing dog looked better than one that was sitting.
"Go!" Hudson said.

Bart took off like he was chasing a rabbit. He jumped over two bars and went under a third. Hudson raced beside the dog, calling out commands. Bart leaped onto a table and stopped. As soon as Hudson gave the command, Bart leaped down and barreled ahead. He went through a tunnel and over a long jump.
"Yip!" Howler pranced excitedly.
"No. Stand and wait," Jackie said. Howler obeyed, but Jackie could still feel his tense excitement as they watched Bart cross the finish line.
"Nice!" Jackie called.
"Thanks." Hudson gave Bart a treat. "Bart didn't even flinch when Howler barked."
"His focus is amazing!" Jackie said.
"So how's it going with Howler?" Hudson asked.
"He's doing okay. He doesn't always pay attention—I have to really watch him."
"That's what a good handler does—adjusts to the dog," Hudson said. "Let's see you stack him. Do you want to use the platform?"
"Let's try the ground," Jackie said. "We have to learn both methods. Will you keep Bart in the ring while I practice with Howler? That'll test his focus."
"Sure. Good idea."
Jackie led Howler into the ring with Bart walking behind them. First, they circled the ring. Whenever Howler tried to look back, Jackie commanded, "Go," to bring his attention forward.
"That was good," Hudson said after a few times around the ring. "Now bring him up," he called in an official tone, like a judge's.
Jackie brought Howler to the center of the ring to stack him. She knelt and slipped one hand beneath Howler's jaw to control his head. Her other hand was on his tail. "Stay."
"Speak," Hudson whispered to Bart.
Bart obeyed. "Yip!"
"Yip! Yip!" Howler wanted to see his new friend.
Jackie held the dog's head firmly forward. "Stay."
When Howler finally stayed still, Jackie rewarded him with a treat. "Stay," she commanded again, adjusting his back feet.
Judge Hudson grinned, walking to Howler's side. He ran his hands down Howler's back and legs. He bent to look for wrinkles around the dog's neck. Beagles were supposed to have smooth necks.
"Try holding his head a teeny bit higher," Hudson said.
Jackie gently lifted Howler's head a fraction of an inch.
"That's better." Hudson stepped back. Howler looked at him, his face showing his excitement. "Yip!"
"Stay," Jackie commanded. Howler didn't move and Jackie smiled.

"That was great!" Hudson said. "Remember what I said about beagles showing a lot of personality? The judge won't deduct points for it, as long as the handler maintains control. And that's what you did."
Jackie nodded, pleased.
"Go around the ring again," Hudson said. "We'll judge his gait now."
"Go!" Jackie commanded, starting off quickly.
Jackie was halfway around the ring, when Hudson said, "Stop."
Jackie halted, knowing what was coming.
"He's pacing instead of trotting," Hudson said.
Jackie frowned. "Am I going too slow or too fast? I can't figure it out."
"I'm not sure. Why don't you try a courtesy circle first."
"Okay." A courtesy circle was a tight circle, which handlers often did before starting around the ring. It helped them to get a dog moving properly before the judges started watching.
"Go," Jackie said, turning Howler in a small circle before going around the ring.
"Yes!" she thought. "We're trotting!" Then she felt a change in the dog's movement. He was pacing again! She stopped, letting out a heavy groan.
"Let me try," Hudson said.
Howler and Hudson circled the ring, the dog smoothly trotting the entire time.
Jackie tried again. Halfway around, Howler started pacing.
Jackie stopped, frustrated. "Grr," she complained. "What's the matter with this dog?"
Hudson shrugged. "I'm not sure. But it's not a dog problem—it's a handler problem."
Jackie felt stung. "I never had this problem with Poke—or any of Grandma's other dogs!" she snapped.
"You've never handled this dog before," Hudson replied calmly. "You're still getting used to working together."

Tears suddenly pricked at Jackie's eyes. She'd thought Hudson was going to help her, not criticize her. Plus, the show was just a few weeks away, and she had no clue how to fix this problem with Howler.
"I made a big mistake," she blurted out. "I should have listened to Grandma instead of you. I don't like this breed."
Hudson cocked his head and gave her a puzzled look. "That's ridiculous, Jackie. You can't blame an entire breed because you're having trouble handling one of them."
Her temper flared. "Oh, so you think I'm not a good handler?"
"I didn't say that," Hudson said. "You just need to—"
Jackie didn't hear the rest. She was already running back to the farm with Howler.
Jackie worried all week about her problem with Howler. She felt bad about her argument with Hudson too, but the show was coming up fast.
"I'll focus on my dog problem first," she told herself. Later she'd fix the friend problem.

On Friday she tried running Howler uphill. For once, he trotted the entire time—but it was hard for a dog to run uphill without trotting. As soon as she brought him back to the show ring, he started pacing again.

Jackie woke up on Saturday morning with a heavy heart. She rolled over and pulled the pillow over her head. Priscilla and Fluffy had registered for the show too. It had been a close contest last time. But this time Priscilla was going to blow past Jackie. Then Priscilla would advance to open class—leaving Jackie behind.
"What a disaster," she thought miserably.
"Time for breakfast!" Grandma called.
A few minutes later, Jackie slumped into her kitchen chair.
"Are you feeling all right?" Grandma asked.
Jackie stared at the steaming plate of pancakes in front of her. "I'm just worried. I've tried everything with Howler. But he's still not trotting."
"You'll figure it out," Grandma said.

"You keep saying that, Grandma," Jackie mumbled. "But what if I don't? Gaiting is basic stuff. I'm going to look like a total newbie at this show." Jackie gave Grandma her most pleading look. "Can't I take Poke to one more show? Please?"
Grandma shook her head. "Sorry."
Jackie slumped farther down. "Maybe I'll just skip this show. Obviously, I'm not ready."
Grandma gave her a stern look. "You've already registered and your parents paid the fees. Stop thinking about your friends. And start thinking about Howler."
"He's so different from Poke," Jackie grumbled.
"So stop treating him like Poke!"
Jackie flushed. Grandma didn't approve of quitting—on anything, especially dogs.
"Okay." Jackie pushed her chair back with a sigh. "I'll get started."
Soon Jackie was heading for the kennels with Poke trotting eagerly at her side. When they got there, Jackie patted him. "Sorry, buddy. I'm going to work with Howler today."
"Whoof!" Poke lay down by the gate.

As Jackie approached, Howler spun in circles. Jackie couldn't help laughing. Howler was frustrating, but it was impossible to resist his enthusiasm. She bent over to look into his soulful eyes. "You're a good dog."
"Yip!" Howler raced off, nose to the ground.
Jackie went to get Howler's leash and some treats. As she left the kennels, she spotted Hudson riding his bike up the long driveway. Bart was trotting at his side. She stopped to wait for her friend.
"Um, I'm sorry about last weekend," she murmured. "I acted like a jerk."
"Yep." Hudson grinned and nodded. "You acted like a jerk."
"I'm so nervous about the show," Jackie mumbled. "I can't get used to Howler, and I don't know what I'm doing."
Howler came running over. "Yip! Yip!" He danced happily around Jackie.
"You might not like beagles," Hudson said. "But this one really loves you!"
Jackie laughed and scooped him up. "I love him too. I'm just not sure I'm the right handler for him."
By now Grandma had joined them. "Well, the team's all here," she said. "Let's get this situation fixed."

Jackie slipped the leash over Howler's ears and tightened it high on his neck. In the ring they made a courtesy circle, and then Jackie began running. Howler started off trotting, but he was soon pacing.
She stopped and looked at her coaches. "Well?"
"Try bumping him gently when he starts pacing," Grandma suggested. "The secret is to throw him a little off-balance. That will make pacing harder."
Jackie tried the suggestion. Howler trotted for a few yards, but then he was back to pacing.
Jackie looked up again for advice. But Hudson and Grandma were huddled together, both shaking their heads. They looked frustrated too.
"Ugh," Jackie thought. Was it worse to make a fool of herself at the show or give up completely? Neither choice felt good.
Just then she realized Poke had entered the ring. Ignoring Howler, he took his place by Jackie's side and looked up at her expectantly.
She looked down at him with a sad face. "Sorry, Poke. I'm working with Howler now."
"Whoof!" Poke nudged her hand with the leash.
"Hey!" Jackie thought. She ran over to Hudson. "Can you hold Howler's leash for a second?" Then she ran to get Poke's leash.

She quickly led Poke to the starting point inside the ring, and the two of them began to run. Beside the familiar dog, her own movements felt smooth and automatic. When running with Poke, she didn't even have to think about what to do. They completed a couple of turns around the ring.
Hudson was nodding at her. "Awesome idea! You can see what feels different between the two dogs."
Next, Jackie started around the ring with Howler. The beagle began in a trot. Then, just as Jackie expected, he moved into a pace.
"It's not a dog problem—it's a handler problem."

Hudson's words suddenly flashed in her mind. Jackie took a deep breath and ignored Howler, concentrating on her own body instead. She could feel a pull in her right side as she dropped her left shoulder to accommodate the shorter dog. Then she straightened up, and Howler was trotting!
"Of course!" she thought. Her leaning toward the shorter dog had signaled him to pace. When she straightened up, he began to trot.
The dog and handler made three more rounds. Jackie kept her posture straight and upright.
Grandma and Hudson broke into loud applause.
Jackie stopped and hugged Howler. She had figured it out! She gave the little beagle a treat and slipped off the leash. Hudson released Bart, and the two beagles followed their noses across the yard.
"Whoof!" Poke said.
Jackie's next hug was for the Labrador. "Thank you, Poke!" She gave him a treat. "And thank you, Team Howler," she said to Grandma and Hudson.
"That was amazing," Hudson said.
"It was," Grandma agreed. "But don't get too excited yet. You have only one more weekend before the show."
Hudson grinned. "Once you advance to open class, we'll be competing against each other."
Jackie punched his shoulder. "When that time comes, may the best handler win!"
"No problem, Howler," Jackie whispered nervously. "We're going to do great."

Jackie stood in a line of seven handlers with their dogs. She was petting Howler to keep him—and herself—calm. She had bathed him yesterday, so this morning he had needed just a quick brush. It had taken longer to get herself ready. Handlers had to dress up, but the idea was to show the dog, not the person. Jackie was wearing her favorite green skirt with a matching jacket.
"Handlers, enter the ring," an official called.
Jackie took a deep breath. It was time.

With her friends and family watching, Jackie led Howler into the ring, behind another beagle. Priscilla and Fluffy were the last ones to enter. Howler, so far, was on his best behavior. He trotted around the ring with the other dogs, and then stood at her side.
"Good boy." Jackie slipped him a treat.
Jackie watched as the first girl showed her German shepherd before the judge. Jackie couldn't tell if the judge was impressed or not.
"Tough judge," the girl murmured as she took her place behind Priscilla and Fluffy.
Jackie nodded but kept her eyes forward. She needed to appear focused and confident in front of the judges.

"Bring him up," said the judge to the next handler. One by one, the kids showed their dogs. Jackie felt sorry for some kids as they made dumb mistakes. She had made the same mistakes when she first started as a novice. She hoped she had learned enough by now to advance to open class after today.

Finally, only one handler remained before Jackie's turn. The kid looked terrified, tangling himself in his leash as he entered the ring. Priscilla burst out laughing, but Jackie kept a straight face. She knew from experience—everyone made mistakes.

The boy lifted his beagle to the table. As the judge approached, the hound lunged forward and nearly fell off the table. The judge gave them a moment to get stacked and then circled the table. The dog twisted with the judge, watching him.
"No, Boomer!" The boy struggled to keep the dog still. "Stand like you did at home!"
"Oops. Newbie mistake," thought Jackie. The dog had probably been fine alone in the backyard. But handlers had to get their dogs used to noisy situations too.
"Up and back," said the judge.
The handler trotted Boomer to the end of the ring. As they made the turn, the dog's nose went up.
"Uh-oh," Jackie thought.
Suddenly, Boomer lunged, yanking the leash from the boy's hand. The dog took off, the boy racing after him. People and dogs scattered, yelling and barking like crazy.
"Yip! Yip!" Howler excitedly followed the action.
"No," Jackie said firmly, bringing him under control. "This is terrible!" she thought in dismay. "Now Howler is completely distracted—and it's almost our turn!"
Finally the boy caught the dog.
The judge looked at Jackie. "I'll give you another minute if you need time to settle your dog after that, er, episode."
Jackie shook her head. There was no use putting it off. "We're ready."
"Good luck," Priscilla whispered.
Howler trotted happily into the ring. Jackie lifted him to the table, positioned his feet, and moved to the side. "Show time, Howler," she whispered.
Howler's tail waved.
The judge ran his hand down Howler's back and legs. Jackie could sense Howler wanting to turn his head. She quickly slipped her hand under his jaw, holding his head steady. He kept his position.
Next the judge examined the dog's head and eyes. Howler leaned forward, his nose quivering.
"Stay," Jackie said.
The dog leaned a little farther but didn't move his feet.
"Stay." Jackie resisted pulling him back with the leash. That would make things look worse, and she had a feeling that Howler would obey her command.
She was right. Howler kept his position until the judge nodded.
"Around," he said.
Jackie took off fast, paying close attention to her own posture. The beagle trotted perfectly beside her.
"Up and back."
Jackie let out a breath. "We're almost done!" she thought. "Please, Howler, no mistakes now!"
She took off and Howler trotted at her side. "Perfect," she said as they made the turn.
"Yow-w-w-l!" Just then a long howl came from Boomer. His handler had brought the runaway beagle back to watch.
"No, no, no," Jackie thought as Howler slowed to look at the other dog. Instantly she moved to Howler's other side to block his view, switching the leash into her other hand. "Go!"
Howler obeyed. But halfway across the ring, Jackie felt him slip into a pace. "Ack!" she thought. When she had switched sides, she had put the leash in her right hand. Now she was leaning again!
"Stop," she said. Howler stopped, giving her a questioning look.
"My fault," she assured him, and gave him a treat. Embarrassed, she hurried to the far side of the ring to start again.
"Go!" This time she had the leash in her left hand. And she kept her posture straight as they ran.
Howler trotted straight to the judge and stopped. "Yip!" He was obviously quite proud of his performance. The judge smiled, motioning Jackie to the back of the line.

Jackie sighed. Her dumb mistake with the leash would cost them first place. That meant she wouldn't be moving up to open class anytime soon. Tears sprang to her eyes, but she brushed them away. Overall, she and Howler had done well for their first show together. She gave Howler a treat.

The handlers and audience grew quiet as the judge started handing out ribbons. He gave third place to the girl with the German shepherd. Then he stood in front of Priscilla and Jackie holding the first- and second-place ribbons. Jackie took a deep breath and prepared to congratulate Priscilla—again.
"The secret to winning first place is to understand your breed and display both ring etiquette and"—he gave Priscilla a stern look—"sportsmanship." He handed Priscilla the second-place ribbon.
Jackie gasped as the judge handed her the rose ribbon. "Nice job," he said. "I don't think many professional handlers could have done better."
Jackie accepted the ribbon and thanked the judge. Then she and Howler bounded over to her cheering family and friends.
"Nice job!"
"Wow, impressive!"
Jackie beamed. Team Howler had done it! She bent down to give her dog a hug. She couldn't wait to start competing in the open class with the best beagle in the world!
"I don't care if this is the best farmers' market in the world," Lissa grumbled. "I still hate living in this city!"

Lissa was with her father, walking around a busy outdoor farmers' market. Bright red tomatoes spilled out of crates next to cucumbers. Perfect fuzzy peaches sat in baskets beside deep red cherries. Ears of sweet-smelling fresh corn were heaped on tables.

"But this is a dream town for a foodie like you, Lissa," Dad said, still looking around in wonder at the colorful fruits and vegetables. "The city has great restaurants, and this farmers' market is known all over the state. See this?" He reached for a huge zucchini and held it in front of her face. "Look at this gorgeous green zucchini! Now, who could resist a good-looking vegetable like this?"
"Ugh!" Lissa swatted it away. " I can resist it. And technically, Dad, a zucchini is a fruit, not a vegetable."
"Oh." He laughed and put it back.
As they continued wandering through the vendors' booths, they bought some food to take home—strawberries, radishes, and some great-smelling fresh basil.
"The food is awesome here, Dad," Lissa blurted out. "It's just not enough to make up for leaving my friends and my old school."

"I know." Dad put an arm around her shoulder. "I promise, honey—you'll make new friends. It's just going to take some time." He flashed a grin at her. "You'd meet them faster if you left the house more often. You can't spend the summer lying on the couch, watching Caroline Cooks ."
"Oh yes, I can!" Lissa retorted. "It's my favorite show! Besides, the only thing I like about this dumb city is that Caroline Cook lives here."
"Hey! Wait a minute." She stopped and looked around. Her father had just said this was a famous farmers' market for foodies. What if—?
"Look!" Dad suddenly grabbed Lissa's arm, and her heart skipped a beat. "Caroline Cook!" she thought. "I knew she'd be here!"
But her father was pointing to something else. It was a large notice board, which was covered with flyers and posters about city events.

"Come on." Dad dragged her closer to the board and started reading the notices. "I bet we can find something for you to do here. Hey, this sounds good—a teen book club meets at the library every Tuesday at two o'clock."
Lissa groaned. "I love to read. But the library here smells like mold. Thanks but no thanks."

"Okay . . ." Dad peered at another notice. "Someone is looking for a babysitter . . . and here's a flyer about taking swimming lessons at a hotel. I heard there's no community pool—they had to close it a few years ago."
Lissa just grunted, thinking about how she could be swimming at the lake right now with her friends back home.

"Okay, here we go!" Dad eagerly pulled a paper off the board and started reading it. "This is a notice about a kids' cooking competition at the Garden restaurant. The flyer says to stop by the restaurant for more information."
Lissa wrinkled her nose. "I like to cook, but I don't know about entering a competition. That sounds like too much pressure."
Her father wasn't listening. Instead he was already rushing toward their car. "Come on, Lissa! Let's go!"

The Garden restaurant was located in a run-down part of the city. But the building itself looked bright and cheerful. It was painted yellow on the outside, with pictures of fruits and vegetables painted on the walls inside. The main dining area was an open space with a small stage at the back, as if musicians performed there sometimes.
"Nice place," Dad said. "And it's lunchtime. Let's see how the food is."
Lissa smiled, even though she still felt unsure about being there. Dad loved good food as much as she did. Trying out new restaurants was a hobby for both of them.

A waitress brought them menus and then came back to take their order. "Thanks for stopping by today," she said. "We just opened, and business is a bit slow. We're trying to spread the word about the restaurant to bring in more business."
Lissa nodded politely, gazing around. Only two other tables had customers. "I hope this isn't a sign that the food is bad," she thought.
But when her pasta arrived a few moments later, it smelled delicious. It was spaghetti, with a sauce made from fresh tomatoes, garlic, and basil.
Lissa ate a forkful. "Yum! This is good!"
Dad nodded enthusiastically. He had ordered the same thing. "The tomatoes are so sweet and ripe."
When they were finished with the pasta, they ordered dessert. Dad had homemade ice cream, and Lissa had a slice of peach pie.
"This is good," she thought. "But it's missing something. Maybe some cinnamon or vanilla."
When they'd finished eating, Dad asked to meet the chef, who turned out to be a large man with a friendly smile.
"My name's Sam." The chef shook Dad's hand. "I hope you enjoyed your meal."
"It was delicious," Dad said.
The chef looked at Lissa. "I hope you enjoyed the food too?"
Lissa nodded. "The pasta was really good," she said. "But I probably would have added some cinnamon to the peach pie. Cinnamon brings out the flavor of fruit."
"Lissa . . . ," Dad murmured.
The chef blinked in surprise. "Oh!" he said. "Well—thank you for the suggestion. I'll think about that next time I make the pie."
Lissa flushed, suddenly feeling embarrassed. She hadn't meant to be rude. She just had strong opinions about food—and some other things.
"My daughter is very interested in cooking," Dad said quickly. "That's actually why we came in for lunch. We saw a flyer about a kids' cooking contest."

The chef nodded. "Yes, the contest is Betty's idea. She's the owner of the restaurant. It's a competition for kids between the ages of 10 and 15. We like to encourage cooking with fresh ingredients, plus we'll attract some customers to the restaurant." He looked at Lissa. "Have you ever heard of Caroline Cook?"
"Of course!" Lissa said.
Dad laughed. "Lissa never misses Caroline Cook's show."
"Well, Caroline lives in the city. And she's agreed to help with judging the final round of the competition," Sam went on. "The winner will get to be a guest on her show."
"Whoa! That's awesome!" Lissa could hardly believe it. "How do I sign up?"
"The cooking competition sounds exciting," Dad said as he and Lissa drove home. "I think it's perfect for you, Lissa."
Lissa nodded. She didn't want to give Dad the wrong impression that she was suddenly happy about their move. But the cooking contest did sound like fun.
"I could probably even win," she thought. Back at home she'd never met any kids who were as interested in food as she was. And if she won, she'd get to meet Caroline Cook.

A sudden worry struck her. "I just realized something, Dad. The chef, Sam, didn't call it a baking competition. He called it a cooking contest. What if they want me to make . . . I don't know. White bean chili instead of an apple pie?"
Dad shrugged. "Simple. Then you'll just make the best chili in the world."

Lissa nodded, but she wasn't persuaded by Dad's confidence. He always acted as if Lissa could do anything. What if she had an epic failure at the contest and messed up a recipe? Or she had to cook something that she'd never even heard of? Worst of all, what if she made a fool of herself in front of Caroline Cook?

With a knot in her stomach, Lissa pulled out her phone and started scrolling through recipes. The first round of the cooking competition was next Saturday. If she started right away, she could practice cooking dozens of things—cookies, pies, tarts, and even some white bean chili!

Over the next few days, Lissa cooked constantly. On Monday she made a huge pot of chili, which Dad said was perfect. On Tuesday she tried Caroline's paprika chicken, with a blueberry gingerbread for dessert.
"Delicious!" Dad said.
But when Lissa tasted the food, she was less impressed. The paprika chicken was bland, and the gingerbread was just okay.
"More practice!" she told herself.

On Wednesday, Lissa made a batch of Caroline's Perfect Double Chocolate Chunk Cookies while watching the show's "Ode to Chocolate" episode. She put the cookies in the oven and then went back to watching Caroline Cooks . The chef was working on her next dessert—a chocolate mousse cake.
Lissa held her breath as Caroline melted dark chocolate into pure white cream. When the cake was done, it looked like a work of art.
Lissa sighed. "Someday I will make something as beautiful as that."
Beep, beep, beep! A sound startled her. Oh no! It was the smoke detector!
Lissa ran into the kitchen and stared in horror at the smoke streaming from the oven. "My cookies!" she cried.
After fumbling with the knob, Lissa managed to switch the oven off. Her eyes watered from smoke as she opened the door. Luckily there were no flames. Just burnt cookies and a blackened baking sheet.
"Ugh." Lissa moaned. She opened the window to air out the room and pulled the baking tray out of the oven. Then she marched out of the house with the burned cookies, heading for the big trash bin.
"Ruined!" Lissa declared. "A whole batch of double chocolate chunk cookies is going into the trash!"
"Whoa, whoa, whoa!" a voice said. "Did somebody say double chocolate chunk cookies?"

Startled, Lissa looked up. It was the boy who lived next door. She had seen him a few times before, shooting hoops in his driveway. He was always laughing, as if nothing ever bothered him. Usually other kids were with him.
He looked a little worried now though. "I could smell smoke. Is your house on fire?"
"Nope," Lissa said. Her tone had sounded sharper than she intended. "It was just, er, a small accident."
"Good." The boy gave her a grin. "I won't call the fire department then." He eyed the cookie tray. "But can I try one of those cookies?"
Lissa blinked in surprise. He wanted to taste a burnt cookie? "Uh, I guess," she said with a shrug. "I mean, as long as you're not expecting something that tastes good."
The boy reached for a cookie and took a bite. "This isn't bad!" He took another bite and grinned at Lissa with chocolatey teeth. "I'm Jason, by the way. You just moved here, right?"
"Yep." Lissa made a face.
"Oh." He looked a little hurt. "You don't like the city?"
Lissa shook her head. "The farmers' market is good," she said. "But nothing else seems very nice. There's only one crummy park, and no community pool."

Jason's face clouded over, and Lissa bit her lip. "You did it again!" she scolded herself. She had a habit of being honest, which her friends liked. But even they said she was too honest sometimes. Jason seemed like a nice kid, and now he probably thought she was a spoiled brat.

But to her surprise, Jason nodded. "I know. It's kind of boring here. The city does have plans to build a new community center—with a swimming pool and some basketball courts. Once the basketball courts are ready, they're even going to start a city basketball league. But it's taking a long time to raise the money. I'm not sure it will ever happen."
He sat down on his stoop with his basketball, still looking glum.
"You should have a bake sale!" Lissa blurted out.
"A bake sale?" Jason echoed with a laugh. "First of all, I can't bake. Second of all, how much money could I raise by selling cupcakes and cookies?"
"At my old school, we raised a ton of money from bake sales," Lissa said. "We had one every month. We made enough money to buy new laptops for all of the fifth- and sixth-graders."
"Impressive," Jason said.
"I could help you," Lissa offered. "Maybe you could organize all the details for the sale. And I'll do all the baking." She shrugged. "It can't hurt to try, right?"
"Actually, that sounds great!" Jason leaped to his feet again. "You're sure you want to do this though? It seems like a lot of work for you."

"Sure," Lissa said. "I love to bake. Besides . . ." She let her words trail off. She wasn't ready to tell Jason about all the practice cooking she was doing this week for the contest. "I . . . um . . . have nothing else to do," she finished. "It's not like I've got any friends here."
"Wrong." He grinned and held up a hand for a high-five. "You've got one friend!"
Lissa smiled back. "Thanks. And I promise—the next batch of cookies you taste will actually taste good!"
"Oh boy," Dad said on Saturday morning when he and Lissa arrived at the Garden restaurant. "There's quite a big turnout for this event."
He was right. The parking lot was filled with cars. Lissa just nodded, not trusting herself to speak. Her voice seemed to have dried up, and her knees were shaking.

"Why am I so nervous?" she asked herself. "I practiced baking all week, and most of my recipes turned out great." She took a deep breath, trying to calm herself. Caroline Cook probably never got nervous before a show.

Inside, a waitress greeted them with a smile. "Competing?" she asked Lissa. She took the registration form Lissa handed her. "Great! All the cooks are going to be onstage. Your father can sit at a table and watch the competition, if he likes."
Lissa joined some other kids on the stage in the back of the dining room. In the audience she saw lots of kids and adults. She wondered nervously if the judges were sitting there too.
Just then she glimpsed a familiar face in the crowd—Jason! Lissa blinked in surprise. What was he doing here? He grinned and waved. Lissa waved back. A few other kids onstage waved at him too.
"Oh, so that's it," she realized. Jason had some friends competing too. Maybe that was a good sign. If he hung out with kids who liked to cook, maybe she could be friends with these kids too.
One of the girls who'd waved to Jason was staring at Lissa.
"Hi." Lissa nodded at her. "My name is Lissa. I guess you love to cook too," she said nervously.
"What a stupid thing to say," she scolded herself. Of course the girl liked to cook. Otherwise she wouldn't be here!
But the girl was staring at Lissa blankly. "I'm only here because my grandmother made me come," she mumbled. "I don't have much interest in cooking."
"Oh, well, that's cool," Lissa said brightly. "I love cooking. In fact, I'm thinking about becoming a pastry chef someday."
The tall boy on the other side of Lissa laughed loudly. "You want to be a pastry chef? Well, guess what—we're not in Paris!"
Lissa felt her face turn beet red.
"I'm going to be a short-order cook at my cousin's diner someday," the boy went on. "Now, that's real cooking!"

Lissa felt a surge of anger. "Well, I like baking," she snapped. "I might even go to Paris to study when I'm older. I'll learn real cooking skills there, not just lessons in how to flip burgers on a grill!"
The boy glared at her, but the girl laughed. "Ha-ha, Rob!"
"Be quiet, Kelly!" he shot back.
A girl with long, smooth hair was staring at them. "Can you guys be quiet? I don't want to miss hearing the instructions."
"Sorry," Lissa mumbled. "I was just trying to be friendly and introduce myself."

The girl with the long hair rolled her eyes. "I'm Mia, that's Rob, and this is Kelly." She gave Lissa a half smile. "Don't get too confident about your cooking skills just because you want to be a pastry chef. I might study in Paris someday too."
"I wasn't . . . I didn't mean . . ." Lissa tried to explain herself, but it was too late. The other kids had turned away to look at a woman who had stepped onstage.
"Yikes," Lissa thought. "How did I get off to such a bad start with these three kids?"
The woman began speaking into a microphone. "Good morning, everyone. My name is Betty Rossi. I'm the owner of the Garden, and I'd like to welcome everyone to our kids' cooking competition!"

She waited for the applause to die down before continuing. "As you may know already, this is a three-part competition. We'll have round one today and another round next Saturday. The third round will be the final one. Oh, and each round will have a different theme. This week's theme . . ."
"I hope it's bread," Lissa thought, crossing her fingers. She'd baked some really delicious breads this week.
"Salads!" Betty finished.
"Salads?" Lissa blurted out. The theme was salads?
Mia giggled. "Uh-oh! I guess the future pastry chef doesn't know how to make a simple salad."
Lissa hung her head. Of course she knew how to make a salad. But making a salad wasn't cooking; it was simply chopping vegetables and throwing them into a bowl.

"Each of you will be given a basket of different ingredients," Betty went on. "You must use these ingredients in your creation." She gestured to a huge table at the back of the stage that was loaded with supplies. "That's our pantry. You can use ingredients from the pantry too. But you must use a bit of everything in your basket."
"What?" Lissa's heart sank even lower as she took in the woman's words. They weren't allowed to choose their own ingredients?
A girl raised her hand. "Do we have to use up all the stuff in our baskets?"

"No," Betty replied. "But as I said, you must use at least a little bit of each ingredient. You'll have 15 minutes total for this challenge. When the timer goes off, please leave your creations at that display table for our wonderful panel of judges." She gestured to some people sitting near the stage.

Lissa stared as Betty introduced the three judges one by one. There was a food writer; a restaurant critic for a local newspaper; and Sam, the chef of the Garden. He met Lissa's eyes and nodded. Suddenly she wished she hadn't spoken up about his peach pie needing cinnamon.
"The judges will leave the room before you start cooking," Betty said. "That way they won't know who has made which salad."
Lissa sighed with relief. So far that was the only good news she'd heard.

"They'll return after the timer goes off," Betty went on, "and they'll award points after each round of cooking. As you probably know, Caroline Cook has agreed to help with the judging during the final round. The cook with the most points will win the grand prize—a guest appearance on the TV show Caroline Cooks !"
The audience clapped while the kids onstage cheered loudly. Then the judges stood up and exited.
Betty turned back to the contestants and beamed. "Okay, young chefs . . . open your baskets, and start making your salads!"
Lissa gulped. This was it!

As the contest began, the kids all ripped the cloths off their baskets. Lissa peered into her basket. She had some fresh greens, which smelled a bit spicy. Lissa didn't know what they were—maybe arugula leaves? She saw some sprigs of mint too, along with raspberries and . . . Ugh. Were those cornflakes?
Panic went through Lissa again. People ate cornflakes for breakfast. Who had ever heard of putting cornflakes in a salad?
She looked up, and Dad flashed her an enthusiastic thumbs-up from his table. She sent back a wobbly smile. Then she realized somebody was whispering to her.
"Are you panicking?" It was Mia at the next workstation, teasing her. "Real chefs can cook with any ingredient," she added with a giggle.

Lissa abruptly raised her chin. Mia was being annoying, but she was actually making a good point. Real cooks, including pastry chefs, did need to know how to work with different ingredients. "No problem," Lissa told herself. "I can figure out a way to make a great salad." She was going to show these kids—and the judges—that she could handle any type of cooking!

Lissa closed her eyes and thought over all the recipes she had memorized over the past week. She had made breads, cakes, pots of chili, casseroles, and spicy dishes. Some recipes had even included unusual combinations of flavors. Caroline Cook always said that good food was all about good flavor.

"Caroline Cook!" Lissa thought, and her eyes flew open. Of course! Lissa had watched an episode of Caroline Cooks called "Salad Surprise." Lissa hadn't followed it closely, but now she struggled to remember every detail. What had Caroline said? A salad should have something crunchy, something creamy, and something sweet.
It wasn't exactly a recipe, but it was an idea to work with. For crunch she could use the cornflakes. Sweetness could come from the raspberries. As for creamy . . .
Lissa rushed to the back of the stage and surveyed the pantry table. "Maybe I can make a dressing with sour cream," she thought. What if she mixed sour cream and mint? How would that taste?

Lissa grabbed the sour cream, as well as a packet of carrots, an apple, and some sugar. As she spun around, she bumped into Rob, who was scooping up bacon bits and an avocado. His eyes were bright with excitement.
"This is so fun!" he whispered.
He raced back to his workstation before Lissa could respond, but silently she found herself agreeing with him. It was fun to cook with a challenge like this!
Betty chatted with the audience with a stream of jokes and comments. As she wandered around the stage with her microphone, she asked each young chef about the ingredients in their baskets.

By the time Betty reached Lissa's station, Lissa's nerves had settled. She answered Betty confidently, showing her the ingredients in her basket. There was a ripple of laughter from the audience when they saw the cornflakes.
"Are you making us a breakfast salad?" Betty asked, grinning.
"Um, not today," Lissa said quickly.
"Well then, Lissa, what kind of salad are you making for us?"
"A good one!" Lissa retorted. The audience laughed again, and Lissa looked up and smiled at the crowd. Being in front of a big audience wasn't as scary as she had expected.

Lissa finished making her salad several minutes before the timer rang. Proudly she brought it up to the display table. Despite her earlier worries, her dish looked polished and appetizing. The greens were fanned out on a platter, dotted with colorful raspberries, and decorated with apple and carrot slices. She'd sprinkled the cornflakes on top of the whole thing, along with a light drizzle of sweet mint-and-sour-cream dressing.
Lissa sat down next to Mia in the first row of chairs. Mia shot Lissa a sly look. "So how did it go, pastry chef?"
Lissa narrowed her eyes. Mia wasn't exactly being mean, but she didn't sound particularly nice either. "We'll soon find out," Lissa replied with a shrug.
The timer dinged.
"Chefs, put down your salad tongs!" Betty joked.
The rest of the contestants put their salads on the display table and then raced to their seats.
A moment later the judges returned to the dining room. "Now for the moment of truth!" Betty boomed into the microphone.
The judges tasted the salads one at a time, starting with Rob's creation.
"Yummy!" the restaurant critic said. "A nice spin on a traditional Cobb salad."
"Really good!" Sam added, and the food writer agreed.
Lissa looked thoughtfully at Rob. She'd dismissed him so quickly because he'd said he wanted to work in a diner. Yet his salad looked delicious, and the judges loved it.
When the judges reached Lissa's salad, she held her breath. Sam took the first forkful. He chewed thoughtfully. Then a wide smile spread across his face.
"Delicious!" he declared. "Just the right amount of tang and crunch, and that creamy mint dressing is a smart addition."
The other judges took their tastes and commented as well. They all liked it!
"Whew!" Lissa sighed with relief. It had been fun to play with flavors, but it was even better to know her experiment had worked.
When the judges moved to Mia's salad, they sounded less impressed.
"Bland," Sam pronounced. "I think this cook could have done more with these ingredients."
Mia let out a low gasp. "Oh no," she whispered.
Lissa looked down. She couldn't help feeling a tiny bit smug.
At last the judging was over. The judges huddled with Betty for a second. Then Betty picked up her microphone again.
"And the top points go to . . . Rob and Lissa!" Betty beckoned them both up to the stage.
"Yes!" Lissa thought. She jumped to her feet, her heart pounding wildly. She shook hands with the judges and Betty, and waved to the applauding audience.

"Congratulations to all our young cooks," Betty said. "You've done a great job today, and I'm looking forward to seeing you next Saturday. Next week you will be baking. Please come with a dessert recipe that includes fruit or vegetables."

Lissa grinned. Her salad had been a big success. And next week's theme was baking, which was her specialty. After showing these judges her baking skills, she'd be one round closer to winning the grand prize!
The next day Lissa sat with Jason in front of her computer. "The judges said to bring a recipe to the contest," she murmured. "I need to find something that will really impress them."
"You make delicious burnt chocolate chunk cookies."
Lissa grinned. "I thought you said you were going to help me, not insult me!"
Jason turned back to the screen. "What about this recipe for chocolate caramel cake?"
"Our recipe needs to have fruit or vegetables in it," she reminded him. "I can make that cake for your bake sale though."
"As long as I get to taste it first." Jason scrolled downward. "So . . . we need something with fruit or vegetables." He wrinkled his nose. "Who would put vegetables in a dessert?"
"Well, lots of people like carrot cake," Lissa said. "And sweet potato pie."
"Right." Jason nodded. "My mom bakes zucchini bread sometimes."
"Yuck." Lissa made a face. "First of all, zucchini is disgusting. And second of all, it's technically a fruit, not a vegetable."
"Okay, so no zucchini recipes!" Jason paused to look at an image of a banana cream pie. "What about this?"
Lissa skimmed the ingredients. "This could work."
"Great." Jason leaped to his feet. "Let's start baking!"

So began another week of cooking. Every day Lissa tried a new recipe. Sometimes Jason helped by cracking eggs or creaming butter and sugar together. Other times he just tasted the results. He wasn't a very critical judge, as Lissa had already seen from his enjoyment of her burnt cookies. But he was very encouraging.
"Delicious!" he said again and again. "Another winner!"
The two of them worked their way through recipes for banana cream pie, a cherry crisp, rhubarb custard bars, and raspberry crumb cake.
Dad shook his head every time he entered the busy kitchen. "I've gained ten pounds since this competition started!"
"It's your fault," Lissa told him. "You're the one who made me sign up!"

While Jason and Lissa experimented with recipes for the contest, they also talked about the bake sale for the community center. Jason was still figuring out the details. Meanwhile, Lissa was thinking about desserts to bake for it, starting with that chocolate caramel cake.

On Thursday, Lissa made a batch of peach hand pies. While the small pies were cooling, she reviewed her ideas for the next round of the cooking competition. "I've got one more day to practice recipes," she thought. "I'll make up my mind about a recipe tomorrow."

When the hand pies were cool, she put some on a tray and headed outside, where Jason was playing basketball. Abruptly, she froze. Rob and Kelly were walking up Jason's driveway. Lissa took a step backward.
Jason stopped playing basketball and waved to his friends. Then he caught sight of Lissa. "Yes! It's snack time! Bring those treats out here, Lissa!"
Lissa took a deep breath and approached the other kids.

On Saturday morning Lissa went right to her workstation. She waved to Mia, Rob, and Kelly, but she kept her head down, staring at her phone until Betty stepped onto the stage.

"Huh?" a girl said.

Lissa quickly assembled the cherry crisp, sneaking glances at her competitors as she worked. She did feel confident about her own recipe, but she couldn't help worrying about the others' desserts. What were they baking? Was her cherry crisp recipe good enough to beat the others.

Betty walked over to Lissa with a sympathetic expression. "I'm sorry, but I don't think we can bring the pan back from the oven now. No second chances, I'm afraid. Besides that, the pan will be very hot—too hot for you to work with for several minutes."

"But . . ." Lissa wanted to argue, but she knew that it was pointless. She walked back to her table in a daze. What a dumb mistake. "My crisp is going to taste terrible!" she whispered. "Sour cherries are so . . . sour!"

After all the desserts had been baked and cooled, the judges began tasting them. They raved over Kelly's peach cake and Rob's cranberry cookies.

"Guess what!" Jason burst out as she approached. "The bake sale's all set. I can't believe this is really coming together. You guys are so awesome!"

Jason glanced at Lissa. "How did your cherry crisp turn out?"
