Mr. Stein scanned his list, searching for Parker's name. "Parker Brantley. You have a good voice—and a decent range too. Why aren't you in chorus?"
"Uh . . . uh . . . I play sports," Parker mumbled. "I don't have time."
"Well, that's a shame." Mr. Stein returned to his list. "Let's see who's next."
Parker stumbled back to where Ray was sitting. "He liked my voice!"
"I know! He never compliments anyone. Maybe you'll get called back to audition for a small speaking part. Make sure you speak loudly and clearly every time you talk to him or Ms. Kwan."

Ray grinned. He was enjoying being the theater expert. He thought of some more helpful advice for Parker. "Try to be more enthusiastic. You're auditioning for a part every minute you're here, not just when you're onstage."
Parker nodded. "Okay, okay, I get it. Can we leave now?"

The next day, when Ray went to check the callback list, Kyla was already in the music room. She ran up to him with her friends. Before she could say anything, he warned her, "Don't get your hopes up. Sixth-graders rarely get speaking parts." He paused ominously. "Sometimes they don't even get a part."
Kyla stuck her tongue out at him. "Ha! I got called back. So did you and Parker."
Her friends giggled.
"Parker got called back?" said Ray in surprise. "Parker?"
"I'm right here behind you, dude. And I'm as shocked as you are!"

Over the next few days, Ray practiced the music by himself and with Parker. As he grew more familiar with the songs and their lyrics, Ray felt more convinced than ever that he was meant to play Warbucks.
"Yup," Parker agreed as they walked into the auditorium for callbacks. "You're perfect for the part. So, how's this going to work today?"
"Basically, we'll all take turns reading different parts, big and small. That helps Ms. Kwan get a good look at everybody. Mr. Stein will be there too. You ready for this?"
"I guess so."
The boys watched while the girls read an orphanage scene over and over. "How many times are they going to do this?" Parker complained.
"Until Ms. Kwan gets an idea of who belongs in which role."
Next, the boys read a scene with Warbucks, Rooster, and some other male characters. Parker spoke loudly and clearly. When he read Warbucks' lines, he strode confidently around the stage.
"Whoa! He's taking my advice!" Ray thought proudly.
Soon the group moved on to the singing and dancing part of the audition. When they were done, Parker and Ray flopped into their seats.
"Whew! Dancing is hard!" Parker rubbed his knee.
"Yeah. I told you I couldn't compete with Ben," Ray said.
At the end of the afternoon, Ms. Kwan made an announcement. "The cast list will be posted on Friday after school, followed by a quick cast meeting."
As Ray and Parker gathered up their backpacks, Ray explained the director's strategy.
"Some kids react badly when they don't get the part they want," he said. "So Ms. Kwan posts the list on Friday. That gives kids a chance to cool down over the weekend."
"Yeah, that happens with soccer tryouts too," Parker said. "Coaches like to give players time to absorb bad news."
On Friday afternoon Ray and Parker joined the kids crowding around the cast list in the music room.
"I got a speaking part!" Kyla was jumping up and down with excitement. "I'm July! One of the orphans!" Her friends gave her a group hug.
Ray and Parker pushed their way past Kyla and her friends to the front of the line.

At first Ray couldn't find his name. It wasn't next to "Oliver Warbucks." It wasn't next to "Rooster." When he finally found it near the bottom of the list, he gasped. "'Policeman . . . Ray Aguilera.' Policeman?" he said. "There must be some mistake."
Meanwhile, Parker was also having trouble finding his name. It wasn't among the ensemble.
"I guess I didn't get a part." Parker shrugged. "Not like I really expected to or anything, but it would've been fun."
"Check the top of the list," Ray said quietly.
"Oh!" Parker was so startled, he took a step backward. "'Oliver Warbucks . . . Parker Brantley.' That can't be right."
"You can say that again," Ray muttered. He couldn't believe this had happened. Parker as Warbucks? What were Ms. Kwan and Mr. Stein thinking?

Ray ran a hand through his hair. "Warbucks was supposed to be my part," he thought miserably. And now Parker, who had absolutely no idea what to do onstage, had stolen it. Parker, who wouldn't even have made it to callbacks without Ray's help.
Ray and Parker were still standing in front of the cast list. They both looked stunned but for different reasons.
"Hey, move out of the way so other people can see!" Ben said.
Parker and Ray moved a few inches apart, and Ben squeezed between them. Ben scanned the list. "I got Rooster! All right!" He pumped his fist in the air. Then he studied the other names for a minute.

"Too bad about Warbucks," Ben said to Ray. "I thought for sure you'd get that." He turned to Parker. "But congrats to you! I know you haven't done a show with us before. Do you do theater someplace else?"
"No, this is my first show ever," Parker said sheepishly. "I was just lucky to get a part."
"Yeah, you're a natural," Ray said mournfully. He hurried away, eager to be by himself for a few minutes.
Parker caught up to him a few seconds later. "Whoa! That was a surprise, huh?"
"Yup."
Parker laughed nervously. "It's as if Coach Wiggins suddenly made you a starter on the soccer team."
"Uh-huh." Ray swallowed hard. He was having trouble speaking.
"I really have no idea how to be an actor." Parker matched his stride to Ray's as they walked down the hall. "You'll help me, right?"
"Sure. Whatever."
"So, what do we do now? Shouldn't we be in the music room to get our scripts?"
"Yup." Ray spun around and headed back to the music room.
When they got there, Mr. Stein was handing out scripts as Ms. Kwan called names.
"Oh, there you are, Parker." Mr. Stein held out a script with one hand and checked off Parker's name with the other.
Ms. Kwan called the actors in the order they appeared in the play. At last she called Ray's name.
"At least I got a script," he said to himself. There were no scripts for people without speaking parts. The director would just tell them what to do.

Ms. Kwan finished handing out scripts. "You'll find your rehearsal schedule inside each script. Members of the ensemble, your schedules are on the table over there. Everybody won't have to come to rehearsal every day. Of course, that could change."
The kids who'd been in shows before laughed knowingly.

"Especially as we get closer to opening night," Ms. Kwan continued. "If you have any scheduling conflicts, please tell me immediately. Don't even think of quitting this show just because you didn't get the part you wanted. And don't have your parents call me to complain."

She paused and looked around the room. "Starting right now, you need to be professional about your part in this production. Everybody can't have a leading role, but everybody is important. Make the most of your part. I'll be watching for the future."
"Like that'll do me any good," Ray mumbled as Ms. Kwan dismissed the cast. "This is my last show before high school."
"What did you say?" Parker asked.
Ray shook his head. "Let's find my sister and get out of here."

On the way home, Kyla sat in the front seat with her mother, while Ray and Parker sat in the back. Parker and Kyla looked at their scripts. Ray was too busy fuming to read anything. He stared out the window, wondering where he’d gone wrong. Mr. Stein had seemed to like his singing. Maybe it was the way he'd read Warbucks’ lines or—
"July has lines!" Kyla announced to her mother. "All my friends are orphans, but they don't have any lines. They don't even have names!"
"You must have done well at the auditions." Mrs. Aguilera smiled at Kyla.
Ray felt even worse. He just wanted to get home and hide in his room forever.
"Oh! Look at that!" Kyla pointed excitedly to her script. "I even have some solos! There are places where I get to sing a line all by myself!"
"Those aren't real solos," Ray said in a grumpy voice.
"Your part isn't so bad, Ray," Parker said, jumping in. "I mean, Drake, the butler, has more lines than you do. But a lot of them are just 'yes, sir.'"
"Humph." Ray snorted. He refused to be cheered up right now, especially by Parker.
Kyla joined in. "You have a scene with Annie and Sandy, the dog."
"Will you have to train the dog?" Mrs. Aguilera asked. "Ms. Kwan probably knew that was something you'd be good at."
Ray sighed. "No, Mom. Sandy is played by a kid, not a real dog."
"Who got that part?" Parker asked.
"Lakshmi," Kyla said. "Ray's girlfriend."
"She's not my girlfriend. She played my girlfriend in last year's show."
"Oh, right," Kyla said.
Everyone was silent for a few minutes.
"Aw, Ray! You have the cutest scene with Sandy at the end." Kyla closed her script.
"That should make you feel better." Mrs. Aguilera sounded encouraging.
Ray sighed again. "I can't get excited about playing a nameless policeman."
"No, he has a name. I know I saw it someplace." Kyla flipped through her script. "Here it is. Officer Ward."
Ray groaned. He hated this show already.

Right from the start of rehearsals, Ray felt left out. Three days a week, he practiced with the ensemble in the music room. They worked on learning the music for the big production numbers. Ray was in only one of those, so he usually didn't have to stay for the whole rehearsal.

Meanwhile, Kyla and Parker went to practice every day and stayed late. Sometimes they worked on learning music with Mr. Stein. Other days they worked on their lines with Ms. Kwan in the auditorium. They were now more involved in Ray's favorite activity than Ray was. Every day one of them had a funny story about rehearsal. Something Ray had missed. And Parker always seemed to have a problem.
"There's so much stuff to learn!" Parker said to Ray. They were standing at their lockers one Friday after classes ended. "Half the time I don't know what's going on."
Ray tried to be sympathetic. "At least Warbucks' dance with Annie is easier than what you'd have to do in the ensemble."

"True, but everything is still hard for me." Parker shifted his books to the other arm. "I guess things will get easier. That's what Ben said when we were playing Frisbee yesterday. Well, the other guys were playing, and I was mostly watching because of my knee." He paused to explain. "We go outside and throw the Frisbee whenever we're not needed onstage."
"You don't have to tell me." Ray sighed. "I know about the Frisbee games. I used to play all the time." Playing Frisbee with his friends was one of the best parts of doing a show.
"So, do you want to see that new spy movie this weekend?" Parker asked.
Ray wasn't sure he wanted to hang out with Parker. It wasn't easy listening to him complain about having the starring role. "Uh, I really can't."
"Okay." Parker suddenly spotted Ben. "Well then, I'll see you Monday. Hey, Ben, wait up!"
Ray watched as Parker hurried to catch up with Ben. Then he slowly walked to the bus by himself.

When Ray woke up on Saturday morning, he was freezing. Without opening his eyes, he snuggled under the covers. But he still felt a cold breeze on his face. He wasn't sure if he was awake or asleep. Then he heard Kyla softly singing "It's the Hard-Knock Life."
"This is a strange dream. That's one of the orphans' songs," Ray said to himself. He opened his eyes a little. Kyla seemed to be in his room. She was very tall.
Ray's eyes flew open. Kyla was standing on a step stool, washing one of his windows. Now he was wide-awake.
"What are you doing in my room?" he shouted. "Close that window and get out of here!"
Kyla was busy concentrating on a stubborn smudge. "I'm working on my character. The orphans do a lot of cleaning. I need to know what that's like so I can play my part realistically."
"So go clean your own windows!" Ray tugged at his covers, trying to pull them up even higher.
"I already did my windows." Kyla dipped a sponge into a bucket full of water.
"Get out of here! Now!"

"All right, all right." Kyla slammed the window shut. She carried the bucket from the room and then returned for the step stool. "By the way, don't go into the bathroom. I just scrubbed the floor, and it's still wet."
Ray moaned and pulled the covers over his head. He could still hear Kyla, who was now singing "Tomorrow."
"I don't know how much more of that song I can take," he mumbled. "And I definitely can't stand being trapped in the house with Kyla. Maybe I'll go to the movies with Parker after all."
At the next rehearsal, Ms. Kwan had an announcement for the whole cast. As usual, Parker sat next to Ray, who was drawing spirals on the cover of his math notebook.
"We're going to try something new with this production." Ms. Kwan paused until she had everyone's attention. Ray kept drawing. "In the past if a lead got sick, we relied on him or her to keep going."
"The show must go on," Mr. Stein said.
"Exactly. Over the weekend I was at a convention for drama teachers. I heard story after story of leads getting sick right before opening night. Especially with that awful virus that's going around."
"And the show couldn't go on!" Mr. Stein seemed pleased with his joke.
Ms. Kwan looked over the top of her red glasses at him. The kids laughed.
"Why is everybody laughing?" Parker whispered.
Ray glanced at Ms. Kwan. "She gives that look whenever a kid interrupts her." He went back to doodling.

Ms. Kwan continued. "I've decided to cast understudies for Warbucks and Annie. It'll be more work to rehearse two actors for each part, but I'll be able to sleep at night. After consulting with Mr. Stein, I've decided that Ray and Lakshmi will be the understudies for Parker and Mariah. And David and Brittany will be understudies for the policeman and Sandy."
"Huh?" Ray was suddenly paying attention. "Did she just say my name?"
"Yes!" Parker slapped him on the back. "You're my understudy!"
Ray was too surprised to say anything.
"What about me?" Ben called out. "Don't I get an understudy?"
"No one dances like you do, Ben." Ms. Kwan looked very serious. "You can't get sick."
"Nobody sneeze on Ben!" Mr. Stein said.
Meanwhile, Ray was feeling better by the minute. "I might get to star in this show after all," he thought.
Parker nudged him. "What exactly does an understudy do?"
"If anything happens to you, I take your place onstage."
"Oh, it's like soccer! I'm the goalie, and you're my backup, ready to go in the net if I get hurt."
"Something like that."
"Cool! Now we can learn the part together. And we can shave our heads together too. I mean, Ms. Kwan said I could wear a bald cap, but I'd rather shave my head. Wouldn't you?"
"Yeah, sure." Ray wasn't thinking about hair. He was thinking that things would be perfect if Parker got sick and missed the show.

But as soon as he'd thought that, Ray felt terrible. Of course he didn't want Parker to get sick. But what if . . . His mind was churning. What if he worked really hard and Ms. Kwan realized something important. She'd made a big mistake when she cast Parker for Ray's part. She might even recast the play.
"Then Parker will be my understudy !" Ray said out loud.
Parker looked at him. "What did you say about me?"
"Oh, nothing," Ray murmured. "I was just talking to myself."

As Parker's understudy, Ray attended rehearsals every day. He never got to leave early. He had plenty of time to play Frisbee with his friends. He was in on every joke and funny thing that happened at rehearsals. All this should have made him happy. But it didn't.

Weeks passed, and Ray was still Parker's understudy, even though he was doing everything he could to get the director to notice him. He'd memorized his lines right away, while Parker was still carrying a script onstage. He'd mastered the songs and the dancing. Plus, he was still playing his regular part, the policeman.

Late one afternoon Ray was sitting next to Lakshmi in the auditorium. In their roles as understudies, they were watching the rehearsal. Both were taking notes whenever Ms. Kwan spoke to Warbucks or Annie.
"Emphasize that last line more," Ms. Kwan said to Parker.
Ray underlined that line in his script.
"Try to look sadder now," she said to Mariah, who played Annie. "You've just found out your parents are dead."
Lakshmi drew a sad face on her script.

"At least you're not onstage with Warbucks for very long," Lakshmi said. "The first time that the dog appears, Annie's there too. So I have to pay attention to what Ms. Kwan is saying to me and to Mariah. All while pretending I'm a dog!"
"Yeah, I like to focus on being Warbucks. And I'd like it even more if . . ." Ray's voice trailed off.
Lakshmi looked at him. "If what?"
"Oh, nothing." Ray didn't want Lakshmi to know he'd be happier as the star. He smiled at her. "So, who do you like better as Warbucks? Parker or me?"
"Hmm. Interesting question." Lakshmi tapped her pencil on the seat in front of her. "I don't think one of you is better than the other. You're just different."
"What do you mean?"

"Parker seems older to me. Maybe it's because he limps sometimes. I don't know, but I can really see him as Annie's father. Like when he says he wants to adopt her, I really believe him. And you have to admit Parker has a great singing voice."
"Uh-huh." Ray felt his smile fade. This wasn't what he'd wanted to hear.

"You're good too!" Lakshmi said quickly. "You make all Warbucks' funny lines even funnier. And you're a better dancer than Parker." She paused. "Though it's kind of sweet that he dances so awkwardly with Annie. More like a real dad."
Ray let out a heavy sigh.
"That's enough for today," Ms. Kwan said. "Thanks, everyone. Parker, please try to learn the difference between stage right and stage left. It's not that hard."
Ray shook his head in disbelief. How could Ms. Kwan and Mr. Stein have chosen Parker for the lead when he—
Lakshmi interrupted his thoughts. "See you tomorrow, Ray."
"Yup. Same time, same place."
"Are we rehearsing our lead roles tomorrow?"
Ray consulted his schedule. "Nope. Not until Friday. We're rehearsing Sandy and Officer Ward again."
After Lakshmi walked away, Ray stood up and stretched.
Parker came offstage and joined him in the audience. He held out his hands. "I know my right hand from my left. I really do. But I can't get this stage right and left business."
"Here's an easy way to remember," Ray said. "It's the opposite of what you think it is."
"So, stage right is to my left and stage left is to my right."
"Right!" Ray said, and they both laughed. "Except that's only for the audience—"
"Hey, did you guys see my phone?" Lakshmi came running back down the aisle.
Ray shook his head.
"Maybe it's under here somewhere." Parker bent down and peered under the seats.
As they searched for Lakshmi's phone, Ray didn't finish what he'd been saying. For an actor onstage, facing the audience, stage left is actually to the left and stage right is to the right.
"He needs to make that mistake again," Ray thought. "Then he'll get it right."

The next day at rehearsal, Parker immediately mixed up stage right and stage left. Ms. Kwan stopped everything to explain the terms to him yet again. "I know you're new to theater, Parker, but you have to pay attention."
"Okay, I've got it now." Parker's face was red. "Left is to the left, right is to the right."
"Exactly. Now let's start this scene again."
When there was a break, Parker stalked over to Ray. "Why did you tell me the wrong thing?"
"I was going to tell you everything later. It was just a joke!" Ray felt himself flush with anger. "You have to know this stuff if you're the lead, and now you do."
"But Ms. Kwan is mad at me!"
"She gets mad at everybody." Ray thought back to something he'd done last year. "If you really want her to like you, add some lines to your part. She loves that."
"Well, okay, but . . . are you sure?"

"Um, sure." Ray couldn't believe Parker was taking his joke seriously. But it would be funny if Parker actually did add some lines. "Show her how creative you are," Ray went on. "Warbucks is a billionaire. Say something about stocks."
"All right, everyone, let's work on the last scene!" Ms. Kwan called out to the cast.
Ray went backstage and took his place in the wings, waiting to go onstage with Sandy and the orphans. He listened as Parker suddenly started talking about the stock market.
"What's he doing?" Lakshmi whispered. "That's not in the script."
Ray smiled. "I told him Ms. Kwan likes it when people add lines."
"No, she doesn't!" Lakshmi's whisper grew louder. "She hates that!"
"It was just a joke!"
"You told Parker to add lines?" Kyla said loudly right behind Ray. Apparently, everyone onstage could hear Kyla because they all turned toward the wings.
"Shh, Kyla!" Ray put his finger to his lips.
He listened as Ms. Kwan scolded Parker, and Parker apologized. Then Parker looked into the wings and locked eyes with Ray.
"I can't believe you did that to him," Lakshmi said to Ray.
"It was just a joke," Ray repeated weakly.
"Excuse me, Ms. Kwan, I'll be right back." Parker flung his script to the stage and started striding toward Ray.
"Uh-oh, you're in trouble," Kyla said. "He looks really mad."
Suddenly all the lights in the auditorium went out. Kyla screamed. It was pitch-black both onstage and off. There was a loud crash onstage.
"Ow!" cried Parker. "My knee!"

The lights were out for only a few seconds. But that was long enough for Parker to get hurt. When the lights came on again, Parker was lying onstage, clutching his knee. A bucket was overturned next to him.
Ray was the first one to reach Parker.
"Ow! My knee! I landed on it when I tripped over that bucket!" Parker moaned with his eyes closed.
"You'll be okay," Ray said. "Shake it off and get back in the game."
Parker's eyes flew open. "Get away from me. You—"
"I didn't do anything! I was over there." Ray pointed offstage. "How can you think I'd do something to hurt you? That's ridiculous! I'd never—"
"Everybody out of the way!" Mr. Stein bounded up the steps to the stage with Ms. Kwan right behind him. "Give him some room to breathe. Are you all right, Parker?"
Parker moaned again.
"I can't believe you did that!" Kyla said to Ray as all the kids stepped back.
"I didn't do anything! I was backstage with you!"
"You admitted you told Parker to add some lines! What were you doing? Trying to steal his part?"
"No! Of course not!"

But Kyla wasn't through with him. "You're a real schemer, Ray! You're worse than Rooster! And we all know where he goes in the end. Jail!" Kyla paused for breath. "Lakshmi isn't trying to hurt Mariah so she can be Annie! You're the worst person in the world, Ray Aguilera!"
"Parker tripped over a bucket," Ray said evenly. "An orphan's bucket. I don't even have a bucket!" Ray looked at the orphans now surrounding him and Kyla. "One of you must have left it out there."
"Not me!" they all said as one.
"Well . . . well . . . well . . ." Kyla stalled, trying to think of what to say. "Then what about the lights?"
"The lights? I couldn't turn off the lights. I was standing right in front of you. I wasn't even near any lights! The power must have gone off for a minute."
Some kids nearby were muttering, and Ray could tell they were taking Kyla's side. At least the teachers hadn't heard Kyla.
"Why couldn't she stay out of my activities?" he thought. "Why did she have to try out for this play?"
"Lakshmi! Ben!" Ms. Kwan called. "I need you to get a bag of ice from the cafeteria."
"Lakshmi!" Ray pleaded. "You believe me, don't you?"
But she just turned and walked away with Ben. Everyone else abandoned Ray too. He stood by himself, watching Mr. Stein talk to Parker.
Ray knew he'd been wrong to give Parker bad advice—even as a joke. "But I'd never hurt him!" he said to himself.
By the time Lakshmi and Ben returned with some ice, Parker was sitting up. After applying ice for a few minutes, he was able to stand with Mr. Stein's help. Everyone in the auditorium applauded.
"Way to go, Parker!" Ray slapped him on the back as he limped past.
"Leave me alone!" Parker snapped.
Ray stayed silent, watching as his friend exited stage left.

Parker took a few days off from rehearsing to rest his knee. He still came to rehearsals, but he sat in the auditorium while Ray played Warbucks. Whenever Ray tried to talk to him, Parker started talking to someone else. One day Ray looked out from the stage and saw Parker surrounded by girls. They included Lakshmi, Kyla, and all of Kyla's friends.
Ray came offstage in time to hear Parker explaining that he had to pay attention. "Just in case Ms. Kwan changes one of the plays onstage."
"This isn't soccer," Ray muttered as he passed. "It's called blocking . That's the right word for how actors move around the stage."
"Did he just call you a blockhead?" Kyla asked.
"Who knows?" Parker smiled and shrugged. "Now, who brought me some cookies today? Those chocolate ones from yesterday were delicious!"
Ray rolled his eyes. While he had lost most of his friends, Parker was making new ones by the minute.

After the break Ray had to rehearse a scene as Officer Ward. He stood in the wings, waiting for his cue. He watched as Annie sang "Tomorrow" with Sandy. He wished he could talk to Lakshmi. But what would he say? That his "jokes" had gone too far? That maybe, if he really thought about it, he had been trying to steal Parker's role? But he would never do anything to hurt Parker?
Yes, that was perfect.
When the orphan and dog stopped singing, Officer Ward entered and confronted them.
"Stop right there!" Ms. Kwan frowned at Ray. "Why are you smiling, Officer Ward? This dog doesn't have a leash or a license. You're trying to enforce the law here."
"Sorry. I was thinking of something else."
"Make your entrance again."
Ray went back offstage. This time he entered as a stern policeman. He looked mean as he threatened to send Sandy to the dog pound.
"Much better, Ray," Ms. Kwan said when they finished the scene. "That's it for today, everybody." She went over to talk to Parker.
Ray waited while Mr. Stein gave Annie and Sandy a few suggestions to improve their duet. Then, as Lakshmi left the stage, Ray approached her.
"Hey, Lakshmi! Can I talk to you for a second?"
"Grr!"
Ray laughed. "Rehearsal is over. You can stop being Sandy now."
"Grr!" She growled at him again and walked away.
"But, Lakshmi—"
"Attention, everyone!" Ms. Kwan clapped her hands. "Before you leave, I have some good news. Parker will be back with us onstage tomorrow. Isn't that right, Parker?"
The kids yelled and applauded for Parker. He stood up and bowed.
"I'd also like to thank Ray for taking Parker's place these past few days."
This time not a single cast member clapped.
Ms. Kwan looked puzzled. "I know it's late and you're all tired, but—"
"Come on, everybody," said Mr. Stein. "A round of applause for Ray."
There was some weak applause. Mr. Stein looked at Ms. Kwan and shrugged. By now Ray was rushing toward the exit.
"How's Parker doing?" Mrs. Aguilera asked as Ray and Kyla got into their car.
"Everybody's happy that he's coming back tomorrow," Kyla said.
"So, Ray, did you have a good time filling in for Parker?"
"Nope," Ray muttered.
"Everybody hates him," Kyla said.
Ray shot her a look. Why couldn't she keep quiet?
"What? Explain, please." Mrs. Aguilera turned toward Ray in the backseat.
"It's horrible being the villain in real life," Ray said. "I don't want to talk about it."

Parker returned to the stage. As the weeks passed, Ray started noticing that something was wrong with Parker. Ray didn't see it all the time, and he couldn't put his finger on what it was. But something was definitely off.

Ray couldn't ask Parker because Parker still wasn't speaking to him. Neither was Lakshmi. She continued to bark and growl whenever he tried to talk to her. One day after they'd finished a scene, Ms. Kwan was talking to the cast.
"Officer Ward, pat Sandy on the head when you let her out of the box." The director turned her attention to the other actors. "Annie, you need to . . ."
Lakshmi was sitting at Ray's feet, so he decided to pat her head. She snarled and tried to bite him.
"Ouch! Did you just snap at me?" he hissed at her.
"Grr," Lakshmi growled.
Kyla laughed out loud. "Serves you right, Ray!"
Ms. Kwan turned around. Ray expected her to yell at them for talking. Instead she smiled.
"Ray and Lakshmi, I'm proud of how hard you've been working as understudies."
"If only she knew," Kyla murmured.
Ms. Kwan went on. "So, as a reward, you'll get to perform the lead roles at the Saturday matinee!"
"Oh!" Lakshmi jumped up. "That's exciting!"

"Wow!" Ray was so surprised, he couldn't say anything more. He'd given up any hope of playing Warbucks during an actual performance. After he'd tried to sabotage Parker, he wasn't sure he even deserved the role.
"Now you'll have to shave your head!" Ben crowed. He punched Ray in the arm. "I can't wait to see how that turns out."
Ray faked a grin. He'd decided against a bald cap, but he wished Parker and he could shave their heads together. No way was that happening now.

That night at home Ray pulled out his cast list. He had managed to convince Ben and a few other people that he wasn't responsible for Parker's accident. They were talking to him. He put a check next to their names.

He put an X next to those who still thought everything was his fault. Ray had no idea which side Kyla was on. Sometimes she seemed disappointed in him. But one time he'd overheard her defending him to her friends. He put a question mark next to her name.
Ray looked at the list. There were a lot of X s.

The set crew finished painting the scenery. The actors' costumes were ready to be tried on. Ray shaved his head. Two Saturdays in a row, the whole cast practiced from ten in the morning until after dark. Tech rehearsals started with the light and sound crews. Opening night was coming soon.

For the final dress rehearsal, Ray was wearing his policeman's uniform. He liked the costume, and he'd grown to like the part too. At the start of the play, he was sort of a villain. But by the end, he was one of the good guys. The part wasn't the lead, but it was fun to play.
Ray sat in the cafeteria, where the actors waited until they had to go backstage. To pass the time, he was playing cards with Ben and some kids in the ensemble.
"Hurry up and shuffle, Ben," Ray said. "I'm in the next scene. This is a run-through, so Ms. Kwan won't be stopping for anything."

"Unless there's an emergency," Ben said. He dealt the cards. "I wish we could see what's happening onstage. My cousin says at his school they have a screen in the cafeteria. That way the actors can watch the show."
"That'd be nice," Ray said as he organized the cards in his hand.
Suddenly an assistant stage manager rushed into the cafeteria.
"Ray!" she said breathlessly. "Ms. Kwan needs you right now."
Ray looked at the clock on the wall. "Already? They did that scene really fast."
"No, they haven't even started yet," said the stage manager. "Parker didn't show up!"
"Okay, that's my definition of an emergency!" Ben said.
Ray dropped his cards on the table and pushed back his chair. "What? Where is he?"

The stage manager shrugged. "No one knows. Ms. Kwan couldn't reach him by phone. You're supposed to change costumes and be ready to go on as Warbucks. Where's David? He has to take your place as Officer Ward."
"Hey, dude, this is your big chance," Ben said to Ray. "Break a leg!"
"Yeah, thanks," Ray said in an absentminded way. He was thinking of other things. Such as: "What's wrong with Parker? Am I going to get the blame?"

Ray changed costumes and stayed in Ms. Kwan's classroom, which served as the boys' dressing room. With the door open, he could hear the music from the auditorium. By paying attention to the songs, he'd know when to go backstage.

Something about putting on Warbucks' costume made Ray feel nervous. "Calm down," he said to himself. "You know this part. You know the nerves will pass as soon as you get onstage." He paused as something suddenly occurred to him. "Ohh! Maybe that's it!"
Ray found his own clothes and pulled his phone from his jeans pocket. He texted Parker and waited a few minutes. No response. He texted again. Nothing.
"Come on!" he said. "I have to go onstage in a minute!"
But Parker still didn't respond. Ray heard Warbucks' servants singing. "That's my cue!" And he ran backstage.
The rehearsal went quickly. At the end of the curtain call, Ms. Kwan signaled for the cast to remain onstage.

"That was a good run-through! Thank you, Ray and David for stepping in. Parker had better have a good excuse for missing this rehearsal. Otherwise, Ray will be Warbucks in all the performances." She turned to Mr. Stein. "I told you we needed understudies!"
Mr. Stein nodded in agreement.
After changing out of their costumes, Ray and Kyla waited for their ride home. Ray scrolled through his messages. He was disappointed to see that there was nothing from Parker.
"I guess you're happy now that you might be Warbucks," Kyla said.
"Not really." Ray was busy texting Parker again. He looked up as their mother pulled in front of the school. "I need Mom to drop me off at Parker's right away. I think he's in trouble."
Kyla nodded. "Yeah, it sounds like Ms. Kwan's really mad at him."
"No, I'm talking about Parker himself. Something's wrong with him."
Kyla sighed as she slung her backpack over her shoulder. "Did you do something else to him?"
Ray shook his head. "No, he did it to himself!"
Ray found Parker lying on the couch, watching a soccer game on TV.
"What are you doing here?" Parker said. "Get out."
"No, what are you doing here, Parker? Nobody misses the final dress rehearsal—unless they're dead."
Parker stared at the TV. "Goal!" shouted the announcer.
"Yes!" Parker pumped a fist.
Ray moved right in front of Parker. "Look, I'm really sorry." He swallowed hard. "I was trying to steal your part. I thought I deserved to be Warbucks."
Parker said nothing for a moment. "And . . . ?"
"I'm sorry I told you Ms. Kwan likes people to add lines."
"Is that it?"
"I shouldn't have tried to confuse you about stage left and stage right. But I didn't leave that bucket onstage. And I know what's wrong with you."
Parker looked at Ray in surprise.

"When I put on the Warbucks costume today, I started feeling nervous. But I knew I'd be okay as soon as I got onstage. That's what always happens. You're suffering from your first case of stage fright," Ray said. "And you don't know how to deal with it."

Parker exhaled loudly. "The whole soccer team is coming on opening night. I don't mind singing at rehearsals. But I can't sing to an auditorium full of people! Especially people I know. My dad says to imagine the audience in their underwear. How can I do that and remember my lines? I'm doomed!"
"Tons of people watch you play soccer—"
"Yeah, but I've been playing soccer for years. This is my first show."

"Look at it like this." Ray pushed Parker's feet out of the way and sat down. "You never know how a soccer game will end—no matter how much you practice. But you know how a show will go because we've practiced every minute of it. Stage fright is just part of doing a show. Everybody gets it. Everybody gets over it."
Ray wasn't sure about that last part, but it sounded good. And Parker appeared to be thinking about what he'd said.
"Okay," Parker finally said. "But what if I forget a line? Or my voice squeaks? Or my friends start laughing really hard? Or . . ."
Ray put his head in his hands and stayed like that as Parker went on about all the terrible possibilities. Then suddenly Ray raised his head. "Can your brother give us a ride to school?"
"I guess so."
Ray took out his phone.
"Who are you calling?" Parker asked.
"Kyla."
When she answered the phone, Ray asked her to text her friends. "Tell them to go back to school right now. I'm calling an emergency rehearsal."
"Does Ms. Kwan know about this?"
"No."
"Why should I help you?" Kyla sounded suspicious of Ray.
"It's not for me—it's for the show. Come on, Kyla, please."
And with that one word— please —Ray revealed how desperate he was.
"I'll do it," Kyla said, "but on one condition. You let me—and all my friends—hang out with you at the cast party."
"No way!"
"Come on, Ray, you need all the friends you can get right now."
Ray was in a hurry. "All right, fine, whatever. I'll text the rest of the cast."
He ended the call and slapped Parker on the leg. "Get up, Parker. The show must go on!"
Back in the auditorium, Ray was happy to see that most of the cast had shown up. "Attention, everybody!"
"You sound just like Ms. Kwan," Ben said.
Ray ignored him. "I called this rehearsal because Parker needs our help. We have to show him we've got his back. Right?"
"Right!" echoed the cast.
"We've had so many practices that everybody knows every line in this show. Right?"
"Right!"
"So let's show Parker that he has nothing to fear. We'll run the last scene. Only I'll be Annie, and, Lakshmi, you'll be Warbucks."
Everyone laughed as Ray recast the show. Kyla played Drake, the butler, while Parker was Grace, Warbucks' secretary. The orphans played Warbucks' servants, and the servants played the orphans.
"Okay, everybody, take it from the top."
Everyone was in good spirits as they made their way through the scene. Whenever someone stumbled, the others helped out.

As they reached the end, Ray turned to Parker. "And that's what'll happen if something goes wrong. If you can't remember a line, somebody will prompt you. If someone messes up a line, just respond like you think Warbucks would respond. You're not onstage by yourself. We're—"
"A team," Parker said.
"Exactly! We're a—"
"Hey, what are you kids doing on that stage?" A janitor hurried down the aisle. "You shouldn't be here without a teacher."
"We're just leaving." Ray motioned to the cast. "Time to go, everyone!"
"Thanks, dude," Parker said quietly.

On opening night the show went off without a hitch—except for one moment when Warbucks' secretary missed a line. Parker had the next line. Ray held his breath while Parker stood there in silence. Parker looked at Ray, who gave him a nod.
"Very good, Grace," Parker said in a strong voice. Then he went on with his lines.
Ray exhaled.
During the curtain call, the audience applauded wildly. "Parker! Parker!" called his soccer teammates. Parker grinned and bowed.
As the cast left the stage, Ray punched Parker's arm. "Way to go! You're a star!"

"So are you!" Parker said. "Hey, everybody, before you go!" he called out to the cast backstage. "You know this was my first show. And I just want to say I couldn't have done it without you—and especially without Ray. He saved me."
The cast clapped and cheered. "Parker! Ray! Parker! Ray!"
The two friends took a bow. Then Parker went in search of the soccer team.
Lakshmi patted Ray's back. "What you did for Parker was really nice—and clever too. Maybe you should be a director."
"He's bossy enough to be a director," Kyla said as she and her friends surrounded them.
Ray and Lakshmi laughed.
"I promise not to growl at you anymore!" Lakshmi walked away.
Ray smiled, feeling better than he had in weeks. He was happy with his role in the play, happy with his friends. Happy with everything—until his little sister interrupted his thoughts.
"We can't wait to hang out with you and your friends at the cast party," Kyla said. Her friends nodded.
Ray groaned. "Are you sure I agreed to that?"
"Of course, I'm sure." Kyla grinned. "I never forget a line!"
